COMPUTER MAINTENANCE PROGRAM OF STUDY STANDARDS
District of Columbia Arts Education Learning Standards

FE21F4C0DFE401316C8668A86D17958E.description: Read biographies and stories about artists and summarize the readings in short reports, telling how the artists mirrored or affected their time periods or culture.

FE211490DFE401316C8468A86D17958E.description: Draw diagrams, maps, graphs, timelines, or illustrations to communicate ideas or tell a story about a historical event.

FE203290DFE401316C8268A86D17958E.description: Identify through research twentieth-century artists who have used symmetry in their work and then create a work of art, using bilateral or radial symmetry.

FE1FCEA0DFE401316C8168A86D17958E.description: Write and illustrate a book (using book arts) implementing the writing process (e.g., prewriting, drafting, revising, editing/proofreading, publishing/presenting) demonstrating a unified drawing style.

FE1EBAD0DFE401316C7F68A86D17958E.description: Connect and apply what is learned in the visual arts to other art forms, subject areas, visual culture and communications and to careers. (Connections, Relationships, Applications)

FE1E5930DFE401316C7E68A86D17958E.description: Using appropriate vocabulary of art, explain the successful compositional and communicative qualities of an artist's work.

FE1DF550DFE401316C7D68A86D17958E.description: Describe how the individual experiences of an artist may influence the development of specific works of art.

FE1D92C0DFE401316C7C68A86D17958E.description: Discuss how the subject and selection of media relate to the meaning or purpose of a work of art.

FE1D2900DFE401316C7B68A86D17958E.description:
Analyze works of art and design using a critique process.:
  • Description of elements (describe)
  • How it was made (explain)
  • How the parts of the artwork are arranged as a whole (analyze)
  • How the work affects feelings or mood, and presents ideas or themes (interpret)
  • How the artwork is related to events in the artist's life themes (investigate/interpret)
  • How it may relate to events or social trends of the period (investigate/interpret)

FE1C47C0DFE401316C7968A86D17958E.description: Respond to, analyze, and make judgments about works in the visual arts. (Aesthetics, Valuing & Perspectives of Art)

FE1BD770DFE401316C7868A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe how a person's own cultural content influences responses to works of art. Create a composition that illustrates a personal cultural celebration.

FE1B5FA0DFE401316C7768A86D17958E.description: Research and describe the influence of religious groups' history on art and architecture, focusing primarily on buildings in the District of Columbia both past and present.

FE1AECB0DFE401316C7668A86D17958E.description: Identify and discuss the content of works of art in the past and present, focusing on the different cultures that have contributed to the District of Columbia's history and art heritage.

FE1A8B70DFE401316C7568A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast art objects that have a similar theme from different part of the world observed in visits to museums or galleries (e.g., puppets, masks, containers).

FE1A2AC0DFE401316C7468A86D17958E.description: Describe a local historical house, sharing observations about how the structure and the objects in it present a picture of life in another era.

FE19BD30DFE401316C7368A86D17958E.description: Describe an historic district observing the architecture and landscape; speculate how it has changed since its original construction.

FE194D20DFE401316C7268A86D17958E.description: Describe the function and meaning of works of art and objects from Europe. View Impressionist, post-Impressionist, and non-representational artists at The Phillips Collection.

FE18E0F0DFE401316C7168A86D17958E.description: Articulate how art and artifacts play a role in reflecting early Native American life (e.g. in photography, quilts, architecture).

FE188390DFE401316C7068A86D17958E.description: Historical Development, Role and Cultural Diversity of the Visual Arts

FE182390DFE401316C6F68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and understand historical and cultural dimensions of the visual arts and to construct meaning in the diverse ways in which human experience is expressed across time and place. (Historical and Cultural Context)

FE17BFC0DFE401316C6E68A86D17958E.description: Use complementary colors in an original compositional to show contrast (light and dark) and emphasis.

FE1758C0DFE401316C6D68A86D17958E.description: Use additive and subtractive processes in making sculptural forms.

FE16DCF0DFE401316C6C68A86D17958E.description: Create a portrait demonstrating personality or a figure drawing or painting, using proportional size relationships.

FE166D90DFE401316C6B68A86D17958E.description: Use the interaction between positive and negative space in a works of art.

FE160AF0DFE401316C6A68A86D17958E.description: Expression Through Original Works of Art

FE15A6A0DFE401316C6968A86D17958E.description: Maintain the workspace, materials, and tools responsibly and safely.

FE153D30DFE401316C6868A86D17958E.description: Work with contemporary technologies (e.g., internet access, library computer card catalogues) to create art.

FE14D950DFE401316C6768A86D17958E.description: Draw people in proportion to objects found in nature or in their environment.

FE146FB0DFE401316C6668A86D17958E.description: Create a self portrait using proportional size relationships.

FE13EBF0DFE401316C6568A86D17958E.description: Use shading (value) to transform a two-dimensional shape into what appears to be a three-dimensional form (e.g., circle to sphere).

FE137AE0DFE401316C6468A86D17958E.description: Create a contour drawing of objects showing convexity.

FE12BF80DFE401316C6268A86D17958E.description: Apply artistic processes and skills in a variety of media to communicate meaning and intent in original works of art. (Production and Creative Expression)

FE126020DFE401316C6168A86D17958E.description: Discuss the style and techniques used to create portraits of the U.S. colonial and American Revolutionary heroes that can be seen at Art museums such as the National Portrait Gallery and/or the National Gallery of Art.

FE11FC80DFE401316C6068A86D17958E.description: Identify and describe a gesture drawing found in a work of art.

FE112550DFE401316C5E68A86D17958E.description: Perceive and describe contrast and emphasis in works of art, nature and in the environment.

FE10C050DFE401316C5D68A86D17958E.description: Identify pairs of complementary colors (e.g. yellow/violet; red/green; blue/orange) and discuss how artists use them to communicate an idea or mood

FE1059F0DFE401316C5C68A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between visual and actual textures using objects in nature, the environment and works of art

FE0FF5D0DFE401316C5B68A86D17958E.description: Identify, name and describe negative shapes and forms and positive shapes and forms seen in a selected work of art.

FE0F8F80DFE401316C5A68A86D17958E.description: Describe and analyze the elements of art, (e.g., line, color, shape, form, texture, space, and value) emphasizing form, as they appear in nature, the environment and works of art found in the classroom, in art reproductions, in students' own work, during online research, or a museum visit, such as the Corcoran Gallery of Art.

FE0F1B40DFE401316C5968A86D17958E.description: Identify various types of lines (e.g., straight/curved, thick/thin, long/short, vertical/horizontal/diagonal, contour, ruled lines, calligraphy, and other freehand studies from observation, imagination, and schematic studies).

FE0EA610DFE401316C5868A86D17958E.description: Develop perceptual skills, analyze elements of art and the principles of design

FE0E2EC0DFE401316C5768A86D17958E.description: Perceive and understand the components of visual language: the elements of art and the principles of design. (Artistic Perception)

FE0D5F60DFE401316C5568A86D17958E.description: Use improvisation and dramatization to explore concepts in other content areas.

FE0CF570DFE401316C5468A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast how live theatre differs from filmed or taped performances.

FE0C7C60DFE401316C5368A86D17958E.description: Apply theatrical concepts to construct meaning and understanding in other subject areas.

FE0C1A90DFE401316C5268A86D17958E.description: Identify themes by analyzing major ideas of stories/short plays.

FE0BB670DFE401316C5168A86D17958E.description: Describe how actors convey meaning or intent, including relationships between characters (conflict and resolution).

FE0B4E80DFE401316C5068A86D17958E.description: Use the vocabulary of theatre, such as plot, conflict, climax, tone, objectives, motivation, and theme to describe theatrical experiences.

FE0AE730DFE401316C4F68A86D17958E.description: Analyze, critique, and respond to theatre and dramatic media.

FE0A7420DFE401316C4E68A86D17958E.description: Stage scenes or monologues that demonstrate spatial awareness.

FE0A03D0DFE401316C4D68A86D17958E.description: Explain the roles and responsibilities of designers and technical artists in theatre.

FE099180DFE401316C4C68A86D17958E.description: Design and create costumes, props, and makeup/masks to communicate a character in formal and informal theatre performances.

FE093020DFE401316C4B68A86D17958E.description: Design and manage theatrical environments for formal and informal dramatizations.

FE08BA00DFE401316C4A68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate confidence in creating and presenting performances in the classroom.

FE0852A0DFE401316C4968A86D17958E.description: Develop problem-solving and communication skills by participating in cooperative scriptwriting that demonstrates knowledge of basic blocking and stage areas.

FE07EF50DFE401316C4868A86D17958E.description: Make acting choices when dramatizing cultural versions of similar stories from around the world.

FE078FE0DFE401316C4768A86D17958E.description: Exemplify the emotional traits of a character through gesture and action.

FE072860DFE401316C4668A86D17958E.description: Write or improvise short plays adapted from classroom literature that demonstrate the role conflict plays in drama.

FE06C280DFE401316C4568A86D17958E.description: Perform and participate in theatre improvisations and dramatizations to learn acting and scriptwriting fundamentals.

FE05FAB0DFE401316C4368A86D17958E.description: Associate aural examples of music to a variety of cultures, styles, and historical periods.

FE051A10DFE401316C4168A86D17958E.description: Research career and vocational options in music using available technology.

FE04AB10DFE401316C4068A86D17958E.description: Analyze concepts common to music and other disciplines.

FE037930DFE401316C3D68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast materials being studied in its historical and cultural context, including music from the 20th and/or 21st century.

FE02A740DFE401316C3B68A86D17958E.description: Research career and vocational options in music using available technology.

FE0242D0DFE401316C3A68A86D17958E.description: Discuss relationships between music concepts and other disciplines.

FE011410DFE401316C3768A86D17958E.description: Describe distinguishing characteristics of representative choral music from a variety of cultures.

FE00A7C0DFE401316C3668A86D17958E.description: Classify an exemplary vocal/choral work by music style.

FDFFC4C0DFE401316C3468A86D17958E.description: Explore careers in music and relate them to careers in the other fine and performing arts.

FDFF59B0DFE401316C3368A86D17958E.description: Examine and evaluate characteristics of various arts from a particular historic period and various cultures, using appropriate terms.

FDFE2CE0DFE401316C3068A86D17958E.description: Associate distinguishing characteristics of representative choral music from a variety of cultures.

FDFDC340DFE401316C2F68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the functions of vocal/choral music in various cultures.

FDFCD320DFE401316C2D68A86D17958E.description: Explore careers in music and relate them to careers in the other fine and performing arts.

FDFC61C0DFE401316C2C68A86D17958E.description: Associate common music elements and descriptive terms with those used in art, dance, and drama.

FDFB35E0DFE401316C2968A86D17958E.description: Connect music to other art forms and subject areas through understanding the historical and cultural context of music.

FDFAC8D0DFE401316C2868A86D17958E.description: Read and notate rhythmic and melodic notation.

FDFA4E20DFE401316C2768A86D17958E.description: Use a symbol system to sight-read melodies in major and minor keys.

FDF9EB50DFE401316C2668A86D17958E.description: Sight-read individual voice parts in a vocal score.

FDF92530DFE401316C2468A86D17958E.description: Read and notate rhythmic and melodic notation.

FDF8B410DFE401316C2368A86D17958E.description: Use a symbol system to sight-read melodies in major keys.

FDF84600DFE401316C2268A86D17958E.description: Sight-read individual voice parts in a vocal score.

FDF748D0DFE401316C2068A86D17958E.description: Read and notate rhythmic patterns in various meters at various tempi.

FDF6CDB0DFE401316C1F68A86D17958E.description: Sight-read, analyze and practice simple phrases of up to eight measures using music notation.

FDF5FAE0DFE401316C1D68A86D17958E.description: Sight-read, analyze and practice simple phrases of up to four measures using music notation.

FDF4A000DFE401316C1A68A86D17958E.description: Compose a selection for two or more voices making use of available technology.

FDF43D50DFE401316C1968A86D17958E.description: Improvise a melody to a 12 bar blues, iii-VI-ii-V, and ii- V7-I chord progression in various key centers.

FDF36B10DFE401316C1768A86D17958E.description: Create harmonies for a given melody.

FDF2F140DFE401316C1668A86D17958E.description: Compose rhythmically interesting melodies within specified guidelines.

FDF28190DFE401316C1568A86D17958E.description: Improvise a melody to a 12 bar blues and ii-V7-I chord progression.

FDF1A160DFE401316C1368A86D17958E.description: Create harmony for a given melody.

FDF11080DFE401316C1268A86D17958E.description: Compose rhythmically interesting melodies within specified guidelines.

FDF089D0DFE401316C1168A86D17958E.description: Embellish a folk song by creating rhythmic and melodic variations based on I, IV, and V (V7) chords.

FDEFBFC0DFE401316C0F68A86D17958E.description: Compose rhythmic patterns and simple melodies within specified guidelines.

FDEF4840DFE401316C0E68A86D17958E.description: Improvise "responses" in a similar style to given rhythmic and melodic phrases.

FDEEDF60DFE401316C0D68A86D17958E.description: Create variations of familiar melodic phrases on a neutral syllable.

FDED7390DFE401316C0A68A86D17958E.description: Play an accompaniment to a voice part on a melodic instrument.

FDECB090DFE401316C0868A86D17958E.description: Sing independently, from memory, a solo from the standard vocal repertoire that is appropriate for an audition.

FDEC4970DFE401316C0768A86D17958E.description: Perform music from various cultures and traditions in a variety of languages.

FDEBDCA0DFE401316C0668A86D17958E.description: Sing music in at least four parts, with and without accompaniment.

FDEB61F0DFE401316C0568A86D17958E.description: Perform literature with complex and non-traditional harmonies and other nontraditional musical elements.

FDEA9E20DFE401316C0368A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate an understanding of phrasing as it effects expression.

FDEA3CF0DFE401316C0268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate blending vocal timbres and matching dynamic levels.

FDE9D9E0DFE401316C0168A86D17958E.description: Incorporate appropriate mood, dynamics, tempo, and tone color into performance.

FDE8F720DFE401316BFF68A86D17958E.description: Sing in English (and any other languages) in a way that can be understood.

FDE88560DFE401316BFE68A86D17958E.description: Use the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) as a resource tool.

FDE7BC10DFE401316BFC68A86D17958E.description: Sing acappella music in a variety of keys.

FDE75350DFE401316BFB68A86D17958E.description: Sing with vowel purity, distinguishing between pure vowel sounds and diphthongs.

FDE6F130DFE401316BFA68A86D17958E.description: Use vocal development exercises to achieve accurate pitch production.

FDE671F0DFE401316BF968A86D17958E.description: Use vocal development exercises to produce a relaxed, open sound.

FDE5E8D0DFE401316BF868A86D17958E.description: Sing with a free, clear tone, demonstrating accurate intonation.

FDE529A0DFE401316BF668A86D17958E.description: Exhibit increased knowledge of breathing physiology and the ability to apply it to singing.

FDE4C620DFE401316BF568A86D17958E.description: Use vocal techniques in the control of dynamics and articulation throughout the vocal range.

FDE45B80DFE401316BF468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of vocal technique and be able to apply it to advanced vocal literature.

FDE2DFA0DFE401316BF068A86D17958E.description: Play an individual voice part on a melodic instrument.

FDE21730DFE401316BEE68A86D17958E.description: Sing in small ensembles with one singer on a part.

FDE1B250DFE401316BED68A86D17958E.description: Perform music from various cultures and traditions in a variety of languages.

FDE130E0DFE401316BEC68A86D17958E.description: Sing music in at least four parts, with and without accompaniment.

FDDAA6E0DFE401316BEB68A86D17958E.description: Perform literature with traditional and nontraditional harmonies and other musical elements.

FDD9CFC0DFE401316BE968A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate an understanding of phrasing as it effects expression.

FDD90590DFE401316BE768A86D17958E.description: Incorporate appropriate mood, dynamics, tempo, and tone color into performance.

FDD83470DFE401316BE568A86D17958E.description: Sing in English (and any other languages) in a way that can be understood.

FDD7CF90DFE401316BE468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the difference between voiced and unvoiced consonants.

FDD6E7C0DFE401316BE268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the use of vowel placement to adjust tone.

FDD66200DFE401316BE168A86D17958E.description: Sing with vowel purity, distinguishing between pure vowel sounds and diphthongs.

FDD5FFC0DFE401316BE068A86D17958E.description: Use vocal development exercises to achieve accurate pitch production.

FDD42590DFE401316BDC68A86D17958E.description: Exhibit knowledge of breathing physiology and the ability to apply it to singing.

FDD12390DFE401316BD568A86D17958E.description: Clap melodic rhythm from simple melodies.

FDD05DD0DFE401316BD368A86D17958E.description: Perform music from various cultures and traditions.

FDCFF480DFE401316BD268A86D17958E.description: Sing literature with and without instrumental accompaniment.

FDCF65B0DFE401316BD168A86D17958E.description: Sing literature in three-part or four-part harmony.

FDCE44F0DFE401316BCE68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate awareness of blend and balance in choral singing.

FDCD18B0DFE401316BCB68A86D17958E.description: Sing in English (and any other languages) in a way that can be understood.

FDCCB7E0DFE401316BCA68A86D17958E.description: Develop skills in articulation and clarity of pronunciation.

FDCBEF60DFE401316BC868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate knowledge of basic terminology related to phonation and knowledge of individual singing ranges.

FDCB77B0DFE401316BC768A86D17958E.description: Sing with purity of vowels, distinguish between vowel sounds, and perform them correctly.

FDCB0F40DFE401316BC668A86D17958E.description: Use vocal development exercises to achieve accurate pitch production.

FDC64EB0DFE401316BBB68A86D17958E.description: Use body percussion to practice and perform rhythms.

FDC57940DFE401316BB968A86D17958E.description: Perform music from various world cultures and traditions.

FDC507C0DFE401316BB868A86D17958E.description: Sing literature with and without instrumental accompaniment.

FDC29370DFE401316BB268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate indicated dynamics and tempo in individual and group singing.

FDC1D080DFE401316BB068A86D17958E.description: Sing in English (and any other languages) in a way that can be understood.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

F4783CC0DFE401315D3C68A86D17958E.description: Compare two decimals to hundredths by reasoning about their size. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two decimals refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual model.

F477F7D0DFE401315D3B68A86D17958E.description: Use decimal notation for fractions with denominators 10 or 100.
comments: For example, rewrite 0.62 as 62/100; describe a length as 0.62 meters; locate 0.62 on a number line diagram.

F477A870DFE401315D3A68A86D17958E.description: Express a fraction with denominator 10 as an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, and use this technique to add two fractions with respective denominators 10 and 100.
comments: Students who can generate equivalent fractions can develop strategies for adding fractions with unlike denominators in general. But addition and subtraction with unlike denominators in general is not a requirement at this grade.
For example, express 3/10 as 30/100, and add 3/10 + 4/100 = 34/100.

F4775A50DFE401315D3968A86D17958E.description: Understand decimal notation for fractions, and compare decimal fractions.

comments: For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
F4770880DFE401315D3868A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

F476AF60DFE401315D3768A86D17958E.description: Understand a multiple of a/b as a multiple of 1/b, and use this understanding to multiply a fraction by a whole number.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to express 3 × (2/5) as 6 × (1/5), recognizing this product as 6/5. (In general, n × (a/b) = (n × a)/b.)
For example, use a visual fraction model to represent 5/4 as the product 5 × (1/4), recording the conclusion by the equation 5/4 = 5 × (1/4).
F4765D70DFE401315D3668A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction a/b as a multiple of 1/b.

F475FC80DFE401315D3568A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction by a whole number.

F475A3D0DFE401315D3468A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole and having like denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

F47553E0DFE401315D3368A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract mixed numbers with like denominators, e.g., by replacing each mixed number with an equivalent fraction, and/or by using properties of operations and the relationship between addition and subtraction.

F4750E00DFE401315D3268A86D17958E.description: Decompose a fraction into a sum of fractions with the same denominator in more than one way, recording each decomposition by an equation. Justify decompositions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

F474CA30DFE401315D3168A86D17958E.description: Understand addition and subtraction of fractions as joining and separating parts referring to the same whole.

F47483E0DFE401315D3068A86D17958E.description: Understand a fraction a/b with a > 1 as a sum of fractions 1/b.

F4743900DFE401315D2F68A86D17958E.description: Build fractions from unit fractions by applying and extending previous understandings of operations on whole numbers.

F473E340DFE401315D2E68A86D17958E.description: Compare two fractions with different numerators and different denominators, e.g., by creating common denominators or numerators, or by comparing to a benchmark fraction such as 1/2. Recognize that comparisons are valid only when the two fractions refer to the same whole. Record the results of comparisons with symbols >, =, or <, and justify the conclusions, e.g., by using a visual fraction model.

F4738EF0DFE401315D2D68A86D17958E.description: Explain why a fraction a/b is equivalent to a fraction (n × a)/(n × b) by using visual fraction models, with attention to how the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions themselves are the same size. Use this principle to recognize and generate equivalent fractions.

F4734B40DFE401315D2C68A86D17958E.description: Extend understanding of fraction equivalence and ordering.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

F472C010DFE401315D2A68A86D17958E.description: Recognize a line of symmetry for a two-dimensional figure as a line across the figure such that the figure can be folded along the line into matching parts. Identify line-symmetric figures and draw lines of symmetry.

F4727B80DFE401315D2968A86D17958E.description: Classify two-dimensional figures based on the presence or absence of parallel or perpendicular lines, or the presence or absence of angles of a specified size. Recognize right triangles as a category, and identify right triangles.

F4723270DFE401315D2868A86D17958E.description: Draw points, lines, line segments, rays, angles (right, acute, obtuse), and perpendicular and parallel lines. Identify these in two-dimensional figures.

F471D5C0DFE401315D2768A86D17958E.description: Draw and identify lines and angles, and classify shapes by properties of their lines and angles.

F4713AC0DFE401315D2568A86D17958E.description: Recognize angle measure as additive. When an angle is decomposed into non-overlapping parts, the angle measure of the whole is the sum of the angle measures of the parts. Solve addition and subtraction problems to find unknown angles on a diagram in real world and mathematical problems, e.g., by using an equation with a symbol for the unknown angle measure.

F470F7C0DFE401315D2468A86D17958E.description: Measure angles in whole-number degrees using a protractor. Sketch angles of specified measure.

F470AFE0DFE401315D2368A86D17958E.description: An angle that turns through n one-degree angles is said to have an angle measure of n degrees.

F4704F20DFE401315D2268A86D17958E.description: An angle is measured with reference to a circle with its center at the common endpoint of the rays, by considering the fraction of the circular arc between the points where the two rays intersect the circle. An angle that turns through 1/360 of a circle is called a "one-degree angle," and can be used to measure angles.

F46FE300DFE401315D2168A86D17958E.description: Recognize angles as geometric shapes that are formed wherever two rays share a common endpoint, and understand concepts of angle measurement:

F46F9FE0DFE401315D2068A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of angle and measure angles.

comments: For example, from a line plot find and interpret the difference in length between the longest and shortest specimens in an insect collection.
F46E30B0DFE401315D1B68A86D17958E.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions by using information presented in line plots.

F46F5BB0DFE401315D1F68A86D17958E.description: Apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real world and mathematical problems.
comments: For example, find the width of a rectangular room given the area of the flooring and the length, by viewing the area formula as a multiplication equation with an unknown factor.

F46F1710DFE401315D1E68A86D17958E.description: Use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, intervals of time, liquid volumes, masses of objects, and money, including problems involving simple fractions or decimals, and problems that require expressing measurements given in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Represent measurement quantities using diagrams such as number line diagrams that feature a measurement scale.

F46ECD50DFE401315D1D68A86D17958E.description: Know relative sizes of measurement units within one system of units including km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz.; l, ml; hr, min, sec. Within a single system of measurement, express measurements in a larger unit in terms of a smaller unit. Record measurement equivalents in a two column table.
comments: For example, know that 1 ft is 12 times as long as 1 in. Express the length of a 4 ft snake as 48 in. Generate a conversion table for feet and inches listing the number pairs (1, 12), (2, 24), (3, 36), …

F46E7F00DFE401315D1C68A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving measurement and conversion of measurements from a larger unit to a smaller unit.

F46BF0E0DFE401315D1468A86D17958E.description: Find whole-number quotients and remainders with up to four-digit dividends and one-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

F46BAE40DFE401315D1368A86D17958E.description: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit whole number, and multiply two two-digit numbers, using strategies based on place value and the properties of operations. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

F46B6B60DFE401315D1268A86D17958E.description: Fluently add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

F46B2420DFE401315D1168A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding and properties of operations to perform multi-digit arithmetic.

F46D6F20DFE401315D1868A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place.

F46D28A0DFE401315D1768A86D17958E.description: Read and write multi-digit whole numbers using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form. Compare two multi-digit numbers based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

comments: For example, recognize that 700 ÷ 70 = 10 by applying concepts of place value and division.
F46CC570DFE401315D1668A86D17958E.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what it represents in the place to its right.

F46C46C0DFE401315D1568A86D17958E.description: Generalize place value understanding for multi-digit whole numbers.

F46AD760DFE401315D1068A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

F46A78E0DFE401315D0F68A86D17958E.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself.
comments: For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.

F469EF80DFE401315D0D68A86D17958E.description: Find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1—100. Recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is a multiple of a given one-digit number. Determine whether a given whole number in the range 1—100 is prime or composite.

F469AD60DFE401315D0C68A86D17958E.description: Gain familiarity with factors and multiples.

F46966C0DFE401315D0B68A86D17958E.description: Solve multistep word problems posed with whole numbers and having whole-number answers using the four operations, including problems in which remainders must be interpreted. Represent these problems using equations with a letter standing for the unknown quantity. Assess the reasonableness of answers using mental computation and estimation strategies including rounding.

F4691DC0DFE401315D0A68A86D17958E.description: Multiply or divide to solve word problems involving multiplicative comparison, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem, distinguishing multiplicative comparison from additive comparison.

F468A820DFE401315D0968A86D17958E.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.

F4686430DFE401315D0868A86D17958E.description: Use the four operations with whole numbers to solve problems.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
F467C8E0DFE401315D0668A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

F4676F80DFE401315D0568A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

F4660E70DFE401315D0168A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

F46572B0DFE401315CFF68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: District of Columbia Science Standards

0B45AB10DFE50131832B68A86D17958E.description: Describe how, as a person matures, the amounts and kinds of food and exercise needed by the body change.

0B4569E0DFE50131832A68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that vitamins and minerals are substances required by the body in small amounts to synthesize essential substances and carry out essential processes

0B451EF0DFE50131832968A86D17958E.description: Recognize that food provides energy as well as materials for growth, maintenance, and repair of body parts.

0B44DB40DFE50131832868A86D17958E.description: Explain that some things people take into their bodies from the environment can hurt them, and give examples of such things.

0B449680DFE50131832768A86D17958E.description: Explain that eating a variety of healthful foods and getting enough exercise and rest help people stay healthy.

0B444B80DFE50131832668A86D17958E.description: Explain that people need water, food, air, waste removal, and a particular range of temperatures, just as other animals do, although different animals can tolerate very different ranges of temperature and other features of their surroundings.

0B440B40DFE50131832568A86D17958E.description: Humans have a variety of mechanisms to stay healthy. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B43CD20DFE50131832468A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast how life cycles vary for different living things.

0B438CE0DFE50131832368A86D17958E.description: Describe the life cycle of some living things, such as the frog and butterfly, including how they go through striking changes of body shape and function as they go through metamorphosis.

0B434C50DFE50131832268A86D17958E.description: Recognize that plants and animals go through predictable life cycles that include birth, growth, development, reproduction, and death.

0B430A60DFE50131832168A86D17958E.description: Plants and animals have predictable life cycles. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B42C440DFE50131832068A86D17958E.description: Explain that characteristics used for classification depend on the purpose of the grouping.

0B427AC0DFE50131831F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that a great variety of living things can be sorted into groups in many ways using various properties, such as how they look, where they live, and how they act, in order to decide which things belong to which group.

0B423DC0DFE50131831E68A86D17958E.description: Plants and animals can be classified according to the physical characteristics that they share. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B41C370DFE50131831C68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that things that make sound do so by vibrating objects, such as vocal cords and musical instruments. Describe that the sound travels as a vibration through the air.

0B418170DFE50131831B68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe how moving air and water (carriers of kinetic energy, the energy of motion) can be used to run machines like windmills and waterwheels.

0B4132E0DFE50131831A68A86D17958E.description: Describe how people use electricity or the chemical energy from burning fuels, such as wood, oil, coal, or natural gas, to obtain heat energy for doing tasks, such as cooking their food and warming their houses.

0B40E3E0DFE50131831968A86D17958E.description: Recognize that energy can be transformed from one form to another.

0B407E50DFE50131831868A86D17958E.description: Describe basic forms of energy, including mechanical (kinetic and potential), light, sound, heat, chemical, nuclear, and electrical.

0B4032C0DFE50131831768A86D17958E.description: Recognize that energy is needed to carry out almost any kind of change.

0B3FEFA0DFE50131831668A86D17958E.description: Energy takes many forms and has many sources. As a basis for understanding these concepts, students:

0B3F44E0DFE50131831468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and describe that sunlight can be blocked to create shadows, and the direction and length of shadows vary at different times of day.

0B3EE0F0DFE50131831368A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe the changes that occur in the observable shape of the moon over the course of a month (i.e., the moon looks a little different every day, but looks the same again about every four weeks).

0B3EA3E0DFE50131831268A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe that the sun can be seen only in the daytime; the moon can be seen sometimes at night and sometimes during the day.

0B3E65B0DFE50131831168A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe how there are more stars in the sky than anyone can easily count, but they are not spaced or spread evenly.

0B3E28B0DFE50131831068A86D17958E.description: Using a globe, demonstrate how the Earth rotates on its axis every 24 hours, producing the night-and-day cycle.

0B3DEB70DFE50131830F68A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe the apparent motion of the sun and moon over a time span of one day.

0B3DAAF0DFE50131830E68A86D17958E.description: Objects in the sky move in regular and predictable patterns. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B4727D0DFE50131833068A86D17958E.description: Construct something to perform a task, by using commonly available materials, such as paper, cardboard, wood, plastic, or metal, or by using existing objects.

0B46E570DFE50131832F68A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate how an invention can be used in different ways, such as a radio or a cell phone that can be used to receive both information and entertainment.

0B46A190DFE50131832E68A86D17958E.description: Define technology as the application of human ingenuity and skill to the solution of practical problems (e.g., typewriter, computer).

0B465270DFE50131832D68A86D17958E.description: Although each of these human enterprises of science and technology has a character and history of its own, each is dependent on and reinforces the other. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B3AEF20DFE50131830468A86D17958E.description: Explain that one way to make sense of something is to think of how it compares to something more familiar (e.g., vibrations of an object in air such as a tuning fork, a plucked string of a string instrument, human vocal cords).

0B3AAE70DFE50131830368A86D17958E.description: Ask, "How do you know?" in appropriate situations, and attempt reasonable answers when others ask the same question.

0B3D2050DFE50131830C68A86D17958E.description: Make sketches and write descriptions to aid in explaining procedures or ideas.

0B3CE430DFE50131830B68A86D17958E.description: Appropriately use simple tools — such as clamps, rulers, scissors, and hand lenses, as well as other technology (e.g., such as calculators and computers) — to help solve problems.

0B3CA840DFE50131830A68A86D17958E.description: Keep a notebook that describes ongoing observations and that is still understandable weeks or months later.

0B3C6CF0DFE50131830968A86D17958E.description: Measure and mix dry and liquid materials in prescribed amounts, following reasonable safety precautions.

0B3C3070DFE50131830868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the ability to work cooperatively while respecting the ideas of others and communicating one's own conclusions about findings.

0B3BF190DFE50131830768A86D17958E.description: Discuss the results of investigations and consider the explanations of others.

0B3BA780DFE50131830668A86D17958E.description: Keep and report records of investigations and observations using tools, such as journals, charts, graphs, and computers.

0B3B4490DFE50131830568A86D17958E.description: Participate in different types of guided scientific investigations (related to content in this grade), such as observing objects and events and collecting specimens for analysis, including longer-term investigations that take place over several days, weeks, or months.

0B3A6CD0DFE50131830268A86D17958E.description: Recognize and explain that when a scientific investigation is repeated, carefully and under the same conditions, a similar (but not necessarily identical) result is expected.

0B3A25C0DFE50131830168A86D17958E.description: Scientific progress is made by asking relevant questions and conducting careful investigations. As a basis for understanding this concept, and to address the content in this grade, students should develop their own questions and perform investigations. Students:

document.title: District of Columbia Science Standards

78FAA24309EF44ADA8DE68EDF2ABE54E.description: Identify common needs of plants and animals. (Children might say, "All animals need air to breathe," or after hearing Anne Morris' Bread, Bread, Bread read aloud, they say, "Everyone eats bread, but there are different kinds.")

8299D8AD27134A208473370E5CDB8915.description: Observe, describe, compare, and categorize plants and animals. (Students might say, "Birds can fly, but cats can't." They notice differences and say, "Some of our plants are tall, and some are short.")

45638598E37646B69ACA6F4AA4C33BA7.description: Explore and observe changes in plants and animals, their life cycles, and habitats. (Children can care for a classroom pet by providing food and water as needed and by helping to clean the cage. On a nature walk, students might observe aloud, "Look, that squirrel is putting something in his mouth.")

7746E618534D433A8DAC4F7FA67C72C7.description: Children are familiar with living things (plants and animals) and what they need to survive. Students:

734F50E64A3E427C931DA3E70459962A.description: Experiment with how things move and change. (Students can create different inclines with blocks to explore the velocity of toy cars. Children can shake cream in a plastic jar until it becomes butter.)

E07A78396ECE4AFAAEF09054ACF3594B.description: Observe, describe, compare, and categorize objects on the basis of qualities such as weight, shape, size, color, and temperature. (Children can use a balance to compare the weights of rocks in a collection, or they can use sorting trays to arrange a collection of bottle caps.)

48FFE1DB11FD4FB69394D3DC36A6B07D.description: Explore the physical properties of objects and materials. (Students can use a magnifying glass to examine sand, and they can pick up some metal objects using a magnet.)

240239656E5949949DEB0B800EAE1660.description: Children are familiar with the physical properties and uses of materials and objects. Students:

A87AAF9AF21D42E08743054241E8E840.description: Explore how their actions can cause changes in the environment. (Students use the recycle bins in the classroom. Children observe aloud, "Look how the dirt gets darker when we put water on it.")

2E311C0EBBC84565A6404BE7203E558E.description: Observe and describe the natural world around them. (Children look at dark clouds and conclude, "It's going to rain." A student says, "I think it's spring because I saw some flowers in our garden.")

192677F292054818976686BC42526E67.description: Children are familiar with the Earth and the natural world. Students:

43763FBAAFA64DEFABE57624C3EC98B4.description: Communicate observations and findings through a variety of methods. (A student explains to a friend how he turned dirt into mud. Children draw a picture of a carrot, showing the root in the soil and the leaves above the soil.)

890A5623559942D3ABA1CDD968EE82CD.description: Discuss and draw conclusions and form generalizations. (Children notice that mixing yellow and blue paint always makes the paint turn green. A student asserts, "I can do things now that I couldn't do when I was a baby because I'm big now.")

1A3AC6C4A9634974893B006831A36672.description: Collect, organize, and record information. (Children draw a picture of worms found outside, or they sort leaves found on the playground and line them up by shape.)

31E922BE1D214EBEB388499A8F8D880C.description: Use tools to explore and investigate. (Students use a pair of binoculars to watch a bird building a nest, or they use a string to measure the growth of a plant.)

E5CB5EC491214F53B22BDCBF927F9CF7.description: Explore cause and effect. (Students add blocks to a tower to see how high it can rise before it falls, or they place pennies, one by one, in two floating boats to see which boat sinks first.)

27B565A8CDEC45EBB4AB7548553D4F97.description: Ask questions and make predictions. (Students ponder, "Where does the sun go at night?" Children put snow in a bucket and conclude, "If we take the bucket inside, the snow's going melt.")

8806D3628E364BD0B509F65560E4FFC7.description: Children develop inquiry and process skills. Students:

document.title: District of Columbia Science Standards

0C579730DFE5013184B168A86D17958E.description: Explain that waves obey the superposition principle: Many waves can pass through the same point at once, and the wave amplitude at that point is the sum of the amplitudes of the individual waves.

0C574A60DFE5013184B068A86D17958E.description: Summarize how something can be "seen" when light waves emitted or reflected by an object enter the eye, just as something can be "heard" when sound waves from an object enter the ear.

0C56FA70DFE5013184AF68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that human eyes respond to a narrow range of wavelengths of the electromagnetic spectrum (red through violet) called visible light.

0C56A190DFE5013184AE68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that vibrations in materials set up wave disturbances, such as sound and earthquake waves, which spread away from the source.

0C564AD0DFE5013184AD68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain how light waves, sound waves, and other waves move at different speeds in different materials.

0C55F500DFE5013184AC68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain how sound in a fluid (e.g., air) is a longitudinal wave whose speed depends on the properties of the fluid in which it propagates.

0C559950DFE5013184AB68A86D17958E.description: Explain how electromagnetic waves differ from mechanical waves in that they do not need a medium for propagation; nevertheless, they can be described by many of the same quantities: amplitude, wavelength, frequency (or period), and wave speed.

0C555040DFE5013184AA68A86D17958E.description: Explain how a mechanical wave is a disturbance that propagates through a medium.

0C550DE0DFE5013184A968A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain how waves carry energy from one place to another.

0C54C7C0DFE5013184A868A86D17958E.description: Waves have characteristic properties that are common to all types of wave. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C5432D0DFE5013184A668A86D17958E.description: Plot and interpret distance versus time graphs for constant speed.

0C53ED70DFE5013184A568A86D17958E.description: Explain that if the net force acting on an object always acts toward the same center as the object moves, the object's path is a curve about the force center. (Motion in a circular orbit is the simplest example of this concept.)

0C53AA30DFE5013184A468A86D17958E.description: Know that the greater the mass of an object, the more force is needed to change its motion.

0C5363D0DFE5013184A368A86D17958E.description: Explain that every object exerts an attractive gravitational force on every other object.

0C530E70DFE5013184A268A86D17958E.description: Explain why an unbalanced force acting on an object changes the object's speed or direction of motion or both.

0C52C6D0DFE5013184A168A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain that when the forces on an object are balanced (equal and opposite forces that add up to zero), the motion of the object does not change.

0C527940DFE5013184A068A86D17958E.description: Recognize that a force has both magnitude and direction.

0C523280DFE50131849F68A86D17958E.description: When an object is subject to two or more forces at once, the effective force is the cumulative effect of all the forces. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C519410DFE50131849D68A86D17958E.description: Know that power is energy per unit of time, expressed in watts, W, and 1 W = 1 J/s. Explain that devices are rated according to their power capacity or consumption.

0C513E10DFE50131849C68A86D17958E.description: Explain how electrical circuits provide a means of transferring electrical energy from sources such as generators to devices in which heat, light, sound, and chemical changes are produced.

0C50F670DFE50131849B68A86D17958E.description: Describe the role that electromagnets play in electric motors, electric generators, and simple devices such as doorbells and earphones.

0C50A380DFE50131849A68A86D17958E.description: Explain that when an electric current flows why there is always a magnetic field associated with it.

0C505500DFE50131849968A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain that an object can be electrically charged either positively or negatively; objects with like charges repel each other, and objects with unlike charges attract each other.

0C500950DFE50131849868A86D17958E.description: Electricity and magnetism are related phenomena that have many useful applications in everyday life. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C4D1C00DFE50131848E68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast how heat energy can be transferred through radiation, convection, or conduction.

0C4CC9B0DFE50131848D68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain that in processes at the scale of atomic size or greater, energy cannot be created or destroyed but only changed from one form into another.

0C4F7240DFE50131849668A86D17958E.description: Explain how electrical energy can be generated using a variety of energy sources and can be transformed into almost any other form of energy, such as mechanical motion, light, sound, or heat.

0C4F2990DFE50131849568A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain that heat energy is a common product of an energy transformation, such as in biological growth, the operation of machines, the operation of a lightbulb, and the motion of people.

0C4EDAD0DFE50131849468A86D17958E.description: Know that the sun's radiation consists of a wide range of wavelengths, mainly visible light, infrared, and ultraviolet radiation.

0C4E91A0DFE50131849368A86D17958E.description: Explain that the sun emits energy in the form of light and other radiation, and only a tiny fraction of that energy is intercepted by the Earth.

0C4E4BE0DFE50131849268A86D17958E.description: Describe that energy may be stored as potential energy in many ways, including chemical bonds and in the nucleus of atoms.

0C4E0550DFE50131849168A86D17958E.description: Recognize and describe that energy is a property of many systems and can take the forms of mechanical motion, gravitational energy, the energy of electrostatic and magnetostatic fields, sound, heat, and light (electromagnetic field energy).

0C4DBE30DFE50131849068A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain how kinetic energy can be transformed into potential energy, and vice versa (e.g., in a bouncing ball).

0C4D7310DFE50131848F68A86D17958E.description: Describe kinetic energy as the energy of motion (e.g., a rolling ball), and potential energy as the energy of position or configuration (e.g., a raised object or a compressed spring).

0C4C7A90DFE50131848C68A86D17958E.description: Explain how energy is the ability to do work and is measured in joules (J).

0C4C2C60DFE50131848B68A86D17958E.description: Energy and matter have multiple forms and can be changed from one form to another. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C4B8CA0DFE50131848968A86D17958E.description: Determine the density of substances (regular and irregular solids, and liquids) from direct measurements of mass and volume, or of volume by water displacement.

0C4B4400DFE50131848868A86D17958E.description: Determine and explain that the buoyant force on an object in a fluid is an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid the object has displaced; this principle can be used to predict whether an object will float or sink in a given fluid.

0C4AFFA0DFE50131848768A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain that equal volumes of different substances usually have different masses and, therefore, different densities.

0C4AB970DFE50131848668A86D17958E.description: Know that density is mass per unit volume.

0C4A59A0DFE50131848568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that the mass of an object is a measure of the quantity of matter it contains (measured in kg or g), and that its weight (measured in N) is the magnitude of the gravitational force exerted between Earth and that much mass.

0C4A0150DFE50131848468A86D17958E.description: All objects experience a buoyant force when immersed in a fluid. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C496E50DFE50131848268A86D17958E.description: Recognize that indicators of chemical changes include temperature change, the production of a gas, the production of a precipitate, or a color change.

0C492860DFE50131848168A86D17958E.description: Recognize that solutions can be acidic, basic, or neutral, depending on the concentration of hydrogen ions in the solution. Understand that because this concentration can vary over a very large range, the logarithmic pH scale is used to describe how acidic or basic a solution is (each increase of one in the pH scale is an increase of 10 times in concentration).

0C48E020DFE50131848068A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain that reactions occur at different rates, slow to fast, and that reaction rates can be changed by changing the concentration of reactants, the temperature, the surface areas of solids, and by using a catalyst.

0C489750DFE50131847F68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain how during endothermic chemical reactions heat energy is absorbed from the surroundings, and in exothermic reactions heat energy is released to the surroundings.

0C484810DFE50131847E68A86D17958E.description: Explain how the idea of atoms, as proposed by John Dalton, explains the conservation of matter: In chemical reactions, the number of atoms stays the same no matter how they are arranged, and the mass of atoms does not change significantly in chemical reactions, so their total mass stays the same.

0C47FBF0DFE50131847D68A86D17958E.description: Describe Antoine Lavoisier's work, including the idea that when materials react with each other, many changes can take place, but that in every case the total amount of matter afterward is the same as before (Law of Conservation of Matter).

0C47A7D0DFE50131847C68A86D17958E.description: Discover and explain how elements and compounds (reactants) react with each other to form products with different properties.

0C475810DFE50131847B68A86D17958E.description: Chemical reactions are processes in which atoms are rearranged into different combinations of molecules. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C445AF0DFE50131847168A86D17958E.description: Describe the contributions of the scientists involved with the development of current atomic theory, including John Dalton, Marie and Pierre Curie, Joseph John Thomson, Albert Einstein, Max Planck, Ernest Rutherford, Niels Bohr, and Erwin Schroedinger.

0C46BC20DFE50131847968A86D17958E.description: Explain that the melting and boiling temperatures of a substance (element or compound) depend on pressure and are independent of the amount of the sample. (Some materials do not melt and others do not boil because they decompose as the temperature is raised; other materials do not have a sharp melting point because they are not homogeneous.)

0C466670DFE50131847868A86D17958E.description: Describe how the atoms, molecules, or ions comprising an object are in constant individual motion, and explain how their average motional (kinetic) energy determines the temperature of the object, and how the strength of the forces between them determines the state of matter at that temperature.

0C461FD0DFE50131847768A86D17958E.description: Understand how an ion is an atom or group of atoms (molecule) that has acquired an electric charge by losing or gaining one or more electrons.

0C45DC20DFE50131847668A86D17958E.description: Describe how elements can be classified, based on similar properties, into categories, including highly reactive metals, less reactive metals, highly reactive nonmetals, less reactive nonmetals, and some almost completely nonreactive (noble) gases.

0C4599F0DFE50131847568A86D17958E.description: Know that there are more than 100 elements that combine in a multitude of ways to produce compounds that make up all the living and nonliving things in the universe.

0C455510DFE50131847468A86D17958E.description: Diagram and describe how atoms may combine (bond) into molecules or into large crystalline arrays.

0C450890DFE50131847368A86D17958E.description: Using a periodic chart, explain that the atoms of any element are similar to each other, but they are different from atoms of other elements. Know that the atoms of a given isotope are identical to each other.

0C44A860DFE50131847268A86D17958E.description: Construct a model of an atom and know the atom is composed of protons, neutrons, and electrons.

0C441330DFE50131847068A86D17958E.description: Explain that all matter is made up of atoms that are far too small to see directly through an optical microscope.

0C43B5E0DFE50131846F68A86D17958E.description: Elements have distinct macroscopic properties and atomic structures. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C40F320DFE50131846568A86D17958E.description: Apply simple mathematical models to problems (e.g., formulas such as F = ma).

0C40AF90DFE50131846468A86D17958E.description: Describe the work of pioneers of physics and cosmology, such as Nicolaus Copernicus, Galileo Galilei, Johannes Kepler, Isaac Newton, Hans Christian Oersted and Andre-Marie Ampère, Dmitry Ivanovich Mendeleyev, Albert Einstein, and Lise Meitner.

0C406950DFE50131846368A86D17958E.description: Identify and criticize the reasoning in arguments in which fact and opinion are intermingled or the conclusions do not follow logically from the evidence given, an analogy is not apt, no mention is made of whether the control group is very much like the experimental group, or all members of a group are implied to have nearly identical characteristics that differ from those of other groups.

0C432D20DFE50131846D68A86D17958E.description: Explain why arguments may be invalid if based on very small samples of data, biased samples, or experiments in which there was no control sample.

0C42DEB0DFE50131846C68A86D17958E.description: Read analog and digital meters on instruments used to make direct measurements of length, volume, weight, elapsed time, rates, or temperatures, and choose appropriate units. Explain how to interpolate on analog scales.

0C429BF0DFE50131846B68A86D17958E.description: Use tables, charts, and graphs in making arguments and claims in presentations about lab work.

0C425950DFE50131846A68A86D17958E.description: Participate in group discussions on scientific topics by restating or summarizing accurately what others have said, asking for clarification or elaboration, and expressing alternative positions.

0C421400DFE50131846968A86D17958E.description: Write clear step-by-step instructions (procedural summaries) for conducting investigations.

0C41CFA0DFE50131846868A86D17958E.description: Explain why accuracy and openness in record keeping and replication are essential for maintaining an investigator's credibility with other scientists and society.

0C418BC0DFE50131846768A86D17958E.description: Describe how if more than one variable changes at the same time in an experiment, the outcome of the experiment may not be attributable to a change in any single variable.

0C414250DFE50131846668A86D17958E.description: Test hypotheses that pertain to the content under study.

0C401D90DFE50131846268A86D17958E.description: Describe how scientific knowledge is subject to modification and refinement as new information challenges prevailing theories.

0C3FCE80DFE50131846168A86D17958E.description: Scientific progress is made by asking relevant questions and conducting careful investigations. F42820E0DFE401315CAC68A86D17958E.description: Draw a picture graph and a bar graph (with single-unit scale) to represent a data set with up to four categories. Solve simple put-together, take-apart, and compare problems using information presented in a bar graph.

F421A5E0DFE401315C9668A86D17958E.description: Use addition and subtraction within 100 to solve one- and two-step word problems involving situations of adding to, taking from, putting together, taking apart, and comparing, with unknowns in all positions, e.g., by using drawings and equations with a symbol for the unknown number to represent the problem.

F4215970DFE401315C9568A86D17958E.description: Represent and solve problems involving addition and subtraction.

F420BF50DFE401315C9368A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

F4206F80DFE401315C9268A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

F3FC34E0DFE401315C8E68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

F3FB9410DFE401315C8C68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary.
