comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
F3DDEF10DFE401315C6268A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

F3DDA3D0DFE401315C6168A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

F3DC4F40DFE401315C5D68A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

78ACC8BE75B348778675AD1E12C6761C.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

5DF003AEF8A145059138F102FCE1A2AD.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

document.title: District of Columbia Social Studies Standards

0EE238B0DFE5013188DD68A86D17958E.description: Students know the distinction between sound generalizations and misleading oversimplifications and stereotypes, such as the attribution of individual perspectives on historical events to entire demographic groups.

0EE1DE10DFE5013188DC68A86D17958E.description: Students detect the different historical points of view on historical events and determine the context in which the historical statements were made (the questions asked, sources used, and author's perspectives).

0EE16CA0DFE5013188DB68A86D17958E.description: Students assess the credibility and reliability of Internet sources.

0EE11E00DFE5013188DA68A86D17958E.description: Students assess the credibility of primary and secondary sources, draw sound conclusions from them, and cite sources appropriately.

0EE0DC90DFE5013188D968A86D17958E.description: Students distinguish relevant from irrelevant information, essential from incidental information, and verifiable from unverifiable information in historical narratives and stories.

0EE09920DFE5013188D868A86D17958E.description: Students distinguish fact from opinion in historical narratives and stories. They know facts are true statements because they are supported by reliable evidence and can cease to be facts if new evidence renders previous evidence wrong or unreliable.

0EE4AF70DFE5013188E568A86D17958E.description: Students frame questions that can be answered by historical study and research.

0EE456E0DFE5013188E468A86D17958E.description: Students interpret basic indicators of economic performance, and they conduct cost-benefit analyses of economic and political issues.

0EE40A10DFE5013188E368A86D17958E.description: Students recognize that interpretations of history are subject to change as new information is uncovered.

0EE3ACE0DFE5013188E268A86D17958E.description: Students recognize the role of chance, oversight, and error in history.

0EE351D0DFE5013188E168A86D17958E.description: Students explain the sources of historical continuity and how the combination of ideas and events explains the emergence of new patterns.

0EE30AF0DFE5013188E068A86D17958E.description: Students understand and distinguish cause, effect, sequence, and correlation in historical events, including the short-term causes or sparks from long-term causes.

0EE2C7B0DFE5013188DF68A86D17958E.description: Students explain the central issues and problems from the past, placing people and events in a matrix of time and place.

0EE28400DFE5013188DE68A86D17958E.description: Students construct various time lines of key events, people, and periods of the historical era they are studying.

0EE05600DFE5013188D768A86D17958E.description: Students explain how major events are related to one another in time.

0EDD8DA0DFE5013188CD68A86D17958E.description: Students use geographic knowledge and skills to analyze historical and contemporary issues.

0EDD4BB0DFE5013188CC68A86D17958E.description: Students apply the concept of region and their patterns of change to the study of the natural and human characteristics of places.

0EDFBDB0DFE5013188D568A86D17958E.description: Students explain the effects of interactions between humans and natural systems, including how humans depend on natural resources and adapt to and affect the natural environment.

0EDF7960DFE5013188D468A86D17958E.description: Students identify and explain the process of conflict and cooperation (political, economic, religious, etc.) among people in the contemporary world at local, national, regional, and international scales.

0EDF3330DFE5013188D368A86D17958E.description: Students assess how people's changing perceptions of geographic features have led to changes in human societies. They study current events to describe how people's experiences of diverse cultures and places influences their perceptions and viewpoints.

0EDEF180DFE5013188D268A86D17958E.description: Students study current events to identify the characteristics, distribution, and complexity of earth's cultural mosaics.

0EDEAF40DFE5013188D168A86D17958E.description: Students explain the historical migration of people, expansion and disintegration of empires, and the growth of economic systems. Identify spatial patterns in the movement of people, goods, and ideas throughout history.

0EDE6980DFE5013188D068A86D17958E.description: Students categorize characteristics of places in terms of whether they are physical (natural) or cultural (human). Know and apply the subcategories of physical and cultural characteristics when describing any given place.

0EDE1E30DFE5013188CF68A86D17958E.description: Students create maps that show the growth and decline of empires.

0EDDD210DFE5013188CE68A86D17958E.description: Students use a variety of maps and documents to identify physical and cultural features of neighborhoods, cities, states, and countries. Students interpret historical maps and charts.

0EDD0900DFE5013188CB68A86D17958E.description: Students explain Earth's grid system and are able to locate places using degrees of latitude and longitude.

0EDC69F0DFE5013188C968A86D17958E.description: Historical and Social Sciences Analysis Skills

0EF49420DFE50131891A68A86D17958E.description: Describe the foreign trade through the Silk Roads and the sea. (G, E)

0EF37740DFE50131891668A86D17958E.description: Explain China's reunification under the Qin Dynasty after the disunification of the warring states period. (P, M)

0EF332D0DFE50131891568A86D17958E.description: Summarize the development of Chinese cultural, economic, political, and social institutions and China's influence on other developing civilizations.

0EF2E950DFE50131891468A86D17958E.description: Describe the growth of trade and commerce in the ancient civilization. (G, E)

0EF29880DFE50131891368A86D17958E.description: Describe the achievements of the emperor Ashoka and his contribution to the expansion of Buddhism in the Indian subcontinent. (G, P, R)

0EF23890DFE50131891268A86D17958E.description: Describe the story and teachings of the Buddha.

0EF1F230DFE50131891168A86D17958E.description: Explain the growth of the Mauryan Empire in the context of rivalries among Indian states. (G, P)

0EF1AAC0DFE50131891068A86D17958E.description: Identify the major beliefs and practices of Brahmanism and how they evolved into early Hinduism. (G)

0EF16490DFE50131890F68A86D17958E.description: Explain the religious and cultural developments on the Indian Subcontinent during the Gangetic states and the Mauryan Dynasty.

0EFAD160DFE50131892F68A86D17958E.description: Describe how inner forces (including the rise of autonomous military powers, political corruption, unemployment, and economic and political instability) and external forces (shrinking trade, external attacks, and barbarian invasions) led to the disintegration of the Roman Empire. (P, E)

0EFD35B0DFE50131893768A86D17958E.description: Explain the spread and influence of the Roman alphabet and the Latin language, the use of Latin as the language of education for more than 1,000 years, and the role of Latin and Greek in scientific and academic vocabulary. (I)

0EFCEE70DFE50131893668A86D17958E.description: Describe the legacies of Roman art and architecture, technology and science (e.g., roads, bridges, arenas, baths, aqueducts, central heating, plumbing, and sanitation), literature and poetry, language, and law. (I)

0EFCA5F0DFE50131893568A86D17958E.description: Describe the circumstances that led to the spread of Christianity in Europe and other Roman territories. (G, R)

0EFC5B90DFE50131893468A86D17958E.description: Explain the origins of Christianity in the Jewish Messianic prophecies, the life and teachings of Jesus of Nazareth as described in the New Testament, and the contribution of St. Paul the Apostle to the definition and spread of Christian beliefs (e.g., belief in the Trinity, Resurrection, and Salvation). (R)

0EFC16B0DFE50131893368A86D17958E.description: Trace the migration of Jews around the Mediterranean region and the effects of their conflict with the Romans, including the Romans' restrictions on their right to live in Jerusalem. (G, P)

0EFBCD00DFE50131893268A86D17958E.description: Describe the influence of Julius Caesar and Augustus in Rome's transition from republic to empire. (P)

0EFB7320DFE50131893168A86D17958E.description: Explain the government of the Roman Republic and its significance (e.g., written constitution, separation of powers, rule of law, representative government, the notion of civic duty, and checks and balances) and why it was inadequate to administer Roman affairs by the end of the second century B.C. (B.C.E.). (P)

0EFB2160DFE50131893068A86D17958E.description: Describe the rise of the Roman Republic, including the importance of such mythical and historical figures as Aeneas, Romulus and Remus, Cincinnatus, Julius Caesar, and Cicero. (P)

0EFA8110DFE50131892E68A86D17958E.description: Locate and describe the major river system and the physical setting that supported the rise of this civilization and the expansion of its political power in the Mediterranean region and beyond through the use of currency and trade routes. (G, E)

0EFA34B0DFE50131892D68A86D17958E.description: Students analyze the geographic, political, religious, social, and economic structures during the development of Rome.

0EF78C40DFE50131892468A86D17958E.description: Identify key Greek figures in the arts and sciences (e.g., Hypatia, Hippocrates, Homer, Socrates, Sophocles, Plato, Pythagoras, Aristotle, Euclid, Euripedes, and Thucydides). (I)

0EF9E480DFE50131892C68A86D17958E.description: Trace the rise of Alexander the Great and the spread of Greek culture eastward and into Egypt. (P, S)

0EF99510DFE50131892B68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast life in Athens to Sparta, with emphasis on the daily life of women and children, the games and sports of the Olympiad, the education of youths, the trial of Socrates, and their roles in the Persian and Peloponnesian wars. (S, M)

0EF94DA0DFE50131892A68A86D17958E.description: Explain the significance of Greek mythology to the everyday life of people in the region and how Greek literature continues to permeate our literature and language today, drawing from Greek mythology and epics, such as Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, and from Aesop's Fables. (S, I)

0EF906A0DFE50131892968A86D17958E.description: Outline the founding, expansion, and political organization of the Persian Empire. (G, P)

0EF8C110DFE50131892868A86D17958E.description: State the key differences between Athenian, or direct democracy, and representative democracy. (P)

0EF87210DFE50131892768A86D17958E.description: Explain the democratic political concepts developed in ancient Greece (i.e., the polis, or city-state; civic participation and voting rights; legislative bodies; constitution writing; and rule of law). (P)

0EF82570DFE50131892668A86D17958E.description: Trace the transition from tyranny and oligarchy to early democratic forms of government and back to dictatorship in ancient Greece, including the significance of the invention of the idea of citizenship (e.g., from Pericles' Funeral Oration). (P)

0EF7CE80DFE50131892568A86D17958E.description: Describe the connections between geography and the development of city-states in the region of the Aegean Sea, including patterns of trade and commerce among Greek city-states and within the wider Mediterranean region. (G, E)

0EF67A80DFE50131892068A86D17958E.description: Describe the origins and significance of Judaism as the first monotheistic religion based on the concept of one God who sets down moral laws for humanity. (R)

0EF62690DFE50131891F68A86D17958E.description: Describe how the ideas of the Hebrew traditions are reflected in the moral and ethical traditions of Western civilization. (P, S)

0EF5CA50DFE50131891E68A86D17958E.description: Identify the sources of the ethical teachings and central beliefs of Judaism (the Hebrew Bible, the Commentaries): belief in God; emphasis on individual worth; personal responsibility; the rule of law; observance of law; and practice of the concepts of righteousness and justice; and importance of study. (P, R)

0EF57530DFE50131891D68A86D17958E.description: Describe the settlements and movements of Hebrew peoples, including the exodus and their movement to and from Egypt, and the significance of the exodus to the Jewish and other peoples. (G)

0EF52BB0DFE50131891C68A86D17958E.description: Identify the location of ancient Israel. (G)

0EF4D8E0DFE50131891B68A86D17958E.description: Students analyze the geographic, political, religious, social, and economic structures of the Ancient Hebrews.

0EF08EF0DFE50131890C68A86D17958E.description: Explain the religious traditions, including the worship of gods, goddesses, and Shamanistic rituals. (R)

0EF03ED0DFE50131890B68A86D17958E.description: Describe the creation of syllabic and hieroglyphic writing systems and an accurate calendar. (I)

0EEFF770DFE50131890A68A86D17958E.description: Explain its complex society that is governed by kings and priests with impressive ceremonial centers and artworks. (P, I)

0EEFAF00DFE50131890968A86D17958E.description: Describe the Olmecs' highly developed agricultural system. (G, E)

0EEF25F0DFE50131890768A86D17958E.description: Describe the development of a writing system based on ideographs of characters that symbolize conceptual ideas. (I)

0EEED5A0DFE50131890668A86D17958E.description: Describe the government in the Shang Dynasty, the development of social hierarchy and religious institutions, and Zhou political expansion. (P, S, R)

0EEE7A60DFE50131890568A86D17958E.description: Identify the uses and significance of bronze-making technology. (I, E)

0EEE2B10DFE50131890468A86D17958E.description: Describe the importance of the fertile valleys of the Huang He River to the location of early Chinese agricultural societies. (G)

0EEDD740DFE50131890368A86D17958E.description: Identify the location of the early Chinese agrarian societies that emerged. (G)

0EED79F0DFE50131890268A86D17958E.description: Students analyze the geographic, political, religious, social, and economic structures in Northern China.

0EED1980DFE50131890168A86D17958E.description: Identify the causes of the decline and collapse of this civilization (the first successive waves of Aryans invade portions of the subcontinent). (G, P, M)

0EECB260DFE50131890068A86D17958E.description: Describe the development of Sanskrit literature and its relationship to the development of the caste system. (R, I, S)

0EEC70C0DFE5013188FF68A86D17958E.description: Describe the Vedic hymns and the beginnings of what would later become Hinduism. (R)

0EEC2E60DFE5013188FE68A86D17958E.description: Identify the origins of Indus or Harappan civilization in the Indus Valley, and describe how the major river system and the physical setting supported the rise of the civilization. (G)

document.title: District of Columbia Physical Education Standards

12C6D7C0DFE50131907768A86D17958E.description: Accommodate individual differences in others' physical abilities when planning and participating in small-group activities.

12C63130DFE50131907568A86D17958E.description: Model support towards individuals of all ability levels and encourage others to be supportive and inclusive of all individuals.

12C5B420DFE50131907368A86D17958E.description: Act in a safe and healthy manner when confronted with negative peer pressure during physical activity.

12C574A0DFE50131907268A86D17958E.description: Abide by the decisions of the officials, accept the outcomes of the game and show appreciation towards participants.

comments: Modeling is best interpreted not as a collection of isolated topics but in relation to other standards. Making mathematical models is a Standard for Mathematical Practice, and specific modeling standards appear throughout the high school standards indicated by a star symbol (★). The star symbol sometimes appears on the heading for a group of standards; in that case, it should be understood to apply to all standards in that group.

comments: For example, we define 5<sup>1/3</sup> to be the cube root of 5 because we want (5<sup>1/3</sup>)³ = 5(<sup>1/3</sup>)³ to hold, so (5<sup>1/3</sup>)³ must equal 5.

F530CCD0DFE401315E5368A86D17958E.description: Extend the properties of exponents to rational exponents.

comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.
3FB493E0D1624BEE9AE78FE2C300BA5C.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.

8A80ECF302464AD7BB6F74923E899635.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

387DDC1169F94DE08985B09F8373443A.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.
comments: Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.

Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.
D2FDE329B4A54FAA9A29A8FBD520BA07.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.

document.title: District of Columbia Health Education Standards

1173A350DFE501318E5968A86D17958E.description: Design a purposeful personal health goal (e.g., healthy eating), evaluate how family and peers might support or hinder its achievement, and evaluate progress toward its achievement.

11730280DFE501318E5768A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate the ability to implement decision-making and goal-setting skills to enhance health.

1172C5C0DFE501318E5668A86D17958E.description: Analyze the possible causes of conflict in families, such as hurt feelings, jealousy, desire for independence, and privacy; and discuss possible solutions.

11724C90DFE501318E5468A86D17958E.description: Describe how to demonstrate care and concern toward ill and disabled persons in one's family, school, and community.

1171CD70DFE501318E5268A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate the ability to utilize interpersonal communication skills to enhance and protect health.

11718780DFE501318E5168A86D17958E.description: Analyze how societal messages from all media, including music, television programs, movies, advertising, and the Internet influence adolescents' perceptions and behaviors related to sexual activity, diet and body image, alcohol, drug use and violence.

1170FF10DFE501318E4F68A86D17958E.description: Explain that children learn most of their values from parents and other family members regarding important decisions about friends, sexual relationships, family, education, and a range of other issues.

11708190DFE501318E4D68A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate the ability to analyze the influence of family, culture, media, and technology on health and health behaviors.

11704190DFE501318E4C68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the short-term and long-term impacts of injuries on individuals and families, and develop strategies to reduce the incidence of such injuries.

116F69C0DFE501318E4968A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate the ability to apply self-management skills to enhance personal health and safety.

116F2930DFE501318E4868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate the ability to access valid mental health information from schools (e.g., the school psychologist) and community sources (e.g., a local mental health association).

116E9230DFE501318E4668A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate the ability to access and evaluate health information, products, and services.

116C0ED0DFE501318E3D68A86D17958E.description: Describe the signs and symptoms of substance abuse, factors that contribute to the abuse, stages that lead to dependency, and ways that family and friends can support a drug-free lifestyle.

116BB1A0DFE501318E3C68A86D17958E.description: Explain the physical, legal, financial, social, and psychological cost of the use, sale, and possession of illegal substances.

116A7020DFE501318E3768A86D17958E.description: Describe the benefits of a high-fiber diet (e.g., plenty of grains and fruit) to help food and waste products move through the body systems and prevent diseases.

116A2A80DFE501318E3668A86D17958E.description: Explain that a body mass index is a general indicator of overall fitness.

116B3290DFE501318E3A68A86D17958E.description: Assess the use of public health strategies to prevent diseases and improve health conditions.

116AF250DFE501318E3968A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast prevention and treatment of diseases and health conditions prevalent in adolescents, including obesity, diabetes, Lyme disease, STIs, and HIV/AIDS.

116D8D60DFE501318E4368A86D17958E.description: Describe the symptoms of, prognosis for, and ways to assist family members and friends who suffer from HIV/AIDS, including how to decrease acts of discrimination and stigma.

116D47C0DFE501318E4268A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the major symptoms of most STIs, indicating that many have no symptoms, and explain the serious consequences of going untreated.

116D09E0DFE501318E4168A86D17958E.description: Analyze the social, cultural, religious, and legal factors that influence the choice and use of contraception; and the choice to remain abstinent.

116CCC40DFE501318E4068A86D17958E.description: Differentiate healthy sexual behaviors (abstinence) from those that are harmful (date rape, sexual promiscuity); and identify barriers and supports.

116C8E70DFE501318E3F68A86D17958E.description: Describe short-term and long-term consequences of adolescent sexual activity, and the benefits of abstinence as the most effective means of contraception.

116E44F0DFE501318E4568A86D17958E.description: Describe the components, functions, and processes of the reproductive system, and key developmental and body changes during puberty, including menstruation.

1169A020DFE501318E3468A86D17958E.description: Analyze how unhealthy social environments influence personal health.

11692510DFE501318E3268A86D17958E.description: Assess the effects of peer pressure and offer -effective ways to cope with negative influences and -bullying.

1168E380DFE501318E3168A86D17958E.description: Explain how appropriate mental health care can help prevent, detect, and treat serious mental health problems, such as anxiety disorders, mood disorders, and suicide.

11684D00DFE501318E2F68A86D17958E.description: Students comprehend concepts related to health promotion and disease prevention.

document.title: District of Columbia Science Standards

0D577F10DFE5013186AE68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and describe important legislation enacted to protect environmental quality, such as the Clean Air Act and the Clean Water Act.

0D5708B0DFE5013186AD68A86D17958E.description: Identify natural Earth hazards, such as earthquakes and hurricanes, and identify the regions in which they occur, as well as the short-term and long-term effects on the environment and on people.

0D567F10DFE5013186AC68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the beneficial and harmful effects of an environmental stressor, such as herbicides and pesticides, on plants and animals. Give examples of secondary effects on other environmental components such as humans, water quality, and wildlife.

0D560AD0DFE5013186AB68A86D17958E.description: Understand and explain that waste management includes considerations of quantity, safety, degradability, and cost.

0D559D20DFE5013186AA68A86D17958E.description: Describe the historical and current methods of water management and recycling, including the waste treatment practices of landfills, incineration, reuse/recycle, and source reduction.

0D552C50DFE5013186A968A86D17958E.description: Describe sources of air and water pollution, and explain how air and water quality impact wildlife, vegetation, and human health.

0D54C8E0DFE5013186A868A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between natural pollution and pollution caused by humans, and give examples of each.

0D546360DFE5013186A768A86D17958E.description: Environmental quality is linked to natural and human-induced hazards, and the ability of science and technology to meet local, national, and global challenges. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D5390E0DFE5013186A568A86D17958E.description: Describe how the chemical elements that make up the molecules of living things pass through food webs and are combined and recombined in different ways.

0D5302F0DFE5013186A468A86D17958E.description: Illustrate the flow of energy through various trophic levels of food chains and food webs within an ecosystem. Describe how each link in a food web stores some energy in newly made structures and how much of the energy is dissipated into the environment as heat. Understand that a continual input of energy from sunlight is needed to keep the process going.

0D527B70DFE5013186A368A86D17958E.description: Describe how the energy derived from the sun is used by green plants to produce chemical energy in the form of sugars (photosynthesis), and this energy is transferred along a food chain from producers (plants) to consumers to decomposers.

0D5212B0DFE5013186A268A86D17958E.description: Understand and describe how layers of energy-rich organic material have been gradually turned into great coal beds and oil pools by the pressure of the overlying earth. Recognize that by burning these fossil fuels, people are passing stored energy back into the environment as heat and releasing large amounts of carbon dioxide.

0D51AC20DFE5013186A168A86D17958E.description: Explain the meaning of radiation, convection, and conduction (three mechanisms by which heat is transferred to, through, and out of the Earth's system).

0D513F80DFE5013186A068A86D17958E.description: Explain that energy cannot be created or destroyed; however, in many processes energy is transformed into the microscopic form called heat energy, that is, the energy of the disordered motion of atoms.

0D50D7B0DFE50131869F68A86D17958E.description: Energy and matter have multiple forms and can be changed from one form to another. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D500500DFE50131869D68A86D17958E.description: Explain the dynamics of oceanic currents, including upwelling, density, and deep water currents, the local Labrador Current and the Gulf Stream, and their relationship to global circulation within the marine environment and climate.

0D4F90E0DFE50131869C68A86D17958E.description: Collect, record, and interpret data from physical, chemical, and biological sources to evaluate the health of the Chesapeake Bay watershed and wetlands, and describe how the Bay supports a wide variety of plant and animal life that interact with other living and nonliving things.

0D4F2120DFE50131869B68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe how point and nonpoint source pollution can affect the health of a bay's watershed and wetlands.

0D4EA060DFE50131869A68A86D17958E.description: Describe the causes of, and the efforts to control, erosion in the Chesapeake Bay.

0D4E29B0DFE50131869968A86D17958E.description: Examine the dynamics of diverse ecosystems in watersheds and wetlands. Identify various organisms found in Potomac River wetlands and watersheds.

0D4DB720DFE50131869868A86D17958E.description: Describe how wetlands store excess water and filter sediments and excess nutrients.

0D4D2EB0DFE50131869768A86D17958E.description: Describe the physical characteristics of wetlands and watersheds and explain how water flows into and through a watershed (e.g., precipitation, aquifers, wells, porosity, permeability, water table, capillary water, and runoff).

0D4C9AD0DFE50131869668A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the processes of the hydrologic cycle, including evaporation, condensation, precipitation, surface runoff and groundwater percolation, infiltration, and transpiration.

0D4C3270DFE50131869568A86D17958E.description: Water is continually being recycled by the hydrologic cycle through the watersheds, oceans, and the atmosphere by processes such as evaporation, condensation, precipitation runoff, and infiltration. This life-giving cycle is continually and increasingly affected by human affairs. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D4B5CA0DFE50131869368A86D17958E.description: Understand and describe the concept of integrated natural resource management and the values of managing natural resources as an ecological unit.

0D4AEF40DFE50131869268A86D17958E.description: Identify specific tools and technologies used to adapt and alter environments and natural resources to meet human physical and cultural needs.

0D4A7F50DFE50131869168A86D17958E.description: Analyze the trade-offs among different fuels, such as how energy use contributes to the rising standard of living in the industrially developing nations, yet also leads to more rapid depletion of Earth's energy resources and to increased environmental risks associated with the use of fossil and nuclear fuels.

0D4A0410DFE50131869068A86D17958E.description: Recognize and describe the role of natural resources in providing the raw materials for an industrial society.

0D498D20DFE50131868F68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate knowledge of the distribution of natural resources in the United States and the world, and explain how natural resources influence relationships among nations.

0D491870DFE50131868E68A86D17958E.description: Give examples of the various forms and uses of fossil fuels and nuclear energy in our society, and describe alternative sources of energy provided by water, the atmosphere, and the sun.

0D48AA20DFE50131868D68A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between renewable and nonrenewable resources (including sources of energy), and compare and contrast the pros and cons of using nonrenewable resources.

0D483D90DFE50131868C68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that the Earth's resources for humans, such as fresh water, air, arable soil, and trees, are finite. Explain how these resources can be conserved through reduction, recycling, and reuse.

0D47CF20DFE50131868B68A86D17958E.description: Numerous Earth resources are used to sustain human affairs. The abundance and accessibility of these resources can influence their use. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D46F5F0DFE50131868968A86D17958E.description: Explain how the size and rate of growth of the human population in any location is affected by economic, political, religious, technological, and environmental factors.

0D4681D0DFE50131868868A86D17958E.description: Describe current and historical trends in human population growth in different regions of the world.

0D461C20DFE50131868768A86D17958E.description: Describe the effect of overpopulation (i.e., resource depletion and potential elimination of species), the role of predators in maintaining ecosystem stability, and methods of population management.

0D45B380DFE50131868668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and explain how fluctuations in population size and population growth rates are determined by such factors as birth rate, death rate, and migration rate.

0D4548E0DFE50131868568A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate how resources, such as food supply, the availability of water, and shelter influence populations.

0D44C9C0DFE50131868468A86D17958E.description: Explain the concept of carrying capacity.

0D4451F0DFE50131868368A86D17958E.description: The amount of life any environment can support is limited by the available energy, water, oxygen, and minerals, and by the ability of ecosystems to recycle organic materials from the remains of dead organisms. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D3FD350DFE50131867968A86D17958E.description: Explain how soil, water, and pest management are achieved in various agricultural systems (conventional and organic). Describe the tenets of sustainable agriculture.

0D3F3E90DFE50131867868A86D17958E.description: Describe the concepts of niche and habitat, and explain the effects of loss of habitat on a species' survivability.

0D3ECE30DFE50131867768A86D17958E.description: Describe how adaptations in physical structure or behavior may improve an organism's chance for survival and impact an ecosystem.

0D3E6470DFE50131867668A86D17958E.description: Explain the process of succession, both primary and secondary, in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems.

0D437C40DFE50131868168A86D17958E.description: Locate, identify, and explain the role of the major Earth biomes (e.g., grasslands, rainforests, arctic tundra, deserts) and discuss how the abiotic and biotic factors interact within these ecosystems.

0D430A50DFE50131868068A86D17958E.description: Describe the role of nitrogen and carbon cycles in the improvement of soils for agriculture.

0D429DC0DFE50131867F68A86D17958E.description: Explain how water, carbon, phosphorus, and nitrogen cycle between abiotic resources and organic matter in an ecosystem, and how oxygen cycles via photosynthesis and respiration. Diagram the cycling of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and water in an ecosystem.

0D4228D0DFE50131867E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and describe the difference between systems in equilibrium and systems in disequilibrium.

0D418300DFE50131867D68A86D17958E.description: Know that organisms may interact in a competitive or cooperative relationship, such as producer/consumer, predator/prey, parasite/hosts, or as symbionts, and explain how these interactions contribute to the stability of an ecosystem.

0D411710DFE50131867C68A86D17958E.description: Understand and explain that ecosystems tend to have cyclic fluctuations around a state of rough equilibrium, and change results from shifts in climate, natural causes, human activity, or when a new species or non-native species appears.

0D40AE30DFE50131867B68A86D17958E.description: Understand and describe that if a disaster such as flood or fire occurs, the damaged ecosystem is likely to recover in stages that eventually results in a system similar to the original one.

0D4041D0DFE50131867A68A86D17958E.description: Know and describe how ecosystems can be reasonably stable over hundreds or thousands of years.

0D3DFD10DFE50131867568A86D17958E.description: Explain that biodiversity is the sum total of different kinds of organisms in a given ecological community or system, and is affected by alterations of habitats.

0D3D8BD0DFE50131867468A86D17958E.description: Stability in an ecosystem is a balance between competing effects. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D3CA980DFE50131867268A86D17958E.description: Recognize and explain that in evolutionary change, the present arises from the materials of the past and in ways that can be explained (e.g., formation of soil from rocks and dead organic matter).

0D3C1C90DFE50131867168A86D17958E.description: Describe how the global environment is affected by national policies and practices relating to energy use, waste disposal, ecological management, manufacturing, and population growth.

0D3BA400DFE50131867068A86D17958E.description: Explain how environmental change in one part of the world can impact seemingly distant places and systems.

0D3B42C0DFE50131866F68A86D17958E.description: Understand and explain that human beings are part of Earth's ecosystems, and that human activities can, deliberately or inadvertently, alter ecosystems.

0D3ADE80DFE50131866E68A86D17958E.description: The environment is a system of interdependent components affected by natural phenomena and human activity. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D30F130DFE50131866468A86D17958E.description: Observe natural phenomena and analyze their location, sequence, or time intervals (e.g., relative ages of rocks and succession of species in an ecosystem).

0D307740DFE50131866368A86D17958E.description: Apply mathematical relationships involving linear and quadratic equations, simple trigonometric relationships, exponential growth and decay laws, and logarithmic relationships to scientific situations.

0D2FDB30DFE50131866268A86D17958E.description: Analyze situations and solve problems that require combining concepts from more than one topic area of science and applying these concepts.

0D2F6EA0DFE50131866168A86D17958E.description: Formulate and revise explanations using logic and evidence.

0D2F04B0DFE50131866068A86D17958E.description: Select and use appropriate tools and technology to perform tests, collect data, analyze relationships, and display data. (The focus is on manual graphing, interpreting graphs, and mastery of metric measurements and units, with supplementary use of computers and electronic data gathering when appropriate.)

0D3A0320DFE50131866C68A86D17958E.description: Identify discrepant results and possible sources of error or uncontrolled conditions.

0D3997E0DFE50131866B68A86D17958E.description: Identify and communicate the sources of error (random and systematic) inherent in an experiment.

0D392ED0DFE50131866A68A86D17958E.description: Use hypotheses to choose what data to pay attention to and what additional data to seek, and to guide the interpretation of the data.

0D38BFF0DFE50131866968A86D17958E.description: Plan and conduct scientific investigations to explore new phenomena, to check on previous results, to verify or falsify the prediction of a theory, and to use a crucial experiment to discriminate between competing theories.

0D384950DFE50131866868A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between a conjecture (guess), a hypothesis, and a theory as these terms are used in science.

0D37D310DFE50131866768A86D17958E.description: Recognize the use and limitations of models and theories as scientific representations of reality.

0D376350DFE50131866668A86D17958E.description: Recognize the cumulative nature of scientific evidence.

0D36EC00DFE50131866568A86D17958E.description: Know that scientists cannot always control all conditions to obtain evidence, and when they are unable to do so for ethical or practical reasons, they try to observe as wide a range of natural occurrences as possible so as to be able to discern patterns.

0D2E96B0DFE50131865F68A86D17958E.description: Know the elements of scientific methodology (identification of a problem, hypothesis formulation and prediction, performance of experimental tests, analysis of data, falsification, developing conclusions, reporting results) and be able to use a sequence of those elements to solve a problem or test a hypothesis. Also, understand the limitations of any single scientific method (sequence of elements) in solving problems.

0D2E2C10DFE50131865E68A86D17958E.description: Scientific progress is made by asking relevant questions and conducting careful investigations. As a basis for understanding this concept, and to address the content in this grade, students should develop their own questions and perform investigations. Students:

0D2941D0DFE50131865368A86D17958E.description: Explain that if lighter atoms are fused to form atoms closer to iron, or heavier atoms are split to form atoms closer to iron, there is a mass loss. Explain that according to the principle of conservation of mass-energy, this mass loss must be accompanied by a release of energy according to Einstein's mass-energy equation. Know that because c² is such a large number (≈ 9 x 10<sup>20</sup> m²/s²), a small mass loss leads to a large energy release.

0D2CE6F0DFE50131865B68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate how the mass of a stable nucleus is always less than the sum of the masses of the protons and neutrons comprising it. Know this is especially true of the elements in the region of the periodic table around iron (26 protons, 30 neutrons) and generally less so of elements with greater or lesser atomic numbers than this.

0D2C7D50DFE50131865A68A86D17958E.description: Explain the principle of special relativity and some of its implications, including the mass-energy equivalence equation, E = mc².

0D2C1970DFE50131865968A86D17958E.description: Describe the Heisenberg uncertainty principle and how it arises naturally from the fact that matter has wavelike properties.

0D2BB2B0DFE50131865868A86D17958E.description: Describe Louis de Broglie's insight into the wave-particle duality.

0D2ACDD0DFE50131865668A86D17958E.description: Describe Niels Bohr's model of the atom, its electron arrangement, and the correlation with the hydrogen spectrum.

0D2A4640DFE50131865568A86D17958E.description: Explain how the mass of a neutron or a proton is about 2,000 times greater than the mass of an electron.

0D29B8C0DFE50131865468A86D17958E.description: Recognize that the nucleus, although it contains nearly all of the mass of the atom, occupies less of the atom than the proportion of the solar system occupied by the sun.

0D28D5A0DFE50131865268A86D17958E.description: Explain how the research of Marie Curie, later in collaboration with her husband, Pierre, spurred the study of radioactivity, and led to the realization that one kind of atom may change into another kind, and so atoms must be made up of smaller parts. Rutherford, Geiger, and Marsden found these parts to be small, dense nuclei surrounded by much larger clouds of electrons.

0D285D60DFE50131865168A86D17958E.description: Nuclear processes are those in which an atomic nucleus changes; they include radioactive decay of naturally occurring and manmade isotopes and nuclear fission and fusion processes. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D2454B0DFE50131864868A86D17958E.description: Explain the operation of electric generators, motors, and transformers in terms of Ampère's law and Faraday's law.

0D237730DFE50131864668A86D17958E.description: Determine the direction of a magnetic field produced by a current flowing in a straight wire and in a coil (use the right-hand rule).

0D230FB0DFE50131864568A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving Ohm's law in series and parallel circuits.

0D22A6F0DFE50131864468A86D17958E.description: Predict the current in simple direct current electric circuits constructed from batteries, wires, and resistors.

0D223BA0DFE50131864368A86D17958E.description: Calculate the power dissipated in any resistive circuit element by using Joule's law in the appropriate form.

0D21D5E0DFE50131864268A86D17958E.description: Describe the advantages to alternating current over direct current for power distribution networks.

0D216AE0DFE50131864168A86D17958E.description: Explain the magnitude of the force on a moving particle with charge, q, in a magnetic field, B, is qvB sin θ , where v is the speed of the particle, B is the magnitude of the magnetic field, and θ is the angle between the directions of v and B.

0D20EBF0DFE50131864068A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain how various wavelengths in the electromagnetic spectrum have many useful applications such as radio, TV, microwave radars and ovens, cellular telephones, infrared detectors, optical cables, and X-ray machines.

0D206220DFE50131863F68A86D17958E.description: Explain how electric and magnetic fields are vector fields that contain energy.

0D1FFAA0DFE50131863E68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate how changing magnetic fields produce electric fields (Faraday's law), thereby inducing currents in nearby conductors.

0D1F9010DFE50131863D68A86D17958E.description: Explain that magnetic materials and electric currents (moving electric charges) are sources of magnetic fields, and they experience forces due to magnetic fields of other sources.

0D278990DFE50131864F68A86D17958E.description: Explain the properties of transistors and their role in electric circuits.

0D272090DFE50131864E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that plasmas, the fourth state of matter, contain ions and free electrons in such numbers that they are electrically neutral overall, but the many free charges they contain make them good conductors of electricity. Recognize that the glowing gas in a neon light is plasma.

0D26B980DFE50131864D68A86D17958E.description: Explain that any resistive element in a DC circuit transforms electrical energy into thermal energy at a rate (power) given by Joule's law, P = IV, which in an ohmic element has the special form P = I²R = V²/R.

0D264430DFE50131864C68A86D17958E.description: Give evidence that metals are almost all good electrical conductors; nevertheless, they do offer some resistance (friction) to the flow of current. Know that the greater the potential difference between the ends of the conductor, the greater the current; the greater the resistance, the less the current. Know, too, that for most metals and many other conductors, the current is determined by Ohm's law, V = IR. A conductor that conforms to this rule is called an ohmic conductor.

0D25C280DFE50131864B68A86D17958E.description: Explain that a source of electromotive force (EMF) is any device (such as a battery) that furnishes a steady potential between two terminals. Know that if a conducting loop is supplied between the two terminals, an electric current, I, will flow. Know, too, that current is measured in the number of coulombs per second that flow past a given point in the conductor, I = q/t, and that the unit of electric current is the ampere (A); 1 A = 1 C/s.

0D254570DFE50131864A68A86D17958E.description: Know that most materials fall into one of two categories: electrical conductors, through which an electric charge can flow easily under the influence of an electric field, and electrical insulators (or dielectrics), through which a charge cannot flow easily.

0D24DAC0DFE50131864968A86D17958E.description: Calculate electric potential (voltage): When a charge, q, is pulled through a field, E, over a distance, d, work, W = qd, is done. The work done per unit charge, W/q, is the electric potential, V. Thus, V = Ed. The unit of electric potential is the volt, V; 1 V = 1 N(m/C).

0D23E000DFE50131864768A86D17958E.description: Explain that around any point charge, Q, there is an electric field, E = k Q/r². Know that another charge, q, located in this field will experience a force of magnitude F = qE and that the unit of electric field is the newton per coulomb (N/C).

0D1F1E00DFE50131863C68A86D17958E.description: Determine how an electric charge, q, exists in two kinds: positive (+) and negative (–). Know that like charges repel each other, and unlike charges attract each other with an electrostatic force whose magnitude is given by Coulomb's law, F = kq<sub>1</sub>q<sub>2</sub> /r<sub>12</sub>² , where k is a constant. Know that the unit of electric charge is the coulomb (C).

0D1E96E0DFE50131863B68A86D17958E.description: The phenomena that fall into the categories known as electrostatics and electromagnetism are due respectively to the behavior of stationary and moving charged particles. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D1A3FD0DFE50131863168A86D17958E.description: Identify electromagnetic radiation as a wave phenomenon after observing interference, diffraction, and polarization of such radiation.

0D19B8C0DFE50131863068A86D17958E.description: Use Snell's law to calculate refraction angles and analyze the properties of simple optical systems.

0D1917A0DFE50131862F68A86D17958E.description: Identify the phenomena of interference (beats), diffraction, refraction, the Doppler effect, and polarization, and that these are characteristic wave properties.

0D18ABA0DFE50131862E68A86D17958E.description: Identify transverse and longitudinal waves in mechanical media such as springs, ropes, and the Earth (seismic waves).

0D184170DFE50131862D68A86D17958E.description: Describe waves in terms of their fundamental characteristics of speed, v; wavelength, λ; frequency, f; or period, T, and amplitude, A, and the relationships among them. For example, fλ= v, f = 1/T. Solve problems involving wavelength, frequency, and wave speed.

0D17D650DFE50131862C68A86D17958E.description: Explain that when a light ray passes from air into a transparent substance, such as glass, having index of refraction, n, it is refracted through an angle given by Snell's law, n sin θ<sub>i</sub> = n sin θ<sub>r</sub> , where θ<sub>i</sub> is the angle of incidence of the ray and θ<sub>r</sub> is the angle of refraction.

0D176A10DFE50131862B68A86D17958E.description: Predict and explain how light travels through a transparent medium at a speed, v, less than c. The index of refraction of the medium is defined to be n = c/v.

0D1DC630DFE50131863968A86D17958E.description: Explain how Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell used Ampère's law and Faraday's law to predict the existence of electromagnetic waves and predict that light was just such a wave. Know that these predictions were confirmed by Heinrich Hertz, whose confirmations thus made possible the fields of radio, TV, and many other technologies.

0D1D5860DFE50131863868A86D17958E.description: Know that radio waves, visible light, and X-rays are different wavelength bands in the spectrum of electromagnetic waves whose speed, c, in a vacuum is approximately 3x10<sup>8</sup> m/s (186,000 miles/second).

0D1CE8A0DFE50131863768A86D17958E.description: Differentiate electromagnetic waves from mechanical waves. (Electromagnetic waves are not disturbances in a medium; rather, such waves are a combination of a varying electric field and a varying magnetic field, each of which, in varying, gives rise to the other. Electromagnetic waves can therefore propagate in empty space.)

0D1C7EB0DFE50131863668A86D17958E.description: Describe that sound in a fluid medium is a longitudinal wave whose speed depends on the properties of the medium in which it propagates.

0D1C0F10DFE50131863568A86D17958E.description: Explain that longitudinal waves can propagate in any medium, but transverse waves can propagate only in solids.

0D1B98D0DFE50131863468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate how standing waves on a stretched string are the result of the superposition of the wave moving away from the source and the wave reflected back from the other end of the string.

0D1B1780DFE50131863368A86D17958E.description: Explain that waves conform to the superposition principle: Any number of waves can pass through the same point at the same time, and the amplitude, A, of the resulting wave at that point at any time is the sum of the amplitudes of the superposed waves. Use the principle of superposition to describe the interference effects arising from propagation of several waves through the same medium.

0D1AAD50DFE50131863268A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe that a mechanical wave is a disturbance in a medium. For example, a sound wave in air is a slight variation in the pressure of the air surrounding a vibrating object, such as a bell.

0D170600DFE50131862A68A86D17958E.description: Explain that waves carry energy from one place to another.

0D169B40DFE50131862968A86D17958E.description: Waves carry energy from place to place without the transfer of matter. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D120C60DFE50131861F68A86D17958E.description: Describe a refrigerator as a heat engine operated "in reverse."

0D1189F0DFE50131861E68A86D17958E.description: Given heat input and work output data, calculate the efficiency of a real heat engine or human being (e.g., a well-trained athlete working out for eight hours may consume 7,000 kcal of food (20 MJ) a day and do work at the rate of 1/4 HP (187 W) over an eight-hour period during that day. What is his or her thermodynamic efficiency?).

0D1121E0DFE50131861D68A86D17958E.description: Use the second-law-based Carnot efficiency formula, η = (T<sub>in</sub> – T<sub>out</sub>)/T<sub>in</sub>, to calculate the maximum possible efficiency for a heat engine.

0D10A100DFE50131861C68A86D17958E.description: Use a p-V diagram to graph simple thermodynamic processes for an ideal gas (for which pV = nRT); for example, an isothermal process is described by a hyperbola, an isobaric process by a horizontal straight line, and an isochoric process by a vertical straight line.

0D1030D0DFE50131861B68A86D17958E.description: Explain the law, "the entropy of a closed system will always either increase or remain the same," based on the statistics of the behavior of immense numbers of atoms or molecules that governs all closed systems (second law of thermodynamics).

0D0FB7D0DFE50131861A68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that entropy is a quantity that measures the order or disorder of a system and that it is larger for a more disordered system.

0D0F4C00DFE50131861968A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that in all internal energy transfers, the overall effect is that the energy is spread out uniformly.

0D0ED300DFE50131861868A86D17958E.description: Explain that all objects emit electromagnetic radiation at a rate that rises very rapidly with their temperature. As a result, know that a warmer body that is in the line of sight with a cooler one will transfer net energy to it, cooling down while the cooler object warms up.

0D0E5AC0DFE50131861768A86D17958E.description: Explain the process of convection: Because the density of fluids varies with temperature, the warmer parts of a fluid tend to move into and mix with the cooler parts, resulting in a transfer of heat energy from place to place.

0D15CB90DFE50131862768A86D17958E.description: Describe that when two objects at different temperatures are in contact, heat energy always flows from the object at a higher temperature to the object at a lower temperature by the process of conduction until the two are at the same (intermediate) temperature.

0D1558A0DFE50131862668A86D17958E.description: Explain that on the everyday Celsius scale, 0° C = 273.15 K, which is very close to the freezing point of pure water at atmospheric pressure, 100° C = 373.15 K is very close to the temperature at which pure water boils at a pressure of 1 atmosphere.

0D14F000DFE50131862568A86D17958E.description: Recognize that the absolute temperature is measured in kelvins (K); 0 K is the temperature at which the average kinetic energy of the microscopic parts of the system is an irreducible minimum.

0D147E90DFE50131862468A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe how the absolute temperature of an object is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the thermal motion of its microscopic parts.

0D140940DFE50131862368A86D17958E.description: Describe how in everyday practice, temperature is measured with a thermometer, a device containing a part that has a thermometric parameter (a quantity that changes with temperature).

0D138280DFE50131862268A86D17958E.description: Explain that thermal energy (commonly called heat) consists of random motion and the vibrations and rotations of atoms, molecules, or ions.
