0D12EA50DFE50131862168A86D17958E.description: Describe and measure the work, W, done by a heat engine as the difference between the heat flow, Q<sub>in</sub>, into the engine at high temperature and the heat flow, Q<sub>out</sub>, out at a lower temperature: W = Q<sub>in</sub> – Q<sub>out</sub>.

0D127DD0DFE50131862068A86D17958E.description: Describe and measure that the change U in the internal energy of a system is equal to the sum of the heat flow, Q, into the system and the work, W, done on the system: U = Q + W (first law of thermodynamics).

0D0DC7F0DFE50131861668A86D17958E.description: Recognize that heat flow and work are two forms of energy transfer between a system and its surroundings.

0D0D3AF0DFE50131861568A86D17958E.description: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; however, in many processes energy is transformed into the microscopic form called heat energy, that is, the energy of the disordered motion of atoms. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D0C68F0DFE50131861368A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving a confined, isothermal gas using Boyle's law.

0D0BFA80DFE50131861268A86D17958E.description: Understand that Bernoulli's principle, p + 1/2ρv² = constant, is a consequence of conservation of mechanical energy applied to a moving, incompressible fluid, and apply it accurately.

0D0B91F0DFE50131861168A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving floating and sinking bodies using Archimedes' principle.

0D0B2230DFE50131861068A86D17958E.description: Identify that the pressure in an incompressible fluid (e.g., water) is a function of density, r; depth, y; and gravitational acceleration, g.

0D0AB460DFE50131860F68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that a change in the pressure at any point in a fluid is accompanied by an equal change at all other points (Pascal's principle).

0D0A4190DFE50131860E68A86D17958E.description: Explain that the buoyant force on an object in a fluid is an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it has displaced.

0D09D3C0DFE50131860D68A86D17958E.description: All objects experience a buoyant force when immersed in a fluid. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0D057C50DFE50131860368A86D17958E.description: Calculate the changes in motion of two bodies in one-dimensional elastic collisions in which both energy and momentum are conserved.

0D050790DFE50131860268A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving perfectly inelastic collisions in one dimension using the principle of conservation of momentum.

0D0490B0DFE50131860168A86D17958E.description: Calculate the momentum of an object as the product p = mv.

0D041A60DFE50131860068A86D17958E.description: Apply the law of conservation of mechanical energy to simple systems.

0D039FF0DFE5013185FF68A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving conservation of energy in simple systems such as that of falling objects.

0D08D420DFE50131860B68A86D17958E.description: Calculate changes in gravitational potential energy, U, due to elevation changes, h, near the Earth, using the relation U = mgh.

0D086C60DFE50131860A68A86D17958E.description: Calculate kinetic energy using the formula K = 1/2 mv².

0D080280DFE50131860968A86D17958E.description: Describe the conditions under which each conservation law applies.

0D079370DFE50131860868A86D17958E.description: Identify the joule, J, as the SI unit for work and energy; the unit for power is the watt, W; and the unit for impulse and momentum is the kg(m/s).

0D0726B0DFE50131860768A86D17958E.description: Define power as the rate at which work is done: P = W/t.

0D06B3C0DFE50131860668A86D17958E.description: Explain that momentum is a separately conserved quantity that is defined in one dimension as p = mv. Know that the momentum of a system can be changed only by application of an external impulse, J = Ft. Know that the total momentum of a closed system cannot change, regardless of the interchange of momentum within it.

0D064E80DFE50131860568A86D17958E.description: Describe how kinetic energy can be transformed into potential energy and vice versa (e.g., a bouncing ball).

0D05E5E0DFE50131860468A86D17958E.description: Describe how an unbalanced force, F, acting on an object over time, t, results in a change, p = Ft, in the object's momentum.

0D032FA0DFE5013185FE68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that when a net force, F, acts through a distance, x, on an object of mass, m, which is initially at rest, work, W = Fx, is done on the object; the object acquires a velocity, v, and a kinetic energy, K = 1/2 mv² = W = Fx.

0D02C3C0DFE5013185FD68A86D17958E.description: The laws of conservation of energy and momentum provide independent approaches to predicting and describing the motion of objects. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CFE0C20DFE5013185F368A86D17958E.description: Create and interpret graphs of speed versus time and the position and speed of an object undergoing constant acceleration.

0CFD9D10DFE5013185F268A86D17958E.description: Solve problems in circular motion, using the formula for centripetal acceleration in the following form: a = v²/r.

0CFD3380DFE5013185F168A86D17958E.description: Use and mathematically manipulate appropriate scalar and vector quantities (F, v, a, r, m, g) to solve kinematics and dynamics problems in one and two dimensions.

0CFCC560DFE5013185F068A86D17958E.description: Apply the law F = ma to solve one-dimensional motion problems involving constant forces (Newton's second law).

0D01A980DFE5013185FB68A86D17958E.description: Solve kinematics problems involving constant speed and average speed.

0D013260DFE5013185FA68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that a motion at constant speed in a circle requires a force that is always directed toward the center of the circle.

0D00BE70DFE5013185F968A86D17958E.description: Explain how a force acting on an object perpendicular to the direction of its motion causes it to change direction but not speed.

0D005790DFE5013185F868A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain how the Newtonian model — the three laws of motion plus the law of gravitation — makes it possible to account for such diverse phenomena as tides, the orbits of the planets and moons, the motion of falling objects, and Earth's equatorial bulge.

0CFFE6A0DFE5013185F768A86D17958E.description: Explain that every object in the universe exerts an attractive force on every other object. Know the magnitude of the force is proportional to the product of the masses of the two objects and inversely proportional to the distance between them: F = G m<sub>1</sub>m<sub>2</sub>/r².

0CFF68F0DFE5013185F668A86D17958E.description: Explain that Newton's laws of motion are not universally applicable, but they provide very good approximations, unless an object is moving close to the speed of light, has a very large mass, or is small enough that quantum effects are important.

0CFEF6F0DFE5013185F568A86D17958E.description: Predict and explain how when one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object always exerts a force of equal magnitude but of opposite direction and force back on the first: F<sub>1 on 2</sub> = –F<sub>2 on 1</sub> (Newton's third law).

0CFE79F0DFE5013185F468A86D17958E.description: Explain that only when a net force is applied to an object will its motion change; that is, it will accelerate (according to Newton's second law, F = ma).

0CFC2210DFE5013185EF68A86D17958E.description: Explain that when the net force on an object is zero, no acceleration occurs; thus, a moving object continues to move at a constant speed in the same direction, or, if at rest, it remains at rest (Newton's first law).

0CFBA840DFE5013185EE68A86D17958E.description: Newton's laws of motion and gravitation describe and predict the motion of a vast variety of objects. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CF74C20DFE5013185E468A86D17958E.description: Recognize and deal with the implications of statistical variability in experiments, and explain the need for controls in experiments.

0CF6DE20DFE5013185E368A86D17958E.description: Apply mathematical relationships involving linear and quadratic equations, simple trigonometric relationships, exponential growth and decay laws, and logarithmic relationships to scientific situations.

0CF66760DFE5013185E268A86D17958E.description: Analyze situations and solve problems that require combining concepts from more than one topic area of science and applying those concepts.

0CF601A0DFE5013185E168A86D17958E.description: Formulate and revise explanations using logic and evidence.

0CF59730DFE5013185E068A86D17958E.description: Select and use appropriate tools and technology to perform tests, collect data, analyze relationships, and display data. (The focus is on manual graphing, interpreting graphs, and mastery of metric measurements and units, with supplementary use of computers and electronic data gathering when appropriate.)

0CFAD3F0DFE5013185EC68A86D17958E.description: Identify discrepant results and identify possible sources of error or uncontrolled conditions.

0CFA5CB0DFE5013185EB68A86D17958E.description: Identify and communicate the sources of error inherent in an experiment.

0CF9DF90DFE5013185EA68A86D17958E.description: Use hypotheses to choose what data to pay attention to and what additional data to seek and to guide the interpretation of the data.

0CF960A0DFE5013185E968A86D17958E.description: Plan and conduct scientific investigations to explore new phenomena, to check on previous results, to verify or falsify the prediction of a theory, and to use a crucial experiment to discriminate between competing theories.

0CF8F7A0DFE5013185E868A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between a conjecture (guess), hypothesis, and theory as these terms are used in science.

0CF88CF0DFE5013185E768A86D17958E.description: Recognize the use and limitations of models and theories as scientific representations of reality.

0CF81F00DFE5013185E668A86D17958E.description: Recognize the cumulative nature of scientific evidence.

0CF7B4F0DFE5013185E568A86D17958E.description: Know that scientists cannot always control all conditions when obtaining evidence, and when they are unable to do so for ethical or practical reasons, they try to observe as wide a range of natural occurrences as possible so as to be able to discern patterns.

0CF53040DFE5013185DF68A86D17958E.description: Know the elements of scientific methodology (identification of a problem, hypothesis formulation and prediction, performance of experimental tests, analysis of data, falsification, developing conclusions, reporting results) and be able to use a sequence of those elements to solve a problem or test a hypothesis. Also, understand the limitations of any single scientific method (sequence of elements) in solving problems.

0CF4C2A0DFE5013185DE68A86D17958E.description: Scientific progress is made by asking relevant questions and conducting careful investigations. As a basis for understanding this concept, and to address the content in this grade, students should develop their own questions and perform investigations. Students:

0CF38200DFE5013185DB68A86D17958E.description: Convert between chemical formulas, structural formulas, and names of simple common organic compounds (hydrocarbons, proteins, fats, carbohydrates).

0CF30DE0DFE5013185DA68A86D17958E.description: Explain that amino acids are the building blocks of proteins.

0CF28690DFE5013185D968A86D17958E.description: Describe how large molecules (polymers) such as proteins, nucleic acids, and starch are formed by repetitive combinations of simple subunits (monomers).

0CF21000DFE5013185D868A86D17958E.description: Explain how the bonding characteristics of carbon lead to a large variety of structures ranging from simple hydrocarbons to complex polymers and biological molecules.

0CF19900DFE5013185D768A86D17958E.description: The bonding characteristics of carbon lead to the possibility of many different molecules of many sizes, shapes, and chemical properties. This provides the biochemical basis of life. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CF08BD0DFE5013185D568A86D17958E.description: Use Hess's law to determine the heat of a reaction and to calculate enthalpy change in a reaction.

0CF023A0DFE5013185D468A86D17958E.description: Solve problems involving heat flow and temperature changes, using given values of specific heat and latent heat of phase change.

0CEFB950DFE5013185D368A86D17958E.description: Explain how energy is released when a material condenses or freezes and is absorbed when a material evaporates or melts.

0CEF4F60DFE5013185D268A86D17958E.description: Determine and explain that chemical processes release (exothermic) or absorb (endothermic) thermal energy.

0CEEDF80DFE5013185D168A86D17958E.description: Describe the concepts of temperature and heat flow in terms of the motion and energy of molecules (or atoms).

0CEE78B0DFE5013185D068A86D17958E.description: Energy is exchanged or transformed in all chemical reactions and physical changes of matter. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CED8F10DFE5013185CE68A86D17958E.description: Use titration data to calculate the concentration of an unknown solution.

0CED1440DFE5013185CD68A86D17958E.description: Prepare a specified volume of a solution of given molarity.

0CECA6B0DFE5013185CC68A86D17958E.description: Calculate the theoretical freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation of an ideal solution as a function of solute concentration.

0CEC3BA0DFE5013185CB68A86D17958E.description: Determine the concentration of a solution in terms of molarity and molality.

0CEBC640DFE5013185CA68A86D17958E.description: Calculate the concentration units of solutions such as molarity, percent by mass or volume, parts per million (ppm), or parts per billion (ppb).

0CEB45A0DFE5013185C968A86D17958E.description: Explain that, for a closed system at constant temperature and pressure, a solid in contact with its saturated solution may reach dynamic equilibrium when the rate of solid dissolving equals the rate of solid precipitating.

0CEADCA0DFE5013185C868A86D17958E.description: Predict and describe how the temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area of solids affect the dissolving process.

0CEA0E60DFE5013185C668A86D17958E.description: Solutions are mixtures of two or more substances that are homogeneous on the molecular level. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CE93B50DFE5013185C468A86D17958E.description: Write the equilibrium expression for a given reaction and calculate the equilibrium constant for the reaction from given concentration data.

0CE8CCA0DFE5013185C368A86D17958E.description: Use LeChâtelier's principle to predict the effect of changes in concentration, temperature, volume, and pressure on a system at equilibrium.

0CE83DA0DFE5013185C268A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe the role of activation energy and catalysts in a chemical reaction.

0CE7AC10DFE5013185C168A86D17958E.description: Explain why rates of reaction are dependent on the frequency of collisions, energy of collisions, and orientation of colliding molecules.

0CE74850DFE5013185C068A86D17958E.description: Describe the factors that affect the rate of a chemical reaction (temperature, concentration) and the factors that can cause a shift in equilibrium (concentration, pressure, volume, temperature).

0CE6DE20DFE5013185BF68A86D17958E.description: Explain how equilibrium is established when forward- and reverse-reaction rates are equal.

0CE66F90DFE5013185BE68A86D17958E.description: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic process at the molecular level. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CE4EF50DFE5013185BB68A86D17958E.description: Apply Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures.

0CE48430DFE5013185BA68A86D17958E.description: Solve problems using the Ideal Gas law, pV = nRT, and the combined gas law, p<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub>= p<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>.

0CE41260DFE5013185B968A86D17958E.description: Apply the relationship between pressure and volume at constant temperature (Boyle's law, pV = constant at constant temperature and number of moles), and between volume and temperature (Charles' law or Gay-Lussac's law, V/T = constant at constant pressure and number of moles) and the relationship between pressure and temperature that follows from them.

0CE3AB50DFE5013185B868A86D17958E.description: Explain the kinetic molecular theory and use it to explain changes in gas volumes, pressure, and temperature.

0CE34400DFE5013185B768A86D17958E.description: The behavior of gases can be explained by the kinetic molecular theory. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CDEE060DFE5013185AD68A86D17958E.description: Describe the effect of changes in reactant concentration, changes in temperature, the surface area of solids, and the presence of catalysts on reaction rates.

0CDE77B0DFE5013185AC68A86D17958E.description: Use changes in oxidation states to recognize electron transfer reactions, and identify the substance(s) losing and gaining electrons in an electron transfer reaction.

0CE26B60DFE5013185B568A86D17958E.description: Define oxidation and reduction and oxidizing and reducing agents.

0CE204C0DFE5013185B468A86D17958E.description: Use Avogadro's law to make mass-volume calculations for simple chemical reactions.

0CE19BF0DFE5013185B368A86D17958E.description: Convert the mass of a molecular substance to moles, number of particles, or volume of gas at standard temperature and pressure.

0CE12FC0DFE5013185B268A86D17958E.description: Determine molar mass of a molecule given its chemical formula and a table of atomic masses.

0CE0B4C0DFE5013185B168A86D17958E.description: Calculate the percent of composition by mass of a compound when given the formula.

0CE03DB0DFE5013185B068A86D17958E.description: Calculate the masses of reactants and products in a chemical reaction from the mass of one of the reactants or products and the relevant atomic or molecular masses).

0CDFB960DFE5013185AF68A86D17958E.description: Classify reactions of various types such as single and double replacement, synthesis, decomposition, and acid/base neutralization.

0CDF4E60DFE5013185AE68A86D17958E.description: Describe chemical reactions by writing balanced chemical equations and balancing redox equations.

0CDE1110DFE5013185AB68A86D17958E.description: Name substances and describe their reactions based on Lavoisier's system and explain how this system contributed to the rapid growth of chemistry by enabling scientists everywhere to share their findings about chemical reactions with one another without ambiguity.

0CDDA5E0DFE5013185AA68A86D17958E.description: The microscopic conservation of atoms in chemical reactions implies the macroscopic principle of conservation of matter and the ability to calculate the mass of products and reactants. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CD8FC40DFE5013185A068A86D17958E.description: Identify solids held together by London dispersion forces or hydrogen bonding.

0CD89110DFE50131859F68A86D17958E.description: Predict the formulas of ionic compounds based on the charges on the ions.

0CDCC6D0DFE5013185A868A86D17958E.description: Predict the chemical formulas based on the number of valence electrons.

0CDC4330DFE5013185A768A86D17958E.description: Predict the geometry and polarity of simple molecules, and explain how these influence the intermolecular attraction between molecules.

0CDBD480DFE5013185A668A86D17958E.description: Draw Lewis dot structures for atoms, molecules, and polyatomic ions.

0CDB5450DFE5013185A568A86D17958E.description: Explain that in solids, particles can only vibrate around fixed positions, but in liquids, they can slide randomly past one another, and in gases, they are free to move between collisions with one another.

0CDADBD0DFE5013185A468A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and explain that chemical bonds between identical or similar atoms in molecules such as H<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub>, CH<sub>4</sub>, NH<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>O and many large biological molecules tend to be covalent; some of these molecules may have hydrogen bonds between them. In addition, molecules have other forms of intermolecular bonds, such as London dispersion forces and/or dipole bonding.

0CDA6DD0DFE5013185A368A86D17958E.description: Explain the hydrogen bond as an intermolecular attraction that can exist between a hydrogen atom on one molecule and an electronegative element like fluorine, oxygen, or nitrogen on another molecule.

0CD9D600DFE5013185A268A86D17958E.description: Recognize names and chemical formulas for simple molecular compounds (such as N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>), ionic compounds, including those with polyatomic ions, simple organic compounds, and acids, including oxyacids (such as HClO<sub>4</sub>).

0CD96730DFE5013185A168A86D17958E.description: Predict and explain how atoms combine to form molecules by sharing electrons to form covalent or metallic bonds, or by transferring electrons to form ionic bonds.

0CD824B0DFE50131859E68A86D17958E.description: Explain how Arrhenius' discovery of the nature of ionic solutions contributed to the understanding of a broad class of chemical reactions.

0CD7B6E0DFE50131859D68A86D17958E.description: The enormous variety of physical, chemical, and biological properties of matter depends upon the ability of atoms to form bonds. This ability results from the electrostatic forces between electrons and protons and between atoms and molecules. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CD6E690DFE50131859B68A86D17958E.description: Explain that the half-life of a radioactive element is the time it takes for the radioactive element to lose one-half its radioactivity, and calculate the amount of radioactive substance remaining after an integral number of half-lives have passed.

0CD659E0DFE50131859A68A86D17958E.description: Predict and explain that the alpha, beta, and gamma radiation produced in radioactive decay produce different amounts and kinds of damage in matter and have different ranges of penetration.

0CD5C7A0DFE50131859968A86D17958E.description: Describe the process of radioactive decay as the spontaneous breakdown of certain unstable (radioactive) elements into new elements (radioactive or not) through the spontaneous emission by the nucleus of alpha or beta particles, or gamma radiation.

0CD55C00DFE50131859868A86D17958E.description: Know that many naturally occurring isotopes of elements are radioactive, as are isotopes formed in nuclear reactions.

0CD4EEC0DFE50131859768A86D17958E.description: Describe that the energy release per gram of material is roughly six orders of magnitude larger in nuclear fusion or fission reactions than in chemical reactions. Know that a small decrease in mass produces a large amount of energy in nuclear reactions as well as in chemical reactions, but the mass change in chemical reactions is negligibly small.

0CD45C20DFE50131859668A86D17958E.description: Explain how protons and neutrons in the nucleus are held together by strong nuclear forces that just balance the electromagnetic repulsion between the protons in a stable nucleus.

0CD3CBD0DFE50131859568A86D17958E.description: Nuclear processes are those in which an atomic nucleus changes; they include radioactive decay of naturally occurring and man-made isotopes and nuclear fission and fusion processes. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CD2FAF0DFE50131859368A86D17958E.description: Use an element's location in the periodic table to determine its number of valence electrons, and predict what stable ion or ions an element is likely to form in reacting with other specified elements.

0CD292A0DFE50131859268A86D17958E.description: Use the periodic table to compare trends in periodic properties, such as ionization energy, electronegativity, electron affinity, and relative size of atoms and ions.

0CD21F90DFE50131859168A86D17958E.description: Relate the position of an element in the periodic table and its reactivity with other elements to its quantum electron configuration.

0CD1AE30DFE50131859068A86D17958E.description: Relate an element's position on the periodic table to its atomic number (number of protons).

0CD13560DFE50131858F68A86D17958E.description: Periodicity of physical and chemical properties relates to atomic structure and led to the development of the periodic table. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CD0AD50DFE50131858E68A86D17958E.description: Describe that spectral lines correspond to photons with a frequency related to the energy spacing between levels by using Planck's formula (E = hv) in calculations.

0CD03950DFE50131858D68A86D17958E.description: Describe that spectral lines are the result of transitions of electrons between energy levels.

0CCFCF10DFE50131858C68A86D17958E.description: Construct a diagram and describe the number and arrangement of subatomic particles within an atom or ion.

0CCF60B0DFE50131858B68A86D17958E.description: Explain the historical importance of the Bohr model of the atom.

0CCEEFD0DFE50131858A68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and explain how chemical properties depend almost entirely on the configuration of the outer electron shell, which in turn depends on the proton number.

0CCE78E0DFE50131858968A86D17958E.description: Explain Dalton's atomic theory in terms of the laws of conservation of matter, definite composition, and multiple proportions.

0CCE1350DFE50131858868A86D17958E.description: Detail the development of atomic theory from the ancient Greeks to the present (Democritus, Dalton, Rutherford, Bohr, quantum theory).

0CCDAAA0DFE50131858768A86D17958E.description: An atom is a discrete unit. The atomic model can help us to understand the interaction of elements and compounds observed on a macroscopic scale. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CCCC780DFE50131858568A86D17958E.description: Explain the Brønsted-Lowry theory of acids and bases: An acid is a hydrogen ion (proton) donor, and a base is a hydrogen ion (proton) acceptor.

0CCC5E30DFE50131858468A86D17958E.description: Explain the Arrhenius theory of acids and bases: An acid donates hydrogen ions (hydronium) and a base donates hydroxide ions to a water solution.

0CCBF430DFE50131858368A86D17958E.description: Describe the observable properties of acids, bases, and salt solutions.

0CCB84E0DFE50131858268A86D17958E.description: Illustrate and explain the pH scale to characterize acid and base solutions: Neutral solutions have pH 7, acids are less than 7, and bases are greater than 7.

0CCB11D0DFE50131858168A86D17958E.description: Define pH as the negative of the logarithm of the hydrogen (hydronium) ion concentration, and calculate pH from concentration data.

0CCA9C50DFE50131858068A86D17958E.description: Explain that strong acids (and bases) fully dissociate and that weak acids (and bases) partially dissociate.

0CCA33E0DFE50131857F68A86D17958E.description: Acids, bases, and salts are three classes of compounds that form ions in water solutions. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CC93EE0DFE50131857D68A86D17958E.description: Classify substances as metal or nonmetal, ionic or molecular, acid or base, and organic or inorganic, using formulas and laboratory investigations.

0CC8C530DFE50131857C68A86D17958E.description: Write equations that describe chemical changes and reactions.

0CC83880DFE50131857B68A86D17958E.description: Infer and explain that physical properties of substances, such as melting points, boiling points, and solubility, are due to the strength of their various types of bonds (interatomic, intermolecular, or ionic).

0CC7C950DFE50131857A68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between the three familiar states of matter (solid, liquid, and gas) in terms of energy, particle motion, and phase transitions, and describe what a plasma is.

0CC76140DFE50131857968A86D17958E.description: Know the concept of a mole in terms of number of particles, mass, and the volume of an ideal gas at specified conditions of temperature and pressure.

0CC6F990DFE50131857868A86D17958E.description: Determine the definitions of and use properties such as mass, volume, temperature, density, melting point, boiling point, conductivity, solubility, and color to differentiate between types of matter.

0CC69160DFE50131857768A86D17958E.description: Investigate and classify properties of matter, including density, melting point, boiling point, and solubility.

0CC623F0DFE50131857668A86D17958E.description: Physical and chemical properties can be used to classify and describe matter. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CC1B270DFE50131856C68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and deal with the implications of statistical variability in experiments, and explain the need for controls in experiments.

0CC14860DFE50131856B68A86D17958E.description: Apply mathematical relationships involving linear and quadratic equations, exponential growth and decay laws, and logarithmic relationships to scientific situations.

0CC0D7B0DFE50131856A68A86D17958E.description: Analyze situations and solve problems that require combining concepts from more than one topic area of science and applying these concepts.

0CC06190DFE50131856968A86D17958E.description: Formulate and revise explanations using logic and evidence.

0CBFF470DFE50131856868A86D17958E.description: Select and use appropriate tools and technology to perform tests, collect data, analyze relationships, and display data. (The focus is on manual graphing, interpreting graphs, and mastery of metric measurements and units, with supplementary use of computers and electronic data gathering when appropriate.)

0CC532D0DFE50131857468A86D17958E.description: Identify discrepant results and possible sources of error or uncontrolled conditions.

0CC4BA60DFE50131857368A86D17958E.description: Identify and communicate the sources of error inherent in an experiment.

0CC43C70DFE50131857268A86D17958E.description: Use hypotheses to choose what data to pay attention to and what additional data to seek, and to guide the interpretation of the data.

0CC3BED0DFE50131857168A86D17958E.description: Plan and conduct scientific investigations to explore new phenomena, to check on previous results, to verify or falsify the prediction of a theory, and to use a crucial experiment to discriminate between competing theories.

0CC35790DFE50131857068A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between a conjecture (guess), a hypothesis, and a theory as these terms are used in science.

0CC2EBF0DFE50131856F68A86D17958E.description: Recognize the use and limitations of models and theories as scientific representations of reality.

0CC28070DFE50131856E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize the cumulative nature of scientific evidence.

0CC216C0DFE50131856D68A86D17958E.description: Know that scientists cannot always control all conditions to obtain evidence, and when they are unable to do so for ethical or practical reasons, they try to observe as wide a range of natural occurrences as possible so as to be able to discern patterns.

0CBF7BB0DFE50131856768A86D17958E.description: Know the elements of scientific methodology (identification of a problem, hypothesis formulation and prediction, performance of experimental tests, analysis of data, falsification, developing conclusions, reporting results) and be able to use a sequence of those elements to solve a problem or test a hypothesis. Also, understand the limitations of any single scientific method (sequence of elements) in solving problems.

0CBF0750DFE50131856668A86D17958E.description: Scientific progress is made by asking relevant questions and conducting careful investigations. As a basis for understanding this concept, and to address the content in this grade, students should develop their own questions and perform investigations. Students:

0CB9EAF0DFE50131855B68A86D17958E.description: Assess the method for monitoring and safeguarding water quality, including local waterways such as the Anacostia and Potomac rivers, and know that macroinvertebrates can be early warning signs of decreasing water quality.

0CBD9EE0DFE50131856368A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe how point and nonpoint source pollution can affect the health of a bay's watershed and wetlands.

0CBCFA20DFE50131856268A86D17958E.description: Using ecological studies, explain distinct relationships and differences between urban environments and other environmental systems.

0CBC8D50DFE50131856168A86D17958E.description: Explain how layers of energy-rich organic material, mostly of plant origin, have been gradually turned into great coal beds and oil pools by the pressure of the overlying Earth and its internal heat.

0CBC2430DFE50131856068A86D17958E.description: Explain that ecosystems tend to have cyclic fluctuations around a state of rough equilibrium, and change results from shifts in climate, natural causes, human activity, or when a new species or non-native species appears.

0CBBB9C0DFE50131855F68A86D17958E.description: Describe how ecosystems can be reasonably stable over hundreds or thousands of years.

0CBB4C30DFE50131855E68A86D17958E.description: Describe how the physical or chemical environment may influence the rate, extent, and nature of the way organisms develop within ecosystems.

0CBAD6F0DFE50131855D68A86D17958E.description: Explore and explain how changes in population size have an impact on the ecological balance of a community and how to analyze the effects.

0CBA5F70DFE50131855C68A86D17958E.description: Describe how factors in an ecosystem, such as the availability of energy, water, oxygen, and minerals, and the ability to recycle the residue of dead organic materials, cause fluctuations in population sizes.

0CB97C00DFE50131855A68A86D17958E.description: Illustrate and describe the cycles of biotic and abiotic factors (matter, nutrients, energy) in an ecosystem.

0CB909E0DFE50131855968A86D17958E.description: Stability in an ecosystem is a balance between competing effects. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CB836E0DFE50131855768A86D17958E.description: Investigate and cite specific examples of how the mammalian immune system is designed to protect against microscopic organisms and foreign (or nonself) substances from outside the body and against some aberrant (e.g., cancer) cells that arise within.

0CB7B8B0DFE50131855668A86D17958E.description: Describe that the nervous and endocrine systems maintain overall regulation of optimal conditions within the body by chemical communication.

0CB72A70DFE50131855568A86D17958E.description: Explain how the nervous system mediates communication between different parts of the body and the environment.

0CB6C080DFE50131855468A86D17958E.description: Analyze the complementary activity of major body systems, such as how the respiratory and circulatory systems provide cells with oxygen and nutrients, and remove toxic waste products such as carbon dioxide.

0CB65610DFE50131855368A86D17958E.description: Explain the major systems of the mammalian body (digestive, respiratory, reproductive, circulatory, excretory, nervous, endocrine, integumentary, immune, skeletal, and muscular) and how they interact with each other.

0CB5D320DFE50131855268A86D17958E.description: As a result of the coordinated structures and functions of organ systems, the internal environment of the mammalian body remains relatively stable (homeostatic), despite changes in the outside environment. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CB4E8A0DFE50131855068A86D17958E.description: Recognize that plants have a greater problem with "unpredictable environments" because they cannot seek shelter as many animals can.

0CB48050DFE50131854F68A86D17958E.description: Describe that plants have broad patterns of behavior that have evolved to ensure reproductive success, including co-evolution with animals that distribute a plant's pollen and seeds.

0CB414F0DFE50131854E68A86D17958E.description: Explain that during the process of photosynthesis, plants release oxygen into the air.

0CB3B170DFE50131854D68A86D17958E.description: Explain the photosynthesis process: Plants make simple sugars and other molecules in their leaves, and chlorophyll found in the leaves can make the food and nutrients that the plant can use from carbon dioxide, water, nutrients, and energy from sunlight.

0CB34F30DFE50131854C68A86D17958E.description: Know that about 250,000 species of flowering plants have been identified.

0CB2EA80DFE50131854B68A86D17958E.description: Identify the roles of plants in the ecosystem: Plants make food and oxygen, provide habitats for animals, make and preserve soil, and provide thousands of useful products for people (e.g., energy, medicines, paper, resins).

0CB28200DFE50131854A68A86D17958E.description: Describe the structure and function of roots, leaves, flowers, and stems of plants.

0CB20FB0DFE50131854968A86D17958E.description: Plants are essential to animal life on Earth. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CADAC40DFE50131853F68A86D17958E.description: Explain that evolution builds on what already exists, so the more variety there is, the more there can be in the future.

0CB14470DFE50131854768A86D17958E.description: Explain how biological evolution is also supported by the discovery that the genetic code found in DNA is the same for almost all organisms.

0CB0D7E0DFE50131854668A86D17958E.description: Explain Gregor Mendel's identification of what we now call "genes," how they are sorted in reproduction, and how this led to an understanding of the mechanism of heredity. Understand how the integration of his concept of heredity and the concept of natural selection has led to the modern model of speciation and evolution.

0CB044E0DFE50131854568A86D17958E.description: Research and explain that Darwin argued that only biologically inherited characteristics could be passed on to offspring, and that some of these characteristics would be different from the average and advantageous in surviving and reproducing; over generations, accumulation of these inherited advantages would lead to a new species.

0CAFDB40DFE50131854468A86D17958E.description: Explain that prior to the theory first offered by Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace, the universal belief was that all known species had been created de novo at about the same time and had remained unchanged.

0CAF7230DFE50131854368A86D17958E.description: Describe how life on Earth is thought to have begun as one or a few simple one-celled organisms about 3.5 billion years ago, and that during the first 2 billion years, only single-cell microorganisms existed. Know that, once cells with nuclei developed about a billion years ago, increasingly complex multicellular organisms could evolve.

0CAF07A0DFE50131854268A86D17958E.description: Explain that biological diversity, episodic speciation, and mass extinction are depicted in the fossil record, comparative anatomy, and other evidence.

0CAE9500DFE50131854168A86D17958E.description: Research and explain how natural selection provides a mechanism for evolution and leads to organisms that are optimally suited for survival in particular environments.

0CAE24B0DFE50131854068A86D17958E.description: Explain how a large diversity of species increases the chance that at least some living things will survive in the face of large or even catastrophic changes in the environment.

0CAD32A0DFE50131853E68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain how molecular evidence reinforces and confirms the fossil, anatomical, behavioral, and embryological evidence for evolution, and provides additional detail about the sequence in which various lines of descent branched off from one another.

0CACB230DFE50131853D68A86D17958E.description: Evolution and biodiversity are the result of genetic changes that occur in constantly changing environments. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CA87A30DFE50131853368A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe how a biological classification system that implies degrees of kinship between organisms or species can be deduced from the similarity of their nucleotide (DNA) or amino acids (protein) sequences. Know that such systems often match the completely independent classification systems based on anatomical similarities.

0CA80B80DFE50131853268A86D17958E.description: Explain how the actions of genes, patterns of inheritance, and the reproduction of cells and organisms account for the continuity of life.

0CA793E0DFE50131853168A86D17958E.description: Explain that genetic variation can occur from such processes as crossing over, jumping genes, and deletion and duplication of genes.

0CA72900DFE50131853068A86D17958E.description: Explain how the sorting and recombination of genes in sexual reproduction result in a vast variety of potential allele combinations in the offspring of any two parents.

0CABD630DFE50131853B68A86D17958E.description: Understand and explain that specialization of cells is almost always due to different patterns of gene expression, rather than differences in the genes themselves.

0CAB6AC0DFE50131853A68A86D17958E.description: Explain the mechanisms of genetic mutations and chromosomal recombinations, and when and how they are passed on to offspring.

0CAB00C0DFE50131853968A86D17958E.description: Understand and describe how inserting, deleting, or substituting short stretches of DNA alters a gene. Recognize that changes (mutations) in the DNA sequence in or near a specific gene may (or may not) affect the sequence of amino acids in the encoded protein or the expression of the gene.

0CAA9C60DFE50131853868A86D17958E.description: Explain how the genetic information in DNA molecules provides the basic form of instructions for assembling protein molecules and that this mechanism is the same for all life forms.

0CAA33B0DFE50131853768A86D17958E.description: Explain the flow of information is usually from DNA to RNA, and then to protein.

0CA9C970DFE50131853668A86D17958E.description: Know every species has its own characteristic DNA sequence.

0CA95E20DFE50131853568A86D17958E.description: Explain how hereditary information is passed from parents to offspring in the form of "genes," which are long stretches of DNA consisting of sequences of nucleotides. Explain that in eukaryotes, the genes are contained in chromosomes, which are bodies made up of DNA and various proteins.

0CA8EC70DFE50131853468A86D17958E.description: Describe how the discovery of the structure of DNA by James D. Watson and Francis Crick made it possible to interpret the genetic code on the basis of a nucleotide sequence. Know the important contribution of Rosalind Franklin's data to this discovery (i.e., the careful X-ray crystallography on DNA that provided Watson and Crick the clue they needed to build the correct structure).

0CA69AD0DFE50131852F68A86D17958E.description: Research and explain the genetic basis for Gregor Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment.

0CA60B80DFE50131852E68A86D17958E.description: Genes are a set of instructions encoded in the DNA sequence of each organism that specify the sequence of amino acids in proteins characteristic of that organism. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0CA18CC0DFE50131852468A86D17958E.description: Describe that all organisms begin their life cycles as a single cell, and in multicellular organisms the products of mitosis of the original zygote form the embryonic body.

0CA11D80DFE50131852368A86D17958E.description: Explain how zygotes are produced in the fertilization process.

0CA09170DFE50131852268A86D17958E.description: Differentiate between the functions of mitosis and meiosis. Mitosis is a process by which a cell divides into each of two daughter cells, each of which has the same number of chromosomes as the original cell. Meiosis is a process of cell division in organisms that reproduce sexually, during which the nucleus divides eventually into four nuclei, each of which contains half the usual number of chromosomes.

0CA018F0DFE50131852168A86D17958E.description: Recognize and describe that cellular respiration is important for the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is the basic energy source for cell metabolism.

0C9FB180DFE50131852068A86D17958E.description: Explain why communication and/or interaction are required between cells to coordinate their diverse activities.

0C9F3C30DFE50131851F68A86D17958E.description: Explain how cell activity in a multicellular plant or animal can be affected by molecules from other parts of the organism.

0C9EC320DFE50131851E68A86D17958E.description: Describe that all growth and development of organisms is a consequence of an increase in cell number, size, and/or products.

0C9E4D80DFE50131851D68A86D17958E.description: Explain that complex interactions among the different kinds of molecules in the cell cause distinct cycles of activities, such as growth and division.

0CA53500DFE50131852C68A86D17958E.description: Explain that a complex network of proteins provides organization and shape to cells.

0CA4C750DFE50131852B68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that most cells function best within a narrow range of temperature and pH; extreme changes usually harm cells by modifying the structure of their macromolecules and, therefore, some of their functions.

0CA45BB0DFE50131852A68A86D17958E.description: Describe that the work of the cell is carried out by structures made up of many different types of large (macro) molecules that it assembles, such as proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, and nucleic acids.

0CA3E680DFE50131852968A86D17958E.description: Explain that some structures in the eukaryotic cell, such as mitochondria, and in plants, such as chloroplasts, have apparently evolved by endosymbiosis (one organism living inside another, to the advantage of both) with early prokaryotes.

0CA36E70DFE50131852868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and explain that cell membranes act as highly selective permeable barriers to penetration of substances by diffusion or active transport.

0CA2D910DFE50131852768A86D17958E.description: Describe the organelles that plant and animal cells have in common (e.g., ribosomes, golgi bodies, endoplasmic reticulum) and some that differ (e.g., only plant cells have chloroplasts and cell walls).

0CA26BB0DFE50131852668A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe that within the cell are specialized parts for the transport of materials, energy capture and release, waste disposal, and motion of the whole cell or of its parts.

0CA1F3E0DFE50131852568A86D17958E.description: Understand the function of cellular organelles and how the organelles work together in cellular activities (e.g., enzyme secretion from the pancreas).

0C9DDE60DFE50131851C68A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the general anatomy and constituents of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and their distinguishing features: Prokaryotic cells do not have a nucleus, and eukaryotic cells do. Know that prokaryotic organisms are classified in the Eubacteria and Archaebacteria Kingdoms and that organisms in the other four kingdoms have eukaryotic cells.

0C9D78F0DFE50131851B68A86D17958E.description: All living things are composed of cells. All the fundamental life processes of a cell are either chemical reactions or molecular interactions. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C9CAA90DFE50131851968A86D17958E.description: Explain the hierarchical organization of living things from least complex to most complex (subatomic, atomic, molecular, cellular, tissue, organs, organ system, organism, population, community, ecosystem, and biosphere).

0C9C4670DFE50131851868A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain the role of enzymatic catalysis in biochemical processes.

0C9BE030DFE50131851768A86D17958E.description: Know that living things have many different kinds of molecules, including small ones such as water; midsize ones such as sugars, amino acids, and nucleotides; and large ones such as starches, proteins, and DNA.

0C9B6700DFE50131851668A86D17958E.description: Know that living things are made of molecules largely consisting of carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur.

0C9AD5D0DFE50131851568A86D17958E.description: Describe the central role of carbon in the chemistry of living things because of its ability to combine in many ways with itself and other elements.

0C9A6E70DFE50131851468A86D17958E.description: Describe the structure and unique properties of water and its importance to living things.

0C9A0740DFE50131851368A86D17958E.description: Describe basic atomic structure using simplified Bohr diagrams to understand the basis of chemical bonding in covalent and ionic bonds.

0C999680DFE50131851268A86D17958E.description: Living things are made of atoms bonded together to form molecules, some of the most important of which are large and contain carbon (i.e., "organic" compounds). As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C94FBC0DFE50131850868A86D17958E.description: Recognize and deal with the implications of statistical variability in experiments, and explain the need for controls in experiments.

0C949560DFE50131850768A86D17958E.description: Explain that science discoveries can have both positive and negative implications, involve different decisions regarding ethics and allocation of resources (e.g., organ transplants, stem cell research, forest management, and land use).

0C942DC0DFE50131850668A86D17958E.description: Observe natural phenomena and analyze their location, sequence, or time intervals (e.g., relative ages of rocks and succession of species in an ecosystem).

0C93BF60DFE50131850568A86D17958E.description: Apply mathematical relationships involving linear and quadratic equations, simple trigonometric relationships, exponential growth and decay laws, and logarithmic relationships to scientific situations.

0C9358D0DFE50131850468A86D17958E.description: Analyze situations and solve problems that require combining concepts from more than one topic area of science and applying these concepts.

0C92F150DFE50131850368A86D17958E.description: Formulate and revise explanations using logic and evidence.

0C928410DFE50131850268A86D17958E.description: Select and use appropriate tools and technology to perform tests, collect data, analyze relationships, and display data. (The focus is on manual graphing, interpreting graphs, and mastery of metric measurements and units, with supplementary use of computers and electronic data gathering when appropriate.)

0C98CC20DFE50131851068A86D17958E.description: Identify discrepant results and possible sources of error or uncontrolled conditions.

0C986860DFE50131850F68A86D17958E.description: Identify and communicate the sources of error (random and systematic) inherent in an experiment.

0C97FB20DFE50131850E68A86D17958E.description: Use hypotheses to choose what data to pay attention to and what additional data to seek, and to guide the interpretation of the data.

0C977D70DFE50131850D68A86D17958E.description: Plan and conduct scientific investigations to explore new phenomena, to check on previous results, to verify or falsify the prediction of a theory, and to use a crucial experiment to discriminate between competing theories.

0C9712D0DFE50131850C68A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between a conjecture (guess), a hypothesis, and a theory as these terms are used in science.

0C9691D0DFE50131850B68A86D17958E.description: Recognize the use and limitations of models and theories as scientific representations of reality.

0C9611F0DFE50131850A68A86D17958E.description: Recognize the cumulative nature of scientific evidence.

0C9583C0DFE50131850968A86D17958E.description: Know that scientists cannot always control all conditions to obtain evidence, and when they are unable to do so for ethical or practical reasons, they try to observe as wide a range of natural occurrences as possible so as to be able to discern patterns.

0C920E60DFE50131850168A86D17958E.description: Know the elements of scientific methodology (identification of a problem, hypothesis formulation and prediction, performance of experimental tests, analysis of data, falsification, developing conclusions, reporting results) and be able to use a sequence of those elements to solve a problem or test a hypothesis. Also, understand the limitations of any single scientific method (sequence of elements) in solving problems.

0C919820DFE50131850068A86D17958E.description: Scientific progress is made by asking relevant questions and conducting careful investigations. As a basis for understanding this concept, and to address the content in this grade, students should develop their own questions and perform investigations. Students:

0C901E40DFE5013184FD68A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain how rivers and streams are dynamic systems that erode and transport sediment, change their course, and flood their banks in natural and recurring patterns.

0C8F7740DFE5013184FC68A86D17958E.description: Explain why, how, and where earthquakes occur, how they are located and measured, and the ways that they can cause damage (directly by shaking and secondarily by fire, tsunami, landsliding, or liquefaction).

0C8F0B50DFE5013184FB68A86D17958E.description: Explain the relationship between convection currents and the motion of the lithospheric plates.

0C8E9B40DFE5013184FA68A86D17958E.description: Trace the development of a lithospheric plate from its growing margin at a divergent boundary (mid-ocean ridge) to its destructive margin at a convergent boundary (subduction zone).

0C8E35A0DFE5013184F968A86D17958E.description: Analyze the evidence that supports the hypothesis of movement of the plates (from paleomagnetism, paleontology, paleoclimate, and the continuity of geological structure and stratigraphy across ocean basins).

0C8DCF40DFE5013184F868A86D17958E.description: Explain the work of Alfred Wegener, including reintroduction of the idea of moving continents, and the skepticism with which his theories were first received and why.

0C8D5F90DFE5013184F768A86D17958E.description: Plate tectonics operating over geologic time has altered the features of land, sea, and mountains on the Earth's surface. As the basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C8C7500DFE5013184F568A86D17958E.description: Trace the evolution of the solid Earth in terms of the major geologic eras.

0C8C00F0DFE5013184F468A86D17958E.description: Recognize and explain geologic evidence, including fossils and radioactive dating, that indicates the age of the Earth.

0C8B9830DFE5013184F368A86D17958E.description: Explain the absolute and relative dating methods used to measure geologic time.

0C8B2720DFE5013184F268A86D17958E.description: Illustrate the various processes and rock types that are involved in the rock cycle, and describe how the total amount of material stays the same throughout formation, weathering, sedimentation, and reformation.

0C8AC150DFE5013184F168A86D17958E.description: Differentiate among the processes of weathering, erosion, transportation of materials, deposition, and soil formation.

0C8A5510DFE5013184F068A86D17958E.description: Rocks and minerals are continually being modified within the rock cycle. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C896DE0DFE5013184EE68A86D17958E.description: Identify and explain the mechanisms that cause and modify the production of tides, such as the gravitational attraction of the moon, the sun, and coastal topography.

0C8907B0DFE5013184ED68A86D17958E.description: Describe the processes of the hydrologic cycle, including evaporation, condensation, precipitation, surface runoff, and groundwater percolation, infiltration, and transpiration.

0C889EA0DFE5013184EC68A86D17958E.description: Explain how water flows into and through a watershed (e.g., properly use terms precipitation, aquifers, wells, porosity, permeability, water table, capillary water, and runoff).

0C882BA0DFE5013184EB68A86D17958E.description: Water is continually being recycled by the hydrologic cycle through the watersheds, oceans, and the atmosphere by processes such as evaporation, condensation, precipitation runoff, and infiltration. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C83B010DFE5013184E168A86D17958E.description: Read and interpret space weather data (solar flares, geomagnetic storms, solar wind).

0C8345D0DFE5013184E068A86D17958E.description: Use computer models to predict the effects of increasing greenhouse gases on climate for the planet as a whole and for specific regions.

0C82D5E0DFE5013184DF68A86D17958E.description: Use weather maps and other tools to forecast weather conditions.

0C826500DFE5013184DE68A86D17958E.description: Explain that the oceans store carbon dioxide mostly as dissolved HCO<sub>3</sub>– and CaCO<sub>3</sub> as precipitate or biogenic carbonate deposits.

0C81FBD0DFE5013184DD68A86D17958E.description: Describe the nitrogen and carbon cycles and their roles in the improvement of soils for agriculture.

0C8745F0DFE5013184E968A86D17958E.description: Describe the development and dynamics of climatic changes over time corresponding to changes in the Earth's geography (plate tectonics/continental drift), orbital parameters (the Milankovitch cycles), and atmospheric composition.

0C86D3F0DFE5013184E868A86D17958E.description: Explain special properties of water (e.g., high specific and latent heats) and the influence of large bodies of water and the water cycle on heat transport and, therefore, weather and climate.

0C866C70DFE5013184E768A86D17958E.description: Investigate and identify the causes and effects of severe weather.

0C85F990DFE5013184E668A86D17958E.description: Determine the origins, life cycles, behavior, and prediction of weather systems.

0C859290DFE5013184E568A86D17958E.description: Explain the possible mechanisms and effects of atmospheric changes brought on by things such as acid rain, smoke, volcanic dust, greenhouse gases, and ozone depletion.

0C8529B0DFE5013184E468A86D17958E.description: Explain the effects on climate of latitude, elevation, and topography, as well as proximity to large bodies of water and cold or warm ocean currents.

0C84B610DFE5013184E368A86D17958E.description: Describe the main agents of erosion: water, waves, wind, ice, plants, and gravity.

0C841750DFE5013184E268A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe the composition of the Earth's atmosphere as it has evolved over geologic time (outgassing, origin of atmospheric oxygen, variations in carbon dioxide concentration).

0C819660DFE5013184DC68A86D17958E.description: Examine and describe the structure, composition, and function of Earth's atmosphere, including the role of living organisms in the cycling of atmospheric gases.

0C812640DFE5013184DB68A86D17958E.description: Interactions among the solid Earth, hydrosphere, and atmosphere have resulted in ongoing evolution of the earth system over geologic time. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C804370DFE5013184D968A86D17958E.description: Explain how Kepler's laws predict the orbits of the planets.

0C7FCD50DFE5013184D868A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe the characteristics and motions of the various kinds of objects in our solar system, including planets, satellites, comets, and asteroids, and the influence of gravity and inertia on these motions.

0C7F4D10DFE5013184D768A86D17958E.description: Understand and describe the nebular theory concerning the formation of solar systems, including the roles of planetesimals and protoplanets.

0C7EC420DFE5013184D668A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast the differences in size, temperature, and age of our sun and other stars.

0C7E3270DFE5013184D568A86D17958E.description: Describe the location of the solar system in an outer edge of the disc-shaped Milky Way galaxy, which spans 100,000 light-years.

0C7DC350DFE5013184D468A86D17958E.description: Our solar system is composed of a star, planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and residual material left from the evolution of the solar system over time. The sun is one of billions of stars residing in one of billions of galaxies in a universe that has been changing and evolving over vast amounts of time. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C7CE630DFE5013184D268A86D17958E.description: Construct a model and explain the relationships among planetary systems, stars, multiple-star systems, star clusters, galaxies, and galactic groups in the universe.

0C7C7F70DFE5013184D168A86D17958E.description: Explain that the redshift from distant galaxies and the cosmic microwave background radiation provide evidence for the big bang model that the universe has been expanding for 13 to 14 billion years.

0C7C1630DFE5013184D068A86D17958E.description: Describe how elements with an atomic number greater than helium have been formed by nuclear fusion processes in stars, supernova explosions, or exposure to cosmic rays.

0C7BA930DFE5013184CF68A86D17958E.description: Analyze the life histories of stars and different types of stars found on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, including the three outcomes of stellar evolution based on mass (black hole, neutron star, white dwarf).

0C7B3680DFE5013184CE68A86D17958E.description: Explain that the mass of a star and the balance between collapse and fusion determine the color, brightness, lifetime, and evolution of a star.

0C7AC480DFE5013184CD68A86D17958E.description: Explain the basics of the fusion processes that are the source of energy of stars.

0C7A4F70DFE5013184CC68A86D17958E.description: Describe Hubble's law, and understand the big bang theory and the evidence that supports it (microwave background radiation, relativistic Doppler effect).

0C79DE60DFE5013184CB68A86D17958E.description: Describe various instrumentation used to study deep space and the solar system (e.g., telescopes that record in various parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, including visible, infrared, and radio, refracting or reflecting telescopes, and spectrophotometer).

0C7966B0DFE5013184CA68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that the universe contains many billions of galaxies, and each galaxy contains many billions of stars.

0C78DA10DFE5013184C968A86D17958E.description: Galaxies are made of billions of stars and form most of the visible mass of the universe. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0C745630DFE5013184BF68A86D17958E.description: Describe the contributions of key scientists throughout history, including Claudius Ptolemy, Nicholas Copernicus, Johannes Kepler, Tycho Brahe, Galileo Galilei, Nicholas Steno, Sir Charles Lyell, James Hutton, Henrietta Leavitt, Alfred Wegener, and Edwin Powell Hubble.

0C73DCF0DFE5013184BE68A86D17958E.description: Construct and interpret a simple scale map and topographic cross-section.

0C737010DFE5013184BD68A86D17958E.description: Read a topographic map and a geologic map for information provided on the maps.

0C72CE10DFE5013184BC68A86D17958E.description: Observe natural phenomena, and analyze their location, sequence, or time intervals (e.g., relative ages of rocks, locations of planets over time, and succession of species in an ecosystem).

0C726550DFE5013184BB68A86D17958E.description: Recognize the implications of statistical variability in experiments, and explain the need for controls in experiments.

0C71ECA0DFE5013184BA68A86D17958E.description: Apply mathematical relationships involving proportionalities, linear relations, quadratic equations, simple trigonometric relationships, exponential growth and decay laws, and logarithmic relationships to scientific situations.

0C7178A0DFE5013184B968A86D17958E.description: Analyze situations and solve problems that require combining concepts from more than one topic area of science and applying these concepts.

0C711170DFE5013184B868A86D17958E.description: Formulate and revise explanations using logic and evidence.

0C70A380DFE5013184B768A86D17958E.description: Select and use appropriate tools and technology to perform tests, collect data, analyze relationships, and display data. (The focus is on manual graphing, interpreting graphs, and mastery of metric measurements and units, with supplementary use of computers and electronic data gathering when appropriate.)

0C77E450DFE5013184C768A86D17958E.description: Identify discrepant results and identify possible sources of error or uncontrolled conditions.

0C7775B0DFE5013184C668A86D17958E.description: Identify and communicate the sources of error (random and systematic error) inherent in an experiment.

0C770FA0DFE5013184C568A86D17958E.description: Use hypotheses to choose what data to pay attention to and what additional data to seek, and to guide the interpretation of the data.

0C76A700DFE5013184C468A86D17958E.description: Plan and conduct scientific investigations to explore new phenomena, to check on previous results, to verify or falsify the prediction of a theory, and to use a crucial experiment to discriminate between competing theories.

0C763D30DFE5013184C368A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between a conjecture (guess), a hypothesis and a theory as these terms are used in science.

0C75BE10DFE5013184C268A86D17958E.description: Recognize the use and limitations of models and theories as scientific representations of reality.

0C754090DFE5013184C168A86D17958E.description: Recognize the cumulative nature of scientific evidence.

0C7021E0DFE5013184B668A86D17958E.description: Know the elements of scientific methodology (identification of a problem, hypothesis formulation and prediction, performance of experimental tests, analysis of data, falsification, developing conclusions, reporting results) and be able to use a sequence of those elements to solve a problem or test a hypothesis. document.title: District of Columbia Social Studies Standards

AB46C811947F418E8DEEA9A73B99C47B.description: Identify symbols and practices identified with the United States. (Recognizes the American flag. Says, "I saw the president on TV; he was visiting a school in Washington, DC.")

C5CE9043483F454EA85C9C50F4E8E0F6.description: Demonstrate an understanding of rules and the purposes they serve. (Cautions others on the slide, "Go down feet first or you'll get hurt." Says, "I put my name on the sign-up sheet to get a turn at the computer.")

49FBE8541B874D5794D6E12A73ADF566.description: Make choices and decisions. (Chooses which center he will work in. Participates in creating classroom rules.)

82484789C90146788BC932798DB2BE9C.description: Demonstrate appropriate social interactions that include sharing, compromise, and respect for others. (Participates in group activities. Shares toys with classmates.)

75D23F7AF5FB4CD6BB6AFEEE385C8ADF.description: Children begin to learn the basic civic and democratic principles.

88C272F7C8B54A228647D1503F74BA88.description: Demonstrate understanding of how people, things, and ideas move from one place to another. (Comments, "I rode the Metro to school today." Shares, "The mailman brought me a present from my Grandma. She lives far, far away.")

54939267C70A4D51BBF5AF515E40A4A0.description: Demonstrate understanding that maps are tools to help us find where we are and where we are going. (Scribbles a map and uses it on the playground to find a buried treasure. Plays with maps and refers to one on a pretend trip.)

568794CB52D24E898DC0E906E7738206.description: Begin to learn personal geographic information (e.g., street address, neighborhood, city, and country). (Dials toy phone and says, "Quick, doctor, come to 2331, 45th Place, NE. My baby is sick." Comments, "I live in Washington, DC.")

F3BE7CBAB8BE4711B1586C56EDFE5D35.description: Identify geographic features of their immediate surroundings (e.g., rivers, hills, wetlands, and streams). (Creates a river using sand and water and says, "This river is just like the one we go over near my house." Says, "I get tired running up this hill.")

44368862E1004670A4274B817F6D0AA1.description: Children begin to understand basic geographic concepts.

24DF258002104D339D9FF9540ED7EC6E.description: Track and talk about changes that take place in their families. (Tells the class about the new baby in the family. Says, "I was once a baby, but now I'm a big girl and I go to school.")

C9B6E92D21064530960985FEB0270682.description: Know and follow the established routines of the day. (Turns over the hourglass with sand to see if he can clean up before the sand empties into the next chamber. Makes statements such as, "This afternoon we're all going for a walk to the library.")

B088D3D4373D4480AC1524FF78FEB8F1.description: Demonstrate awareness of changes over time. (Says, "My grandma used to walk with a cane; now she's in a wheelchair." Says, "My mama had to buy me new shoes because my feet keep getting bigger and bigger.")

2E546CB600B941ABBAB3FE12C8908ACA.description: Distinguish the difference between past, present, and future events. (Recalls that yesterday a fire truck came to the school. States, "Tomorrow is my birthday.")

9C9D7580C06146F5816A393EBFECCBA3.description: Demonstrate understanding that time and the passage of time can be measured. (Looks at the sand timer and says, "Hurry, hurry. Cleanup time is almost over." Points to clock in dramatic play area and says, "Time to wake up and go to school!")

19380DED44A140AA94F1CC6263236B85.description: Children begin to understand how people and things change over time.

4876445F34154006B62AB7120B45EA0C.description: Demonstrate understanding of beginning concepts of buying, selling, and trading. (Uses play money to buy groceries in dramatic play area. Sets up toy store and asks teacher how to write a for sale sign.)

BF518C01AB2B4F3D976A318CF25E0741.description: Discuss or dramatize different jobs of people in their community, and demonstrate awareness of their responsibilities. (After studying a picture of a firefighter in a book, comments, "A firefighter came because there was smoke in the kitchen next door." Pretends to be a doctor and says, "Your baby is sick. I need to give her a shot.")

DCEBA7E7B23F44529AC7BEA2F9BBF4E5.description: Children develop a basic understanding of economic concepts.

5AF9B769F01D45CEAD03186C44242E0D.description: Demonstrate emerging awareness and respect for abilities. (Listens to a story about a child with a disability. Includes children with disabilities in play.)

244928FC0D8F4132B12106FA67BAFDD1.description: Demonstrate an emerging respect for culture and ethnicity. (Will learn some words of another language. Tastes a snack that a classmate from another culture brings to school.)

32B33BABEF114AC1BDBB874E30E4E619.description: Begin to identify similarities and differences among people (e.g., gender, race, culture, language, and abilities). (Remarks, "My hair is brown like yours, but yours is curly and mine is straight." Asks, "Do your glasses help you see better?")

AE612B3FFE6B46EA9613F4BE626C440F.description: Children begin to notice and acknowledge diversity.

7644EFFBBE4844CD851F89A4FFB99055.description: Describe how people affect their environment in ways that are negative (litter and pollution) and positive (recycling and planting trees). (Says, "That paper on our playground makes it yucky. I'll pick it up." Asks, "Can we plant some flowers out here so it can be pretty?")

C217C0491B30426DB3734E1A5F62AAF2.description: Participate in group goals and planning. (Participates in morning meeting and sets activities for the day. Makes plans with other children about what they will do when they go outside.)

58FB902DD0A24E07889AE3151A214355.description: Describe or represent their home and other homes in their neighborhood. (Says, "Lots of people live in my apartment building." Comments, "The houses on my street are big with bricks on the outside.")

6E117F42E422401D912BB9DB1C354516.description: Begin to demonstrate respect for others, cooperation, and fairness. (Listens to others during class discussions. Helps classmate sponge the tables after lunch.)

CF9FF9CF49764E668E5D499475ECF5CB.description: Children develop an understanding of self within the context of community.

5D81F7FF4437418FA839C275BDB6AC61.description: Recognize the roles within the home. (Draws a picture of grandmother preparing dinner. While putting away blocks, says: "I have to put away my toys at home before we eat supper.")

8B0AC606A7C146F0820247C87460EF11.description: Identify family members and recognize that families vary. (Points to drawing of family and says, "That's my mommy, that's my daddy, that's my baby sister, and that's me." Looks at photos of families and says, "You have lots of people in your family, but there's just me and my mommy in mine.")

4F53B8829A364B4B99FB60E3FFB3641A.description: Demonstrate knowledge of personal information (e.g., name, birth date, gender, and phone number). (Points to cubby and says, "There's my name … Derrick." Enters block area and says, "I'm a girl, but I can play here, too.")

ECD988C32090448B9934D1660F72B19C.description: Children demonstrate a sense of self within the context of family.

0782F200DFE501317C6668A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

07814F40DFE501317C6168A86D17958E.description: Tell a story or recount an experience with appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details, speaking audibly in coherent sentences.

088EA8C0DFE501317E5268A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate command of the conventions of standard English grammar and usage when writing or speaking.

088D02C0DFE501317E4D68A86D17958E.description: Report on a topic or text or present an opinion, sequencing ideas logically and using appropriate facts and relevant, descriptive details to support main ideas or themes; speak clearly at an understandable pace.

08894450DFE501317E4268A86D17958E.description: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and communicative tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

0888E410DFE501317E4168A86D17958E.description: Make strategic use of digital media and visual displays of data to express information and enhance understanding of presentations.

08886BF0DFE501317E4068A86D17958E.description: Present information, findings, and supporting evidence such that listeners can follow the line of reasoning and the organization, development, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

0887D560DFE501317E3E68A86D17958E.description: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.

08873DB0DFE501317E3C68A86D17958E.description: Prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations and collaborations with diverse partners, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.

08847DA0DFE501317E3368A86D17958E.description: Conduct short research projects that use several sources to build knowledge through investigation of different aspects of a topic.

08831810DFE501317E2F68A86D17958E.description: Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development and organization are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
