031492A0DFE5013173FB68A86D17958E.description: Explore and describe artistic decisions that affect the conceptualization, the expression and the effectiveness of personal performances, improvisations, and choreography. Suggest alternative movement possibilities.

031404F0DFE5013173FA68A86D17958E.description: Defend personal original work using elements of dance, aesthetic principles, choreographic principles, and performance competencies as criteria to assess the work.

031374C0DFE5013173F968A86D17958E.description: Explain conventions of audience etiquette and dance protocols and how they relate to dance and performance in a variety of cultures and settings.

03130470DFE5013173F868A86D17958E.description: Observe major repertory of several famous companies. Analyze the success of the choreography and performances in relation to the intent of the choreographers' artistic statements. Articulate responses in the form of written critical analyses.

03128C10DFE5013173F768A86D17958E.description: Respond - Analyze, critique, and respond to dance.

03120860DFE5013173F668A86D17958E.description: Develop personal strategies/goals in dance and to maintain or achieve personal health and well-being through dance and develop a system of self-assessment to maintain awareness of progress.

03119930DFE5013173F568A86D17958E.description: Remember, repeat, reflect upon, and refine movement in the rehearsal process to perform choreographed dances with technical accuracy and expression, and communicate the meaning of choreography with focused concentration and kinetic awareness. 0310B590DFE5013173F368A86D17958E.description: Clearly and expressively perform dances by a variety of choreographers that use variations of dynamics (energy) to communicate the ideas, feelings, images, and meaning of the choreography.

03102040DFE5013173F268A86D17958E.description: Artistically and musically phrase movement in a variety of dance genres and expressively convey complex concepts or meaning through musical interpretation, rhythm, or phrasing with or without music.

030F77B0DFE5013173F168A86D17958E.description: Accurately perform dances by a variety of choreographers that use complex spatial structures and relationships to convey concepts and meaning.

030F01B0DFE5013173F068A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate kinesthetic awareness, artistic expression, and technical clarity and accuracy in performing dances from a variety of dance genres and choreographers.

030E88E0DFE5013173EF68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate understanding of how dance promotes strength, health, physical safety, provide stress relief, injury prevention, and encourages positive relationships; develop personal strategies to achieve goals in dance and to maintain or achieve personal health and well-being through dance.

030DD5B0DFE5013173EE68A86D17958E.description: Remember, repeat, reflect upon, and refine movement in the rehearsal process to perform choreographed dances expressively, and communicate the meaning of the dance with focused concentration and kinetic awareness. Act responsibly and supportively in all aspects of performance production.

030D61D0DFE5013173ED68A86D17958E.description: Understand how the training in a variety of dance genres prepares the body to perform the movements and techniques inherent in each genre.

030CEA40DFE5013173EC68A86D17958E.description: Expressively perform a dance that uses variations of dynamics (energy) and to communicate the ideas, feelings, images, and meaning of the choreography.

030C7170DFE5013173EB68A86D17958E.description: Understand musical structures and phrasing in a variety of dance genres and convey complex concepts or meaning through musical interpretation, rhythm, or phrasing with or without music.

030C0180DFE5013173EA68A86D17958E.description: Accurately perform a dance that uses complex spatial relationships to convey concepts or meaning.

030B8F20DFE5013173E968A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate technical proficiency in dances from a variety of dance genres (centered alignment, placement, flexibility, endurance, balance, articulation, power, speed, and strength).

030B0CC0DFE5013173E868A86D17958E.description: Perform - Demonstrate dance fundamentals and skills with technical proficiency and spatial, musical, and kinesthetic awareness.

030A8A30DFE5013173E768A86D17958E.description: Research a topic of social conflict and choreograph a dance that makes a meaningful artistic statement about the issue. Receive response and revise the choreography to perform and communicate more clearly.

030A10F0DFE5013173E668A86D17958E.description: Create and perform with accuracy, expression and clarity of meaning, a group dance of personal significance that makes a meaningful artistic statement. Verbally explain how the choreography communicates the meaning of the dance.

03099640DFE5013173E568A86D17958E.description: Synthesize a combination of choreographic strategies and choreographic forms, principles, and structures to create a solo, duet, and group dance and explain how the forms and structures serve to communicate the intent of the dance.

03091C20DFE5013173E468A86D17958E.description: Research a topic of social conflict and use improvisation as a means to experiment and develop a dance that communicates the issues in solo, duet, and group forms. Receive response and revise the choreography to perform and communicate more clearly.

03089DB0DFE5013173E368A86D17958E.description: Use improvisation as a means to experiment with movement possibilities, revise choreography, and develop a dance of personal significance.

03082460DFE5013173E268A86D17958E.description: Synthesize a combination of choreographic principles and structures (such as rondo, palindrome, theme and variation) that demonstrates movement invention and innovation.

0307A8C0DFE5013173E168A86D17958E.description: Create - Understand and create choreographic forms and meaning in dance.

document.title: District of Columbia Physical Education Standards

127FE440DFE501318FFB68A86D17958E.description: Identify and agree on a common goal when participating in a cooperative physical activity.

127F4400DFE501318FF968A86D17958E.description: Use appropriate cues for movement and positive words of encouragement while coaching others in physical activities.

127EF2F0DFE501318FF868A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate respect for individual differences in physical abilities.

127E65D0DFE501318FF668A86D17958E.description: List the benefits of following and the risks of not following safety procedures and rules associated with physical activity.

127DD3B0DFE501318FF468A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate and utilize knowledge of psychological and sociological concepts, principles, and strategies that apply to the learning and performance of physical activity.

127D9410DFE501318FF368A86D17958E.description: Identify healthful choices for meals and snacks that help improve physical performance.

127D0C90DFE501318FF168A86D17958E.description: Differentiate the body's ability to consume calories and burn fat during periods of inactivity and during long periods of moderate physical activity.

127CC9D0DFE501318FF068A86D17958E.description: List and define the components of physical fitness.

127C28C0DFE501318FEE68A86D17958E.description: Identify the body part involved when stretching.

127BC6D0DFE501318FED68A86D17958E.description: Explain that a stronger heart muscle can pump more blood with each beat.

127B86C0DFE501318FEC68A86D17958E.description: Identify characteristics of physical activity that build aerobic capacity and overall fitness.

127B0A10DFE501318FEA68A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate knowledge of physical fitness concepts, principles, and strategies to improve health and performance.

127ACAF0DFE501318FE968A86D17958E.description: Measure and record changes in aerobic capacity and muscular strength, using scientifically based health-related physical fitness assessments.

127A4450DFE501318FE768A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate appropriate warm-up and cool-down exercises before engaging in strength exercises.

127942C0DFE501318FE368A86D17958E.description: Measure and record the heart rate before, during, and after vigorous physical activity.

1278FE80DFE501318FE268A86D17958E.description: Participate in continuous moderate to vigorous physical activities a minimum of three to four days each week that require sustained movement of the large muscle groups to increase breathing and heart rate.

12785BD0DFE501318FE068A86D17958E.description: Record water intake before, during, and after physical activity.

127819E0DFE501318FDF68A86D17958E.description: Participate in physical activity a minimum of four days each week and measure and evaluate changes in health-related physical fitness based on physical activity patterns.

12778110DFE501318FDD68A86D17958E.description: Students assess and maintain a level of physical fitness to improve health and performance through a physically active lifestyle.

12773230DFE501318FDC68A86D17958E.description: Identify the differences between dribbling a ball (with the hand or the foot) while moving forward and when changing direction.

1276E0E0DFE501318FDB68A86D17958E.description: Explain the difference between throwing to a stationary partner and throwing to a moving partner.

12766E90DFE501318FDA68A86D17958E.description: Describe how changing speed and changing direction can allow one person to move freely.

12760280DFE501318FD968A86D17958E.description: Balance while traveling on a ground-level balance beam.

1275BEE0DFE501318FD868A86D17958E.description: Perform an inverted balance (tripod) by evenly distributing weight on body parts.

12757850DFE501318FD768A86D17958E.description: Chase, flee, and move away from others in a constantly changing environment.

1274ED90DFE501318FD568A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate knowledge of movement concepts, principles, and skills that apply to the learning and performance of a variety of physical activities.

1274A140DFE501318FD468A86D17958E.description: Roll a ball for accuracy toward a target and identify the key elements for increasing accuracy.

12742200DFE501318FD268A86D17958E.description: Foot-dribble a ball continuously while traveling and changing direction.

1273E190DFE501318FD168A86D17958E.description: Hand-dribble a ball continuously while moving around obstacles.

12735BB0DFE501318FCF68A86D17958E.description: Kick a ball to a stationary partner, using the inside of the foot.

1272B0D0DFE501318FCD68A86D17958E.description: Throw and catch an object with a partner, increasing the distance from the partner and maintaining an accurate throw that can be easily caught.

127262E0DFE501318FCC68A86D17958E.description: Catch, while traveling, an object thrown by a stationary partner.

127214A0DFE501318FCB68A86D17958E.description: Throw a ball, using the overhand movement pattern with accuracy.

12719440DFE501318FC968A86D17958E.description: Strike a ball from a fixed position using a paddle or racket.

12705FC0DFE501318FC568A86D17958E.description: Jump rope, turning the rope forward as well as backward, while moving.

document.title: Common Core State Standards for Mathematics

comments: For example, how much chocolate will each person get if 3 people share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally? How many 1/3-cup servings are in 2 cups of raisins?
F49E57C0DFE401315D7E68A86D17958E.description: Solve real world problems involving division of unit fractions by non-zero whole numbers and division of whole numbers by unit fractions, e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem.

F49E1230DFE401315D7D68A86D17958E.description: Interpret division of a whole number by a unit fraction, and compute such quotients.
comments: For example, create a story context for 4 ÷ (1/5), and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that 4 ÷ (1/5) = 20 because 20 × (1/5) = 4.

F49DCB10DFE401315D7C68A86D17958E.description: Interpret division of a unit fraction by a non-zero whole number, and compute such quotients.
comments: For example, create a story context for (1/3) ÷ 4, and use a visual fraction model to show the quotient. Use the relationship between multiplication and division to explain that (1/3) ÷ 4 = 1/12 because (1/12) × 4 = 1/3.

F49D81B0DFE401315D7B68A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of division to divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions.
comments: Students able to multiply fractions in general can develop strategies to divide fractions in general, by reasoning about the relationship between multiplication and division. But division of a fraction by a fraction is not a requirement at this grade

F49D2170DFE401315D7A68A86D17958E.description: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.

F49CD340DFE401315D7968A86D17958E.description: Explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction greater than 1 results in a product greater than the given number (recognizing multiplication by whole numbers greater than 1 as a familiar case); explaining why multiplying a given number by a fraction less than 1 results in a product smaller than the given number; and relating the principle of fraction equivalence a/b = (n×a)/(n×b) to the effect of multiplying a/b by 1.

F49C8460DFE401315D7868A86D17958E.description: Comparing the size of a product to the size of one factor on the basis of the size of the other factor, without performing the indicated multiplication.

F49BEA70DFE401315D7668A86D17958E.description: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by tiling it with unit squares of the appropriate unit fraction side lengths, and show that the area is the same as would be found by multiplying the side lengths. Multiply fractional side lengths to find areas of rectangles, and represent fraction products as rectangular areas.

F49B90C0DFE401315D7568A86D17958E.description: Interpret the product (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a × q ÷ b.
comments: For example, use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. (In general, (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.)

F49B4D60DFE401315D7468A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication to multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction.

comments: For example, interpret 3/4 as the result of dividing 3 by 4, noting that 3/4 multiplied by 4 equals 3, and that when 3 wholes are shared equally among 4 people each person has a share of size 3/4. If 9 people want to share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds of rice should each person get? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
F49B0830DFE401315D7368A86D17958E.description: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). Solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.

F49AC6C0DFE401315D7268A86D17958E.description: Apply and extend previous understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide fractions.

F49A7F50DFE401315D7168A86D17958E.description: Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including cases of unlike denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers.
comments: For example, recognize an incorrect result 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7, by observing that 3/7 < 1/2.

F49A3AC0DFE401315D7068A86D17958E.description: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators.
comments: For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.)

F499EB00DFE401315D6F68A86D17958E.description: Use equivalent fractions as a strategy to add and subtract fractions.

comments: Grade 3 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 6, and 8.
Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to fractions with denominators 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 100

F4995630DFE401315D6D68A86D17958E.description: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.

comments: For example, all rectangles have four right angles and squares are rectangles, so all squares have four right angles.
F498F1D0DFE401315D6C68A86D17958E.description: Understand that attributes belonging to a category of two-dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category.

F498B190DFE401315D6B68A86D17958E.description: Classify two-dimensional figures into categories based on their properties.

F4986D80DFE401315D6A68A86D17958E.description: Represent real world and mathematical problems by graphing points in the first quadrant of the coordinate plane, and interpret coordinate values of points in the context of the situation.

F4981B30DFE401315D6968A86D17958E.description: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines, called axes, to define a coordinate system, with the intersection of the lines (the origin) arranged to coincide with the 0 on each line and a given point in the plane located by using an ordered pair of numbers, called its coordinates. Understand that the first number indicates how far to travel from the origin in the direction of one axis, and the second number indicates how far to travel in the direction of the second axis, with the convention that the names of the two axes and the coordinates correspond (e.g., x-axis and x-coordinate, y-axis and y-coordinate).

F497BF60DFE401315D6868A86D17958E.description: Graph points on the coordinate plane to solve real-world and mathematical problems.

F4972AB0DFE401315D6668A86D17958E.description: Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems.

F496E7F0DFE401315D6568A86D17958E.description: Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right rectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems.

F496A1A0DFE401315D6468A86D17958E.description: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole-number products as volumes, e.g., to represent the associative property of multiplication.

F4965390DFE401315D6368A86D17958E.description: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume.

F495F050DFE401315D6268A86D17958E.description: Measure volumes by counting unit cubes, using cubic cm, cubic in, cubic ft, and improvised units.

F495AD60DFE401315D6168A86D17958E.description: A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes is said to have a volume of n cubic units.

F4956A60DFE401315D6068A86D17958E.description: A cube with side length 1 unit, called a "unit cube," is said to have "one cubic unit" of volume, and can be used to measure volume.

F49524E0DFE401315D5F68A86D17958E.description: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement.

F494DFF0DFE401315D5E68A86D17958E.description: Geometric measurement: understand concepts of volume and relate volume to multiplication and to addition.

F493FE80DFE401315D5B68A86D17958E.description: Make a line plot to display a data set of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8). Use operations on fractions for this grade to solve problems involving information presented in line plots.
comments: For example, given different measurements of liquid in identical beakers, find the amount of liquid each beaker would contain if the total amount in all the beakers were redistributed equally.

F4949B90DFE401315D5D68A86D17958E.description: Convert among different-sized standard measurement units within a given measurement system (e.g., convert 5 cm to 0.05 m), and use these conversions in solving multi-step, real world problems.

F4945330DFE401315D5C68A86D17958E.description: Convert like measurement units within a given measurement system.

F4932E80DFE401315D5868A86D17958E.description: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used.

F492DD50DFE401315D5768A86D17958E.description: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models.

F4927F30DFE401315D5668A86D17958E.description: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm.

F4922940DFE401315D5568A86D17958E.description: Perform operations with multi-digit whole numbers and with decimals to hundredths.

F491E660DFE401315D5468A86D17958E.description: Use place value understanding to round decimals to any place.

F491A1E0DFE401315D5368A86D17958E.description: Compare two decimals to thousandths based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons.

F4915C70DFE401315D5268A86D17958E.description: Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form, e.g., 347.392 = 3 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 7 × 1 + 3 × (1/10) + 9 × (1/100) + 2 × (1/1000).

F4911390DFE401315D5168A86D17958E.description: Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths.

F490B0B0DFE401315D5068A86D17958E.description: Explain patterns in the number of zeros of the product when multiplying a number by powers of 10, and explain patterns in the placement of the decimal point when a decimal is multiplied or divided by a power of 10. Use whole-number exponents to denote powers of 10.

F4905F10DFE401315D4F68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.

F48FD9E0DFE401315D4D68A86D17958E.description: Number and Operations in Base Ten
comments: Grade 4 expectations in this domain are limited to whole numbers less than or equal to 1,000,000.

F48F9700DFE401315D4C68A86D17958E.description: Generate two numerical patterns using two given rules. Identify apparent relationships between corresponding terms. Form ordered pairs consisting of corresponding terms from the two patterns, and graph the ordered pairs on a coordinate plane.
comments: For example, given the rule "Add 3" and the starting number 0, and given the rule "Add 6" and the starting number 0, generate terms in the resulting sequences, and observe that the terms in one sequence are twice the corresponding terms in the other sequence. Explain informally why this is so.

F48F0FD0DFE401315D4A68A86D17958E.description: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them.
comments: For example, express the calculation "add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2" as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product.

F48EC000DFE401315D4968A86D17958E.description: Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols.

F48DDAA0DFE401315D4668A86D17958E.description: Look for and express regularity in repeated reasoning.
comments: Mathematically proficient students notice if calculations are repeated, and look both for general methods and for shortcuts. Upper elementary students might notice when dividing 25 by 11 that they are repeating the same calculations over and over again, and conclude they have a repeating decimal. By paying attention to the calculation of slope as they repeatedly check whether points are on the line through (1, 2) with slope 3, middle school students might abstract the equation (y – 2)/(x – 1) = 3. Noticing the regularity in the way terms cancel when expanding (x – 1)(x + 1), (x – 1)(x² + x + 1), and (x – 1)(x³ + x² + x + 1) might lead them to the general formula for the sum of a geometric series. As they work to solve a problem, mathematically proficient students maintain oversight of the process, while attending to the details. They continually evaluate the reasonableness of their intermediate results.

F48D8050DFE401315D4568A86D17958E.description: Look for and make use of structure.
comments: Mathematically proficient students look closely to discern a pattern or structure. Young students, for example, might notice that three and seven more is the same amount as seven and three more, or they may sort a collection of shapes according to how many sides the shapes have. Later, students will see 7 × 8 equals the well remembered 7 × 5 + 7 × 3, in preparation for learning about the distributive property. In the expression x² + 9x + 14, older students can see the 14 as 2 × 7 and the 9 as 2 + 7. They recognize the significance of an existing line in a geometric figure and can use the strategy of drawing an auxiliary line for solving problems. They also can step back for an overview and shift perspective. They can see complicated things, such as some algebraic expressions, as single objects or as being composed of several objects. For example, they can see 5 – 3(x – y)² as 5 minus a positive number times a square and use that to realize that its value cannot be more than 5 for any real numbers x and y.

Mathematically proficient students try to communicate precisely to others. They try to use clear definitions in discussion with others and in their own reasoning. They state the meaning of the symbols they choose, including using the equal sign consistently and appropriately. They are careful about specifying units of measure, and labeling axes to clarify the correspondence with quantities in a problem. They calculate accurately and efficiently, express numerical answers with a degree of precision appropriate for the problem context. In the elementary grades, students give carefully formulated explanations to each other. By the time they reach high school they have learned to examine claims and make explicit use of definitions.

Mathematically proficient students consider the available tools when solving a mathematical problem. These tools might include pencil and paper, concrete models, a ruler, a protractor, a calculator, a spreadsheet, a computer algebra system, a statistical package, or dynamic geometry software. Proficient students are sufficiently familiar with tools appropriate for their grade or course to make sound decisions about when each of these tools might be helpful, recognizing both the insight to be gained and their limitations. For example, mathematically proficient high school students analyze graphs of functions and solutions generated using a graphing calculator. They detect possible errors by strategically using estimation and other mathematical knowledge. When making mathematical models, they know that technology can enable them to visualize the results of varying assumptions, explore consequences, and compare predictions with data. Mathematically proficient students at various grade levels are able to identify relevant external mathematical resources, such as digital content located on a website, and use them to pose or solve problems. They are able to use technological tools to explore and deepen their understanding of concepts.

Mathematically proficient students can apply the mathematics they know to solve problems arising in everyday life, society, and the workplace. In early grades, this might be as simple as writing an addition equation to describe a situation. In middle grades, a student might apply proportional reasoning to plan a school event or analyze a problem in the community. By high school, a student might use geometry to solve a design problem or use a function to describe how one quantity of interest depends on another. Mathematically proficient students who can apply what they know are comfortable making assumptions and approximations to simplify a complicated situation, realizing that these may need revision later. They are able to identify important quantities in a practical situation and map their relationships using such tools as diagrams, two-way tables, graphs, flowcharts and formulas. They can analyze those relationships mathematically to draw conclusions. They routinely interpret their mathematical results in the context of the situation and reflect on whether the results make sense, possibly improving the model if it has not served its purpose.

Mathematically proficient students understand and use stated assumptions, definitions, and previously established results in constructing arguments. They make conjectures and build a logical progression of statements to explore the truth of their conjectures. They are able to analyze situations by breaking them into cases, and can recognize and use counterexamples. They justify their conclusions, communicate them to others, and respond to the arguments of others. They reason inductively about data, making plausible arguments that take into account the context from which the data arose. Mathematically proficient students are also able to compare the effectiveness of two plausible arguments, distinguish correct logic or reasoning from that which is flawed, and—if there is a flaw in an argument—explain what it is. Elementary students can construct arguments using concrete referents such as objects, drawings, diagrams, and actions. Such arguments can make sense and be correct, even though they are not generalized or made formal until later grades. Later, students learn to determine domains to which an argument applies. Students at all grades can listen or read the arguments of others, decide whether they make sense, and ask useful questions to clarify or improve the arguments.
F48C2E80DFE401315D4168A86D17958E.description: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others.

comments: Mathematically proficient students make sense of quantities and their relationships in problem situations. They bring two complementary abilities to bear on problems involving quantitative relationships: the ability to decontextualize—to abstract a given situation and represent it symbolically and manipulate the representing symbols as if they have a life of their own, without necessarily attending to their referents—and the ability to contextualize, to pause as needed during the manipulation process in order to probe into the referents for the symbols involved. Quantitative reasoning entails habits of creating a coherent representation of the problem at hand; considering the units involved; attending to the meaning of quantities, not just how to compute them; and knowing and flexibly using different properties of operations and objects.

F48B92B0DFE401315D3F68A86D17958E.description: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them.
comments: Mathematically proficient students start by explaining to themselves the meaning of a problem and looking for entry points to its solution. They analyze givens, constraints, relationships, and goals. They make conjectures about the form and meaning of the solution and plan a solution pathway rather than simply jumping into a solution attempt. They consider analogous problems, and try special cases and simpler forms of the original problem in order to gain insight into its solution. They monitor and evaluate their progress and change course if necessary. Older students might, depending on the context of the problem, transform algebraic expressions or change the viewing window on their graphing calculator to get the information they need. Mathematically proficient students can explain correspondences between equations, verbal descriptions, tables, and graphs or draw diagrams of important features and relationships, graph data, and search for regularity or trends. Younger students might rely on using concrete objects or pictures to help conceptualize and solve a problem. Mathematically proficient students check their answers to problems using a different method, and they continually ask themselves, "Does this make sense?" They can understand the approaches of others to solving complex problems and identify correspondences between different approaches.

07AD11F0DFE501317C9F68A86D17958E.description: Describe characters in a story (e.g., their traits, motivations, or feelings) and explain how their actions contribute to the sequence of events.

07ACBA50DFE501317C9E68A86D17958E.description: Recount stories, including fables, folktales, and myths from diverse cultures; determine the central message, lesson, or moral and explain how it is conveyed through key details in the text.

07AC66A0DFE501317C9D68A86D17958E.description: Ask and answer questions to demonstrate understanding of a text, referring explicitly to the text as the basis for the answers.

07AB76F0DFE501317C9A68A86D17958E.description: Read and comprehend complex literary and informational texts independently and proficiently.

07AB3090DFE501317C9968A86D17958E.description: Range of Reading and Level of Text Complexity

07AAE8D0DFE501317C9868A86D17958E.description: Analyze how two or more texts address similar themes or topics in order to build knowledge or to compare the approaches the authors take.

07AA9790DFE501317C9768A86D17958E.description: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, including the validity of the reasoning as well as the relevance and sufficiency of the evidence.

07AA3E20DFE501317C9668A86D17958E.description: Integrate and evaluate content presented in diverse media and formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words.
comments: Please see "Research to Build and Present Knowledge" in Writing and "Comprehension and Collaboration" in Speaking and Listening for additional standards relevant to gathering, assessing, and applying information from print and digital sources.

07A9B070DFE501317C9468A86D17958E.description: Assess how point of view or purpose shapes the content and style of a text.

07A96480DFE501317C9368A86D17958E.description: Analyze the structure of texts, including how specific sentences, paragraphs, and larger portions of the text (e.g., a section, chapter, scene, or stanza) relate to each other and the whole.

07A91940DFE501317C9268A86D17958E.description: Interpret words and phrases as they are used in a text, including determining technical, connotative, and figurative meanings, and analyze how specific word choices shape meaning or tone.

07A844C0DFE501317C9068A86D17958E.description: Analyze how and why individuals, events, and ideas develop and interact over the course of a text.

07A7F670DFE501317C8F68A86D17958E.description: Determine central ideas or themes of a text and analyze their development; summarize the key supporting details and ideas.

07A7A360DFE501317C8E68A86D17958E.description: Read closely to determine what the text says explicitly and to make logical inferences from it; cite specific textual evidence when writing or speaking to support conclusions drawn from the text.

07A6E6B0DFE501317C8C68A86D17958E.description: College and Career Readiness Anchor Standards for Reading

document.title: District of Columbia Social Studies Standards

0E761A30DFE5013187F268A86D17958E.description: Students use nontext primary and secondary sources, such as maps, charts, graphs, photographs, works of art, and technical charts.

0E75C5A0DFE5013187F168A86D17958E.description: Students pose relevant questions about events they encounter in historical documents, eyewitness accounts, oral histories, letters, diaries, artifacts, photographs, maps, artworks, and architecture.

0E757D80DFE5013187F068A86D17958E.description: Students differentiate between primary and secondary sources and know examples of each.

0E753270DFE5013187EF68A86D17958E.description: Students analyze societies in terms of the following themes: military, political, economic, social, religious, and intellectual.

0E74E4E0DFE5013187EE68A86D17958E.description: Historical Research, Evidence, and Point of View

0E748990DFE5013187ED68A86D17958E.description: Students identify and explain the process of conflict and cooperation (political, economic, religious, etc.) among people in the contemporary world at local, regional, and national levels.

0E742B00DFE5013187EC68A86D17958E.description: Students explain the causes and effects of settlement patterns, including the effect of rural-to-urban migrations.

0E73E7E0DFE5013187EB68A86D17958E.description: Students trace how changes in technology, transportation, communication, and resources affect the location of economic activities.

0E73A470DFE5013187EA68A86D17958E.description: Students describe the factors that influence the location, distribution, and interrelationships of economic activities in different regions.

0E7360C0DFE5013187E968A86D17958E.description: Students explain the distributions of cultures in places they study and how they create a cultural landscape.

0E731980DFE5013187E868A86D17958E.description: Students identify the human and physical characteristics of the places they are studying, and they explain how those features form the unique character of those places.

0E72C2F0DFE5013187E768A86D17958E.description: Students judge the significance of the relative location of a place (e.g., proximity to a harbor, on trade routes), and they analyze how relative advantages or disadvantages can change over time.

0E727470DFE5013187E668A86D17958E.description: Students define common map and globe terms, including continent, country, mountain, valley, ocean, sea, lake, river; cardinal directions, latitude, longitude, north pole, south pole, tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, equator, 360-degree divisions, time zones; elevation, depth, approximate distances in miles, isthmus, strait, peninsula, island, archipelago, 23-and-a-half-degree global tilt, fall line; and compass rose, scale, and legend.

0E722CD0DFE5013187E568A86D17958E.description: Students use map and globe skills to determine the absolute locations (latitude and longitude) of places, and they interpret information available through a map or globe's legend, scale, and symbolic representations.

0E719F30DFE5013187E368A86D17958E.description: Students conduct cost-benefit analyses of historical and current events.

0E715670DFE5013187E268A86D17958E.description: Students distinguish cause from effect and identify and interpret the multiple causes and effects of historical events.

0E710920DFE5013187E168A86D17958E.description: Students summarize the key events of the era they are studying and explain the historical contexts of those events.

0E70B340DFE5013187E068A86D17958E.description: Students explain how the present is connected to the past, identifying both similarities and differences between the two, and how some things change over time and some things stay the same.

0E7049B0DFE5013187DF68A86D17958E.description: Students know the calendar abbreviations and what they signify (e.g., A.D. and C.E., B.E. and B.C.E., c. and circa).

0E6FE960DFE5013187DE68A86D17958E.description: Students place key events of the historical era they are studying and interpret information contained within time lines and comparative time charts.

0E6F4320DFE5013187DC68A86D17958E.description: Historical and Social Sciences Analysis Skills

0E9F4FE0DFE50131886668A86D17958E.description: Distinguish between waves of immigrant Latino groups and identify the push and pull factors that stimulated their transnational movement (e.g., Cubans in the 1960s and 1980s; Central Americans in the 1980s; Caribbean peoples, especially Haitians and Dominicans, in the 1990s). (G, S)

0E9F09E0DFE50131886568A86D17958E.description: Describe the major Asian immigrant groups who have come to America in the 19th and 20th centuries, locating their countries of origin and where they have tended to settle in large numbers in certain regions (e.g., Koreans, Chinese, and Vietnamese). (G, S)

(G, S)

0B71EB50DFE50131837068A86D17958E.description: Recognize that vaccines can prevent some diseases so that people do not catch them at all.

0B71A010DFE50131836F68A86D17958E.description: Identify diseases that human beings can usually catch only once because their bodies build up an immunity to them.

0B7151E0DFE50131836E68A86D17958E.description: Explain that a healthy body can fight most invasive pathogens; however, some interfere with the body's defenses.

0B711130DFE50131836D68A86D17958E.description: Describe the body's defenses against pathogens, including tears, saliva, skin, some types of white blood cells, stomach secretions, and an internal system of chemical testing.

0B7051B0DFE50131836A68A86D17958E.description: Explain that disease-bearing microorganisms, called pathogens, can enter the body and interfere with the proper function of various parts of the body.

0B700F50DFE50131836968A86D17958E.description: Explain that some diseases are caused by germs (harmful microorganisms such as some bacteria and viruses) and some are not, and those caused by microorganisms may be spread to other people.

0B6FC680DFE50131836868A86D17958E.description: Describe that human beings have body systems very similar to those of other animals, especially other mammals (warm-blooded vertebrate animals that have, in the female, milk-secreting organs for feeding the young).

0B6F7AA0DFE50131836768A86D17958E.description: Humans have a variety of mechanisms to combat disease. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B6CDF70DFE50131835E68A86D17958E.description: Investigate the Chesapeake Bay watershed and wetlands, and describe how they support a wide variety of plant and animal life that interact with other living and nonliving things.

0B6F3020DFE50131836668A86D17958E.description: Explain how dead plants and animals are the food source for many microorganisms.

0B6EE130DFE50131836568A86D17958E.description: Recognize that there are many kinds, and vast numbers, of living things too small to see with the naked eye called microorganisms, but they can be easily seen with the aid of various kinds of microscopes.

0B6E94B0DFE50131836468A86D17958E.description: Explain how in all environments, organisms grow, die, and decay, as new organisms are produced by the older ones.

0B6E4230DFE50131836368A86D17958E.description: Describe the many beneficial attributes of plants, including trees, in improving and sustaining an urban environment.

0B6DF510DFE50131836268A86D17958E.description: Describe the structures in plants (leaves, roots, flowers, stem, bark, wood) that are responsible for food production, support, water transport, growth, and protection.

0B6DA500DFE50131836168A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain that most plants produce far more seeds than actually grow into new plants.

0B6D64A0DFE50131836068A86D17958E.description: Describe how energy derived from the sun is used by green plants to produce chemical energy in the form of sugars (photosynthesis), and this energy is transferred along a food chain from producers (plants) to consumers to decomposers.

0B6D23E0DFE50131835F68A86D17958E.description: Observe and recognize that some source of energy is needed for all organisms to stay alive and grow.

0B6C90C0DFE50131835D68A86D17958E.description: Explain that organisms interact with one another in various ways, such as providing food, pollination, and seed dispersal.

0B6C2E20DFE50131835C68A86D17958E.description: All organisms need energy and matter to live and grow. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B692770DFE50131835268A86D17958E.description: Explain how electrical energy can be used to produce light, heat energy, motion (kinetic energy), or sound energy.

0B6B9290DFE50131835A68A86D17958E.description: Explain that electric current can flow only if there is a complete closed loop of conducting material (called a circuit) for it to flow through. Know that a switch is a device for opening and closing a circuit.

0B6B4DB0DFE50131835968A86D17958E.description: In spite of some similarities, explain how the electrostatic force and the magnetic force are not the same thing.

0B6B0660DFE50131835868A86D17958E.description: Explain that if two electrically charged objects are near each other, each will exert an attractive or repulsive force on the other. Describe that like charges repel each other and unlike charges attract each other.

0B6ABEF0DFE50131835768A86D17958E.description: Recognize that there are two types of electric charge: positive and negative.

0B6A6B90DFE50131835668A86D17958E.description: Explain how an electrically charged object does not have to touch another object to exert a force — called the electrostatic force — on it.

0B6A1210DFE50131835568A86D17958E.description: Describe that magnets have poles; unlike poles of two magnets attract each other while like poles repel.

0B69BE30DFE50131835468A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe that a magnet does not have to touch an object made of magnetic material to exert a force on it.

0B696CC0DFE50131835368A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that magnets attract objects made of iron and a few other substances (called magnetic materials), but they do not attract objects made of most other substances.

0B68E230DFE50131835168A86D17958E.description: Recognize that some materials are electrical conductors and others are electrical insulators.

0B689B20DFE50131835068A86D17958E.description: Electricity and magnetism are related phenomena that have many useful applications in everyday life. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B684E30DFE50131834F68A86D17958E.description: Explain that energy in fossil fuels comes originally from the energy of sunlight used by plants that grew a long time ago.

0B680670DFE50131834E68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that heat energy can be absorbed or given off by both living and nonliving things.

0B67C260DFE50131834D68A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain that when one object rubs against another (such as one's hands rubbing together) the kinetic energy (energy of motion) is transformed into heat energy.

0B677DC0DFE50131834C68A86D17958E.description: Explain when light strikes a surface, it can be reflected, scattered, refracted, and/or absorbed.

0B673670DFE50131834B68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe how light travels through empty space or a transparent medium in a straight line until it strikes an object, and, if the object is transparent, the light will bend (refract) at the interface.

0B66DC10DFE50131834A68A86D17958E.description: Explain that energy comes from the sun in the form of visible light and other radiation we cannot see without special instruments, but some of what we cannot see we can feel as heating (infrared radiation), and some can cause sunburn (ultraviolet radiation).

0B667820DFE50131834968A86D17958E.description: Energy and matter have multiple forms and can be changed from one form to another. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B65FA00DFE50131834768A86D17958E.description: Describe the different properties of soil, including its color, texture (size of particles), and ability to retain water and support the growth of plants.

0B65BAB0DFE50131834668A86D17958E.description: Explain how soil is made partly from rock weathered by water and wind, and partly from decomposition of plant and animal remains, and that it contains many living organisms.

0B6578F0DFE50131834568A86D17958E.description: Define the three categories of rocks (metamorphic, igneous, and sedimentary) based on how they are formed from older rocks.

0B653260DFE50131834468A86D17958E.description: Describe the different layers of the Earth, including the crust, mantle, and core.

0B64E4D0DFE50131834368A86D17958E.description: Explain how weathering breaks rocks up into smaller pieces. Recognize that these pieces may be many sizes and shapes, from jagged boulders to smooth grains of sand and even smaller.

0B649D80DFE50131834268A86D17958E.description: Recognize and describe that most rock is composed of different combinations of one or more minerals.

0B645940DFE50131834168A86D17958E.description: Describe the physical properties of minerals, including hardness, color, luster, cleavage, and streak, and recognize that one mineral can be distinguished from another by use of a simplified key.

0B641620DFE50131834068A86D17958E.description: Define a mineral as a naturally occurring, crystalline inorganic solid substance. Recognize that each mineral has its own characteristic properties (e.g., quartz, mica).

0B63CF10DFE50131833F68A86D17958E.description: The properties of rocks and minerals reflect the processes that formed them. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B638740DFE50131833E68A86D17958E.description: Explain how the surface of the Earth changes over various time scales due to processes, such as erosion and weathering, landslides, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, and mountain building.

0B633C10DFE50131833D68A86D17958E.description: Explain how waves, wind, water, and glacial ice shape and reshape Earth's land surface by eroding rock and soil in some areas and depositing them in other areas.

0B62F7C0DFE50131833C68A86D17958E.description: Waves, wind, water, and ice shape and reshape the Earth's land surface. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B73C280DFE50131837668A86D17958E.description: Make simple and safe electrical circuits with a battery and various plugs, sockets, and terminals.

0B7370E0DFE50131837568A86D17958E.description: Describe how human beings have made tools and machines, such as X-ray cameras, microscopes, satellites, and computers, to observe and do things that they could not otherwise sense or do at all, or as quickly or efficiently.

0B732AC0DFE50131837468A86D17958E.description: Discuss and give examples of how technologies, such as computers and medical Xrays, have improved the lives of people.

0B72DDB0DFE50131837368A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate how scientific tools, such as microscopes, telescopes, and cameras, can be used to gather accurate information for making scientific comparisons of objects and events.

0B729750DFE50131837268A86D17958E.description: Although each of the human enterprises of science and technology has a character and history of its own, each is dependent on and reinforces the other. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0B626870DFE50131833A68A86D17958E.description: Explain how scientific thinking can be distorted by strong feelings, and explain why and when it is appropriate or necessary to separate emotions from the reasoning process.

0B621DA0DFE50131833968A86D17958E.description: Identify better reasons for believing something rather than citing comments such as, "Everybody knows that," "I just know," or "Because they say," and discount such reasons when given by others.

0B61BFD0DFE50131833868A86D17958E.description: Support statements with ideas and data found in print and electronic media, identify and evaluate the sources used, and expect others to do the same.

0B6164A0DFE50131833768A86D17958E.description: Write descriptions of investigations by using observations as support for explanations.

0B610A60DFE50131833668A86D17958E.description: Use numerical data to describe and compare objects and events.

0B60BA00DFE50131833568A86D17958E.description: Explain that clear communication is an essential part of the process of scientific inquiry because it enables scientists to inform others about their work, to expose their ideas to evaluation by other scientists, and to allow scientists to stay informed about scientific discoveries around the world.

0B606CB0DFE50131833468A86D17958E.description: Recognize and describe how results of similar scientific investigations may turn out differently due to inconsistencies in methods, materials, or observations, or the limitations of the tools used.

0B602760DFE50131833368A86D17958E.description: Scientific progress is made by asking relevant questions and conducting careful investigations. As a basis for understanding this concept, and to address the content in this grade, students should develop their own questions and perform investigations. Students:

document.title: District of Columbia Physical Education Standards

121579E0DFE501318F8668A86D17958E.description: Identify and demonstrate the attributes of an effective partner in physical activity.

1214F400DFE501318F8468A86D17958E.description: Describe how positive social interactions can make physical activity with others more fun.

12146030DFE501318F8268A86D17958E.description: Identify the feelings that result from participation in physical activity.

1213DA20DFE501318F8068A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate and utilize knowledge of psychological and sociological concepts, principles, and strategies that apply to the learning and performance of physical activity.

12139AB0DFE501318F7F68A86D17958E.description: Explain the fuel requirements of the body during physical activity and inactivity.

12131B20DFE501318F7D68A86D17958E.description: Identify ways of increasing physical activity in routine daily activities.

12128F50DFE501318F7B68A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate knowledge of physical fitness concepts, principles, and strategies to improve health and performance.

12124E60DFE501318F7A68A86D17958E.description: Identify and use two indicators of increased capacity for vigorous physical activity to measure a change in activity levels.

1211CB60DFE501318F7868A86D17958E.description: Stretch arms, shoulders, back, and legs without hyper flexing or hyper extending the joints.

12114440DFE501318F7668A86D17958E.description: Move from a sitting to a standing position and from a lying to a sitting position without using arms to brace or push oneself off the floor.

1210EDB0DFE501318F7568A86D17958E.description: Travel hand-over-hand along a horizontal ladder or hang from an overhead bar.

121067D0DFE501318F7368A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast changes in heart rate before, during, and after physical activity.

121024C0DFE501318F7268A86D17958E.description: Perform aerobic activity and discuss changes in one's body.

120F9B80DFE501318F7068A86D17958E.description: Participate in physical activity a minimum of three days each week.

120EF510DFE501318F6E68A86D17958E.description: Students assess and maintain a level of physical fitness to improve health and performance through a physically active lifestyle.

120E9810DFE501318F6D68A86D17958E.description: Identify examples of underhand and overhand throwing movement patterns.

120E30C0DFE501318F6C68A86D17958E.description: Identify the placement of the non-kicking foot while kicking a stationary ball from a running approach.

120DDEC0DFE501318F6B68A86D17958E.description: Identify the different points of contact when striking an object to propel it in a given direction.

120D9D40DFE501318F6A68A86D17958E.description: Describe and demonstrate contrasts between slow and fast, heavy and light, and hard and soft while moving.

120D5760DFE501318F6968A86D17958E.description: Identify the base of support of balanced objects and balance oneself, demonstrating momentary stillness, using body parts other than both feet as a base of support.

120D0740DFE501318F6868A86D17958E.description: Identify the right and left sides of the body and move from right to left and left to right.

120CC930DFE501318F6768A86D17958E.description: Identify and independently use personal space, general space, and boundaries while moving in different directions, and discuss why they are important.

120C89C0DFE501318F6668A86D17958E.description: Travel over, under, in front of, behind, and through objects and over, under, in front of, and behind partners.

120C08D0DFE501318F6468A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate knowledge of movement concepts, principles, and skills that apply to the learning and performance of a variety of physical activities.

120BC1F0DFE501318F6368A86D17958E.description: Roll a ball for distance, using proper form.

120B27F0DFE501318F6168A86D17958E.description: Dribble a ball in a forward direction using the inside of the foot.

120AE470DFE501318F6068A86D17958E.description: Dribble a ball continuously with one hand.

120A58F0DFE501318F5E68A86D17958E.description: Kick a rolled ball from a stationary position.

1209C070DFE501318F5C68A86D17958E.description:
Catch:
  • a self-tossed ball
  • a self-bounced ball
  • a gently thrown ball.

12097280DFE501318F5B68A86D17958E.description:
Identify examples of underhand and overhand movement patterns and throw with:
  • the underhand movement pattern using the basic oppositional leg/arm movements.
  • the two-handed overhead pattern.

1208E640DFE501318F5968A86D17958E.description:
Strike a balloon upward and forward continuously using:
  • a large, short-handled paddle
  • arms, hands, and feet.

12083AE0DFE501318F5768A86D17958E.description: Travel in straight, curved, and zigzag pathways while changing speed and direction in response to tempos, rhythms, and signals.

1207A3B0DFE501318F5568A86D17958E.description: Jump a moving rope turned independently or by others continuously.

12075A90DFE501318F5468A86D17958E.description: Jump and land on both feet after taking off on one foot and on both feet.

12071110DFE501318F5368A86D17958E.description: Roll smoothly in a forward direction, without stopping or hesitating, emphasizing a rounded form.

1206C970DFE501318F5268A86D17958E.description: Perform a jog and a run, a hop and a jump, and a gallop and a slide, and explain the key differences and similarities in those movements.

12062D70DFE501318F5068A86D17958E.description: Students demonstrate the motor skills and movement patterns needed to perform a variety of physical activities.

document.title: District of Columbia Science Standards

0AF8B740DFE5013182C368A86D17958E.description: Identify the external features that local plants and animals have (such as those found in schoolyards or in city neighborhoods) that enable them to survive in their environment.

0AF87730DFE5013182C268A86D17958E.description: Recognize that animals (including humans) and plants are living things that grow, reproduce, and need food, air, and water.

0AF83980DFE5013182C168A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain that animals eat plants and/or other animals for food.

0AF7F440DFE5013182C068A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe that there can be differences, such as size or markings, among the individuals within one particular plant or animal group (e.g., maple trees, zebras). Variation is a normal characteristic of many kinds of living things.

0AF7ADB0DFE5013182BF68A86D17958E.description: Explain that most living things need food, water, and air.

0AF76D90DFE5013182BE68A86D17958E.description: Different types of plants and animals inhabit the Earth. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0AF6ECE0DFE5013182BC68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and demonstrate how things near Earth fall to the ground unless something holds them up (i.e., they are subject to the force of gravity).

0AF6A2F0DFE5013182BB68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate and observe that magnets supply a force that can be used to make some things move without touching them.

0AF63DC0DFE5013182BA68A86D17958E.description: Explain that the greater the applied force, the greater the change in the motion of the object.

0AF5EE20DFE5013182B968A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe that the way to make something move (faster or slower or in a different direction) is by giving it a push or a pull, which is called a force.

0AF5B180DFE5013182B868A86D17958E.description: The motion of objects can be observed, measured, and changed. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0AF537A0DFE5013182B668A86D17958E.description: Observe and measure that the sun supplies heat and light to the Earth and is necessary for most life.

0AF4F050DFE5013182B568A86D17958E.description: Investigate and explain that air is a mixture of different gases that surrounds us and takes up space, and whose movement we feel as wind.

0AF4AEC0DFE5013182B468A86D17958E.description: Recognize and explain that water, rocks, soil, and living organisms are found on the Earth's surface.

0AF467C0DFE5013182B368A86D17958E.description: The Earth is composed of land, air, and water. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0AF3CA60DFE5013182B168A86D17958E.description: Write brief informational descriptions of a real object, person, place, or event using information from the observations.

0AF36CE0DFE5013182B068A86D17958E.description: Describe and compare objects in terms of number, shape, texture, size, mass, color, and motion.

0AF31B20DFE5013182AF68A86D17958E.description: Demonstrate that magnifiers help people see small features of objects.

0AF2CEF0DFE5013182AE68A86D17958E.description: Measure the length of objects having straight edges in centimeters or nonstandard units to the nearest unit.

0AF28C30DFE5013182AD68A86D17958E.description: Use tools, such as rulers and magnifiers, to investigate the world and make observations.

0AF24540DFE5013182AC68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and demonstrate what people can learn about plants and animals by observing them closely over a period of time.

0AF20310DFE5013182AB68A86D17958E.description: Investigate and make observations to seek answers to questions.

0AF1BF30DFE5013182AA68A86D17958E.description: Observe, describe, draw, and sort objects as a way of isolating and categorizing some of their properties.

0AF17890DFE5013182A968A86D17958E.description: Scientific progress is made by asking relevant questions and conducting careful investigations. As a basis for understanding this concept, and to address the content in this grade, students should develop their own questions and perform investigations. Students:

document.title: District of Columbia Science Standards

0BF8AE30DFE50131841668A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain that fossils provide evidence of how life and environmental conditions have changed.

0BF86330DFE50131841568A86D17958E.description: Recognize that evidence from geologic layers and radioactive dating indicates that Earth is approximately 4.6 billion years old and life on this planet has existed for more than 3 billion years.

0BF81020DFE50131841468A86D17958E.description: Illustrate and describe that remains of changing life forms are found in successive layers, although the youngest layers are not always found on top because of the folding, breaking, and uplifting of layers.

0BF7C450DFE50131841368A86D17958E.description: Explain how thousands of layers of rock confirm the long history of the changing surface of Earth.

0BF77780DFE50131841268A86D17958E.description: Explain that although weathered rock is the basic component of soil, the composition and texture of soil and its fertility and resistance to erosion are greatly influenced by plant roots and debris, bacteria, fungi, worms, insects, and other organisms.

0BF73490DFE50131841168A86D17958E.description: Describe that the history of life on Earth has been disrupted by major catastrophic events, such as major volcanic eruptions or the impact of asteroids.

0BF6F080DFE50131841068A86D17958E.description: Explain how the Earth's surface is built up and broken down by natural processes, including deposition of sediments, rock formation, erosion, and weathering.

0BF6A830DFE50131840F68A86D17958E.description: Evidence from rocks allows us to understand the evolution of life on Earth. As the basis for understanding this concept, students:

0BF399A0DFE50131840568A86D17958E.description: Explain how physical evidence, such as fossils and surface features of glaciation, supports detailed explanations of how Earth's surface has evolved over geologic time.

0BF34F70DFE50131840468A86D17958E.description: Explain how volcanic activity along the ocean floor may form undersea mountains, which can grow above the ocean's surface to become islands (e.g., the Hawaiian Islands).

0BF30600DFE50131840368A86D17958E.description: Describe that under the ocean basins, molten rock may well up between separating plates to create new ocean floor.

0BF611F0DFE50131840D68A86D17958E.description: Describe how earthquakes and volcanoes often, but not always, occur along the boundaries between plates.

0BF5CEC0DFE50131840C68A86D17958E.description: Explain that earthquakes are sudden motions along breaks in the crust called faults, and volcanoes/fissures are locations where magma reaches the surface as lava.

0BF58C70DFE50131840B68A86D17958E.description: Explain when plates push against each other and neither is dense enough to subduct (both continental), the plates will crumple and fold and form large mountain chains.

0BF54960DFE50131840A68A86D17958E.description: Describe that subducting plates may partially melt and form magma, which rises to the surface as lava to feed volcanoes and form volcanic mountain chains associated with deep-sea trenches.

0BF50400DFE50131840968A86D17958E.description: Explain the process in which plates push against one another, one of them may be dense enough to sink under the other, a process called subduction. Explain that oceanic lithosphere may sink under continental or oceanic lithosphere, but continental lithosphere does not subduct.

0BF4BE00DFE50131840868A86D17958E.description: Compare and contrast oceanic plates and continental plates.

0BF43D40DFE50131840768A86D17958E.description: Explain how lithosphere plates move very slowly, pressing against one another in some places, pulling apart in other places, and sliding past one another in others.

0BF3EB60DFE50131840668A86D17958E.description: Explain why the Earth has a hot interior.

0BF2B830DFE50131840268A86D17958E.description: Describe the solid lithosphere of Earth, including both the continents and the ocean basins, and how it is broken into several plates that ride on a denser, hot, and gradually deformable layer in the mantle called the asthenosphere (weak sphere).

0BCDB0C0DFE50131840168A86D17958E.description: Plate tectonics explain important features of the Earth's surface and major geologic events. As the basis for understanding this concept, students:

0BCD19E0DFE5013183FF68A86D17958E.description: Observe and describe common igneous, metamorphic, and sedimentary rocks, including granite, obsidian, pumice (igneous); slate, schist, marble (metamorphic); sandstone, shale, and limestone (sedimentary).

0BCCCC00DFE5013183FE68A86D17958E.description: Describe how sedimentary rocks are formed when older rocks are subjected to weathering into sediments, and those sediments are eroded, transported, deposited, then compacted and cemented.

0BCC8430DFE5013183FD68A86D17958E.description: Explain how metamorphic rocks are formed when older rocks are heated (short of melting) and/or subjected to increased pressure.

0BCC3140DFE5013183FC68A86D17958E.description: Describe how igneous rocks are formed when older rocks are melted and then recrystallized. Understand they may be cooled deep in the Earth or at or near the surface as part of volcanic systems.

0BCBEFB0DFE5013183FB68A86D17958E.description: Examine and recognize most rocks are made of one or more minerals.

0BCBAD30DFE5013183FA68A86D17958E.description: Recognize minerals are naturally occurring crystalline solids with definite chemical compositions, and identify common minerals using a key to their diagnostic properties.

0BCB5BE0DFE5013183F968A86D17958E.description: Rock materials are continuously recycled in the rock cycle. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0BCA9A40DFE5013183F768A86D17958E.description: Explain the important role of the water cycle within a watershed.

0BCA4350DFE5013183F668A86D17958E.description: Describe that most rainwater that falls in Washington, DC, will eventually drain into the Chesapeake Bay.

0BC9ECA0DFE5013183F568A86D17958E.description: Explain that recycling, reuse, and the development of substitutes can reduce the rate of depletion of many minerals.

0BC99BD0DFE5013183F468A86D17958E.description: Investigate and describe how pollutants can affect weather and the atmosphere.

0BC950F0DFE5013183F368A86D17958E.description: Explain that the atmosphere and the oceans have a limited capacity to absorb wastes and recycle materials naturally.

0BC90C80DFE5013183F268A86D17958E.description: Recognize that the Earth's resources for humans, such as fresh water, air, arable soil, and trees, are finite.

0BC8C220DFE5013183F168A86D17958E.description: Recognize that fresh water is a resource that can be depleted or polluted, making it unavailable or unsuitable for humans.

0BC86960DFE5013183F068A86D17958E.description: Explain that fresh water is limited in supply and uneven in distribution; describe why it is essential for life as we know it and also for most human activities, including industrial processes.

0BC81B80DFE5013183EF68A86D17958E.description: Sources of materials differ in amounts, distribution, usefulness, and the time required for their formation. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0BC770C0DFE5013183ED68A86D17958E.description: Describe how the Earth's atmosphere exerts a pressure that decreases with distance above sea level and, at every point, is the same in all directions.

0BC72B60DFE5013183EC68A86D17958E.description: Describe how climates may have changed abruptly in the past as a result of changes in Earth's crust, such as gas and dust from volcanic eruptions or impacts of meteorites, asteroids, and comets from space.

0BC6E2C0DFE5013183EB68A86D17958E.description: Explain how mountain ranges and other major geographical features affect the climate (e.g., mountains produce rain shadows, land masses interrupt ocean currents).

0BC69020DFE5013183EA68A86D17958E.description: Explain that a great deal of heat energy is absorbed when water evaporates and is released when it condenses. Illustrate that this cycling of water and heat in and out of the atmosphere plays a critical role in climatic patterns.

0BC64B20DFE5013183E968A86D17958E.description: Recognize and describe that the currents in the air and ocean distribute heat energy.

0BC604A0DFE5013183E868A86D17958E.description: Explain how different regions receive different amounts of solar heating because of their latitude, clouds, surface water ice, and other variables. Understand that this results in large-scale convective air flow and weather patterns.

0BC5BA10DFE5013183E768A86D17958E.description: Weather (in the short run) and climate (in the long run) involve the transfer of energy in and out of the atmosphere. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0BC4FE30DFE5013183E568A86D17958E.description: Describe why ocean temperatures, therefore, tend to vary seasonally less than land areas and why coastal areas tend to have cooler summers and warmer winters than inland areas at a similar distance from the poles.

0BC4B240DFE5013183E468A86D17958E.description: Recognize that, compared to other substances such as rock and soil, a given mass of water requires a greater input or output of heat energy to change its temperature by a given amount.

0BC47150DFE5013183E368A86D17958E.description: Explain that much of the heat from the sun is absorbed by the land and oceans and then is released into the atmosphere.

0BC42FB0DFE5013183E268A86D17958E.description: Observe and explain how uneven heating sets up convective cells in the atmosphere and oceans that distribute heat away from the equator.

0BC3EA00DFE5013183E168A86D17958E.description: Describe that the heat from the sun falls on Earth unevenly because of its spherical shape. Describe that regions close to the equator receive more concentrated solar energy than those closer to the poles.

0BC3A5B0DFE5013183E068A86D17958E.description: Explain the meaning of radiation, convection, and conduction (three mechanisms by which heat is transferred to, through, and out of the Earth's system).

0BC35560DFE5013183DF68A86D17958E.description: The transfer of energy through radiation and convection currents affects many phenomena on the Earth's surface. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0BC06850DFE5013183D568A86D17958E.description: Describe that the sun's gravitational attraction holds Earth and the other planets in their orbits, just as the planets' gravitational attraction keeps their moons in orbit around them.

0BC01BF0DFE5013183D468A86D17958E.description: Explain that gravity is a force of attraction that every mass in the universe exerts on every other mass, and everything on or anywhere near Earth is attracted toward and attracts Earth's center by a gravitational force.

0BC2A6C0DFE5013183DD68A86D17958E.description: Recognize that the sun-to-Earth distance is such that it takes about eight minutes for light from the sun to reach Earth. Know that the next nearest star is many thousands of times farther from Earth, and its light takes about four years to reach Earth.

0BC25EF0DFE5013183DC68A86D17958E.description: Recognize and describe the sun as a midsize star located near the edge of a disk-shaped galaxy of stars called the Milky Way. Recognize that the universe contains many billions of galaxies, and each galaxy contains many billions of stars.

0BC20C40DFE5013183DB68A86D17958E.description: Describe that as spring turns to summer at a particular place on Earth, the days grow longer and the sun moves higher in the sky, resulting in more intense heating. In fall and winter, the opposite occurs. Explain how this variation in heating results in the seasons.

0BC1C6C0DFE5013183DA68A86D17958E.description: Construct models or drawings to explain that the seasons are caused by the tilt of the Earth's axis relative to the plane of its orbit and its revolution around the sun. Explain how this results in uneven heating of the various parts of Earth's surface that varies over the course of the year.

0BC17D90DFE5013183D968A86D17958E.description: Describe, as seen from Earth, how planets change their position relative to the background of stars.

0BC131D0DFE5013183D868A86D17958E.description: Explain that large numbers of chunks of rock and ices (asteroids and comets), much smaller than planets, orbit the sun.

0BC0EF70DFE5013183D768A86D17958E.description: Explain that the moon is Earth's only natural satellite, but several of the other planets have natural satellites as well. Understand Earth also has many artificial satellites and that all of these satellites, artificial and natural, are in elliptical orbits around their primaries.

0BC0AD50DFE5013183D668A86D17958E.description: Describe how the planets move around the sun in elliptical orbits, and explain how the near coplanarity of the orbits, along with the principle of conservation of momentum, is evidence essential to our understanding of how the solar system was originally formed.

0BBFABB0DFE5013183D368A86D17958E.description: Recognize that the solar system consists of the Earth, moon, sun, eight generally recognized other planets that orbit the sun and their satellites, and smaller objects, such as asteroids and comets.

0BBF5860DFE5013183D268A86D17958E.description: Astronomy and planetary exploration reveal the structure and scale of the solar system. As a basis for understanding this concept, students:

0BBED280DFE5013183D068A86D17958E.description: Explain that technology is essential to science for such purposes as measurement, data collection, graphing and storage, computation, communication and assessment of information, and access to outer space and other remote locations.

0BBE8E70DFE5013183CF68A86D17958E.description: Explain that computers have become valuable in science because they speed up and extend people's ability to collect, store, compile, and analyze data; prepare research reports; and share data and ideas with investigators all over the world.

0BBE48F0DFE5013183CE68A86D17958E.description: Although each of the human enterprises of science and technology has a character and history of its own, each is dependent on and reinforces the other. Students:

0BBB7610DFE5013183C468A86D17958E.description: Construct and interpret a simple map.

0BBDB3B0DFE5013183CC68A86D17958E.description: Read a topographic map and a geologic map for evidence provided on the maps.

0BBD7170DFE5013183CB68A86D17958E.description: Record and organize information in simple tables and graphs, and identify relationships they reveal. Use tables and graphs as examples of evidence for explanations when writing essays or writing about lab work, fieldwork, etc. Read simple tables and graphs produced by others, and describe in words what they show.

0BBD2B40DFE5013183CA68A86D17958E.description: Draw conclusions based on scientific evidence, and indicate whether further information is needed to support a specific conclusion or to discriminate among several possible conclusions.

0BBCE2F0DFE5013183C968A86D17958E.description: Locate information in reference books, back issues of newspapers and magazines, CD-ROMs, and online databases.

0BBC9CD0DFE5013183C868A86D17958E.description: Write a report of an investigation that includes the problem to be solved, the methods employed, the tests conducted, the data collected or evidence examined, and the conclusions drawn.

0BBC5260DFE5013183C768A86D17958E.description: Recognize and explain that hypotheses are valuable even if they turn out not to be true, but that many investigations are not hypothesis driven.

0BBC04E0DFE5013183C668A86D17958E.description: Identify dependent and independent variables in those investigations that have controls. And, if no controls are used, explain why.

0BBBC030DFE5013183C568A86D17958E.description: Plan and conduct simple investigations based on student-developed questions that pertain to the content under study, and write instructions others can follow in carrying out the investigations.

0BBB2FE0DFE5013183C368A86D17958E.description: Give examples of different ways scientists investigate natural phenomena, and identify processes all scientists use, such as collection of relevant evidence, the use of reasoning, the development and testing of hypotheses, and the use and construction of theory to make sense of the evidence.
