A5685E30B1D945FBB8418B2420A81A4B.description: Analyze the reasons for, and consequences of, choices individuals make when purchasing goods and services.

90695D18E9D3430E9BB6A29193AD7360.description:
Explain how wealth and scarcity affect individual and group power and the ability to make decisions about personal savings
and spending.

F070A968ACCA4B5685AF05816DC97FB8.description:
Describe the goods and services that communities need (e.g., grocery stores, transportation, public safety, etc.) and identify
how they are provided by local government and private businesses.

DE78AB389DEC4B0884546D0E5F2245D6.description:
Explain the varied ways that people labor, define the term income, and describe the kinds of work that people do inside and
outside of the home.

3734862CCC2E47FA87AE54853DCCED11.description:
Describe and locate different human, natural or capital resources in Washington, DC and compare the availability of those
resources across the city.

E60AB5489AC549F7956202B0034BE186.description:
In this driving concept, students will learn basic economic concepts and the various goods, resources and services that meet the
needs of Washingtonians through analyzing how individuals make choices in a free market economy. They will gain an initial
understanding of inequalities across the city by comparing the availability of human, natural, and capital resources.

D048463C93BA4D6482EB97DF13DBF1EB.description: Driving Concept 4: Meeting a Community's Needs

88DB20B529934F6EA137DAD7A9174584.description:
Compare different accounts of the same historical event in Washington, DC and propose possible reasons for the
differences.

663C5BEB034E41899216363BBD74A806.description:
Describe why some groups of people were treated unjustly in the past and identify actions individuals took to promote
greater equality and fairness in society.

04080609760B44A7B5B54E0F3E09BE05.description:
Analyze texts, family, or community stories, and/or historical photographs to compare family, school, and/or community life
in the past and the present.

B994865C9310491891C96FB8CF941896.description: Identify significant events in the history of the school community and explain what makes each event significant.

7A66C1BADC4F48CBB8EFA98B985E9E4F.description:
Analyze maps and images of the Chesapeake region and Washington, DC from different historical periods to describe the
ways the community has changed over time.

16F9F84F130B40039552A248835CF49B.description:
Differentiate between events that happened long ago and events that happened in the not-so-distant past and order the
events on a timeline.

30959C9F7C864A088CD33705D5969158.description:
Through this driving concept, students will analyze the ways Washington, DC has changed over time, using maps, images, and
storytelling about significant events and people in Washington, DC’s history. Students will compare life in the past to life in the
present to build an understanding of how and why people made changes to the city.

A3979D82B1F84D52A2EBE9864B57F127.description: Driving Concept 3: My Community Then and Now

4A0EA78AFCE143C1BEC1B6A4BB34D71A.description: Identify a problem caused by humans to the local environment and propose a solution.

3751D1A6AAD9487B9A431DA8707BED1E.description:
Describe how location, weather, and physical environment affect the way people live, including the effects on their food,
clothing, shelter, transportation, and recreation.

B90D467044F54368B23B8CA52E490F4D.description:
Describe how and why people have changed the physical landscape of the local community and/or the greater Washington,
DC area over time.

F134F1F8D65D48ACBA708B6388BD419C.description:
Construct a simple map of the classroom, school, or local community, using cardinal directions, physical features, and map
symbols.

7FA3AEADAD864389BAE8A09B7E97C285.description:
Describe the absolute and relative locations of Washington, DC area institutions, businesses, or landmarks, and describe the
physical characteristics of those places.

90E68A7C864D433C8A227A625AB1497F.description: Locate and explain physical features on maps (e.g., mountains, oceans, rivers, lakes, etc.).

FBF5FAEAB3694708A18E463D86FEADD1.description: Compare the features of a city, county, state, country, and continent.

953016F602EE4212B8EA19DBC9DC4FD5.description:
Identify the local neighborhood, Washington, DC, the United States, and North America on a map, and identify key political
features of the region.

3EB751E87BF14547A0F678C38EF83973.description: Analyze different representations of Washington, DC to make a claim about different places in the District.

2DB63E17C523412DBF2DA6CFF9A4280A.description:
In this driving concept, students analyze what makes their space in Washington, DC unique, using map skills and historical
sources to clarify how humans changed the landscape of the city over time. Students will evaluate and propose solutions for a
local environmental issue in the city.

A8C05CD0AC8F4DCEAD2D29ED3883F7B2.description:
Identify issues or needs in the school, local, or global community that students care about, and generate possible actions to
create positive change.

AE20EC976703413B8CA6A62041E2E7CA.description:
Identify a source of information about Washington, DC, and explain how the author’s job, training, and/ or experiences
effect the reliability of information.

C89DEAB1780C4456A3E891047EF2433D.description:
Describe how voting and elections can exemplify democratic principles, including but not limited to equality, freedom,
fairness, respect for individual rights, citizen participation, majority rules, and accepting the results of an election.

D0072FBABF6041C98FD30DFBA95D99CC.description: Describe how voting and elections determine who will be president, vice president, and mayor.

A1B667C09D7749618664E130E47EE6BE.description:
Identify community leaders from the past (e.g. George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Susan B. Anthony, Harriet Tubman,
Dolores Huerta, Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., Harvey Milk, Wilma Pearl Mankiller, Lee Yick, and Liliʻuokalani) and compare how
each person created change.

DD4629E690B7418C95F700084F8C8BE9.description:
Identify symbols, songs, and phrases that unify the community of the United States and symbols and songs that unify
different communities within the United States, as well as national holidays that commemorate American history.

7AF10774448B4BA89A8E4AE095DAD7BA.description:
Identify and describe the roles and responsibilities of current leaders, including the president of the United States and the
mayor of Washington, DC.

114823DE2D5E4D1D94B997C71E8685E6.description: Describe the responsibilities of a leader, and identify characteristics of effective and just leaders.

DEB889FCE4DD494FB7D39672A80353FF.description:
Describe how different individuals and groups in a local or global community provide services, uphold rights, and work to
promote the common good for all members.

13240B4979804153817D163685453E14.description: Evaluate the rules and processes of the classroom, and identify characteristics of just and effective rules and laws.

3BD63146D9B54DCFB8FAF834FF4113CE.description:
Identify and define the rights of learners in the classroom community, and describe how individuals can work together to
respect the rights of community members.

82DE4D6A30BB436AAE8AB7F9AF615A59.description:
Describe ways in which groups of people in the same community can hold different beliefs and live their daily lives in
different ways, while still working together toward shared goals.

DFFF0DA95CC0450B984E4E9761AEF690.description:
Explain the ways in which different populations, including but not limited to, Latinx, Black, Asian, immigrant, religious, and
Indigenous communities, have shaped and defined the community of Washington, DC.

2C520BD1406042BEB1A04AFEC751607C.description:
Describe the ways individuals with different backgrounds, including ethnicity, gender, religion, sexual orientation, ability,
economic status, and beliefs are all part of the same community.

6C2C7AF0A66C42D0B1DC8C8D791DFD79.description: Explain what constitutes a community and describe characteristics of different communities.

4902FAA39A56487DA5C99F17DBB06A97.description:
In this driving concept, students will identify and compare different types of community (e.g., their neighborhood, city, and
nation) and the ways that they define leadership, decision-making, conflict resolution, and change-making. Students will
evaluate the various communities that they are a part of (classroom, neighborhood, and world) and analyze the characteristics of
a just, inclusive, and free society. Teachers should use read-aloud texts, images, songs, artifacts, and other materials that detail
the contributions of leaders and community members from the past and present.

document.title: Washington, DC K-12 Social Studies Standards Revised Standards

3637A0F85A3041E9B88D8C536B03185A.description:
Identify a current sustainability challenge and develop an action plan for increasing sustainability in the community or
globally.

6525F8EFC32D4112AF6908891C7C7470.description:
Evaluate local and global methods of human-environment interactions (e.g., farming, other forms of water and land use) to
identify practices that may be considered sustainable.

19405D02EC8E4165A2F71A8EAB75EB4C.description: Explain how the climate has changed from long ago to today and explain how the changing climate impacts life on Earth.

05F03BD19E3E4A5AA9FF25928D22D735.description: Explain how people use water and land today to produce or grow food.

2152C2D9CD9E4886855A88BF10E52D72.description:
In the final driving concept of Grade 2, students will apply what they have learned about the past to analyze the ways people use
land and water today. Students will analyze current agricultural practices to make a claim about the role of sustainability and
make a claim about what kinds of practices best ensure a healthy future.

201D9170460440F6B3D9F41DE6F971D6.description: Compare the social or political structures of societies in Africa, Europe, the Americas, and Asia between 1200 and 1600.

1C61D75F4544440C9966A92D9458524F.description:
Compare gender roles and the daily lives of individuals across societies in Africa, Europe, the Americas, and Asia between
1200 and 1600, and explain how women exercised power in different contexts.

F1EB8EB75AF84073857EDA13CEFA6D09.description:
Analyze primary sources to describe at least two of the significant architectural, cultural, and technological innovations of
the Aztec and Incan Kingdoms between 1200 and 1600

2D82D118F28A4118861FAB3FB0304BC1.description:
Analyze primary sources to describe at least two of the significant architectural, cultural, and technological innovations of
the Ottoman, Safavid, or Mughal Empires between 1200 and 1600.

B18144A03BC142E79F3D9C144B1464DD.description:
Analyze primary sources to describe at least two of the significant architectural, cultural, and technological innovations of
the monarchies in England, Spain, or France between 1200 and 1600.

12B2D787AB6A4AAA9D73A3D51366DBAF.description:
Analyze primary sources to describe at least two of the significant architectural, cultural, and technological innovations of
the empires in Mali, Songhai, or Gedi between 1200 and 1600.

2486679549EF4C9C8A5E995996CBB1BA.description:
In this driving concept, students will analyze the growth of societies between 1200 and 1500. Students will analyze how societies
grew and organized into kingdoms and cities, how they functioned as communities, and the impact of their technology,
government and innovations today.

6EE5AEBC51F7463DBCF7B845D1CF969A.description: Driving Concept 4: Kingdoms, Cities and Communities

F29D61917607423E90E65157CC6B14CE.description:
Analyze the daily lives of different individuals in ancient societies including histories of same-sex relationships and gender
fluidity in civilizations.

4B1F18FCAE084475BF146E6EE77C0862.description:
Describe governing and social structures developed in the Americas, Ancient Rome, and ancient China, including female-led
kingdoms and matriarchal societies.

B94C3125A4764DCDA0E777B02D42930E.description:
Compare the scientific and technological innovations across the Americas, Ancient Rome, and Ancient China (e.g., alphabets
and language systems, roads, aqueducts, etc.).

62CC56BB276D491DAFBB9C866AC37FAA.description:
Compare the physical structures constructed across the Americas, Ancient Rome, and Ancient China and analyze the
purposes of these structures (e.g., temples, pyramids, walls, etc.).

1B29E9A7FE6F4D0F96E772F69BDB1B13.description: Compare the crops grown in ancient civilizations across the Americas, Ancient Rome, and Ancient China.

C9F6C7953D7F477384948A3EF9B3D0CA.description: Explain the utility of different artifacts –– such as photographs, renderings, petroglyphs, cave dwellings, etc. –– and textbased sources in answering questions about the past.

A6CB85C6DFD544AF913C264FE8C6B26D.description:
Locate and identify key geographic characteristics of Central America, South America, Ancient China, and Ancient Rome
(e.g., bodies of water, landforms, climate, etc.).

BD6AE1342BF54301A409A2B98AA7E010.description:
In this driving concept, students will analyze how people lived long ago in other places of the world. Students will study empires
across the Americas, as well as civilizations that developed in other parts of the world, such as Southern Europe, Eastern Asia, or Eastern Africa. Students will evaluate the role physical geography played in the development of scientific and technological
innovations across civilizations.

2B0A8A337AF04576A59FC0321AF0EF5F.description: Driving Concept 3: Innovations of Long Ago

EBBE74FED3C947F9BA5984089B177D38.description:
Compare and describe basic features of government of early civilizations, such as the priesthoods and kings of
Mesopotamia, the pharaohs of Egypt, monarchy of Olmec, and the ruling queens of Kush (e.g., identify patrilineal and
matrilineal practices; Hatshepsut was a female pharaoh of Egypt, etc.).

7C2EA332B70C4940A5655D79631C9A37.description:
Compare scientific, religious, and technological innovations of early civilizations, such as the ziggurats of Mesopotamia, the
pyramids of Egypt and Kush, and Olmec architecture.

5399B509A3674A4CAB4B866073687B8A.description: Compare cultural elements of early civilizations, such as forms of writing or art in Egypt, Kush, Mesopotamia, and Olmec.

E012D220D2C4406A9E2F5A0177137E97.description:
Compare the different kinds of jobs or social roles of ancient people in Egypt, Kush, Mesopotamia, and Olmec and how they
were filled by people of different genders.

42373D02C83B4F2D8FAFC37EBE59B47C.description:
Compare examples of how food was grown in ancient civilizations such as Egypt, Kush, Mesopotamia, and Olmec to how
food is grown by people around the world today.

EAFDF38F3D5F402A83BA17B2BB676C2F.description:
Explain the importance of using water to grow a food source and the importance of developing systems of irrigation,
especially in early civilizations, such as Egypt, Kush, Mesopotamia, and Olmec.

C2489E895AFB48B98485EB3329A91AAC.description:
Describe characteristics of “ancient civilizations,” with a focus on using water and land for large-scale farming and explain
that governments helped oversee the distribution of resources.*

DF836E1FC39F41BEAD0DA06C0AEF52D2.description:
Analyze artifacts –– such as photographs, renderings, petroglyphs, cave dwellings, etc. –– and text-based sources to explain
how historians learn about the past.

3F09B3165F804D5F987286B7F6EB65F6.description:
Through this driving concept, students will develop historical and geographic inquiry skills to evaluate how historians know what
they know about the past. Students will evaluate the accomplishments of ancient Egypt, Kush, Mesopotamia, and Olmec
societies to understand how people used water and land to develop large-scale farming methods. Students will use primary
sources to analyze the scientific and technological innovations of ancient societies, and make comparisons between ancient
societies and contemporary life.

1DB3A8020A57404F8F45E111851E7F6B.description: Compare different ways people get food and water today locally, nationally and globally.

CBA0D406B05E47888EFCC0DA1724CEF8.description: Explain the difference between needs and wants, and identify the essential needs of all humans.

95CC4E60FC9A443DBEB6A1AD2D5FFBE1.description: Analyze data, images, maps, and texts to compare how different people around the world live today.

CD23E2262AF243C5B87DCAE7403351B0.description: Identify and explain the different climate or weather patterns in different global regions.

408BF7E0F64C485ABA628959D118D76E.description:
Identify and locate the seven continents and five oceans using maps, and describe major geographic features around the
world (e.g., coast, bay, gulf, sea, delta, river, lake, peninsula, plain, mountain, canyon, volcano, etc.).

12770E090D3C46189C9DA5AD9346EF47.description:
Create and compare visual representations (e.g., mind maps, concept mapping, spider diagrams) of communities and school
spaces.

18C609757AE7457BA3DA204E2AEFF82C.description:
Compare different kinds of maps, with a focus on physical and political maps, and identify key parts of a map (e.g., title of
map, legend or key, scale, compass or cardinal directions, etc.).

22294EB3061F4328A2035CC0F8A72829.description:
Compare different representations of the Washington, DC and Chesapeake region, including maps representing the political
geography of Indigenous Nations, to develop claims about the changes to the region over time.

5B67587A6DEB4ECE98EFBE2F6468A146.description:
In this driving concept, students will compare life in the past to life in the present using political and physical maps, as well as
other image and text-based resources, to develop their mapping skills and understanding of geography. Beginning with a lens of
inquiry, students will first analyze their own lens or position in the world, identifying their “local” sense of place to position
themselves within the context of the larger world. Students will analyze ways people engage with the environment and the
impact of the environment on human interactions.

9272B041D99F48ED96931CF32CD89A7E.description: Driving Concept 1: Understanding Ourselves in the Larger World

document.title: Washington, DC K-12 Social Studies Standards Revised Standards

432C106F6BBC4F5BB8271D8B9AC6CC83.description: Evaluate the origins and consequences of conflicting narratives about the Civil War and Reconstruction.

6E561A48A54A4111BC4EE5DD13216959.description:
Analyze the legacy of unresolved challenges facing the nation after the Compromise of 1877, including the continued impact
of the Reconstruction era on American Democracy.

B84F2E02FEE34DE28012677F2E17390C.description:
Analyze American military actions against Indigenous Nations during the Civil War and Reconstruction, and the impact of the
Civil War on the sovereignty of Indigenous Nations.

67C6B8DD0DF143238569A303E26516C4.description:
Analyze the rise of white supremacy and racial violence during Reconstruction – including incidents of mass racial violence –
and the impact of so-called “Black Codes” on Black Americans.

7B80F33BE4FC4D7CAD48584A063E40AD.description: Evaluate the reasons for, and tactics of, challenges to federal initiatives begun during Reconstruction, and assess their shortand long-term effects using primary and secondary sources.

85F05AA19227440CAB02A0EA0914539E.description:
Use primary and secondary sources to analyze the ways and means by which formerly enslaved persons created new lives for
themselves in the South, North and West following the legal end of slavery.

A88F4DB906A74FAEA135D6A7BBBC6810.description:
Explain the impact of grassroots efforts by Black Americans to gain access to land and fair labor, participate in political,
economic, and legal systems (including voting), and achieve public education, in reconstituting a multiracial, democratic society.

778F0643633146A5969836ACB0E87B54.description:
Compare different federal approaches toward and policies of Reconstruction (e.g., Abraham Lincoln, Andrew Johnson, and
the Congressional Republican plan), evaluating their rationale and impact.

98FBC62FF2404D18AC49B35741C37420.description:
Evaluate the impact of the 13th, 14th, and 15th amendments on the lived experiences of Black Americans, including the
extent to which each amendment expanded freedom and constitutional protections for Black Americans.

3E36D49E52334F5A8213778CECCAD9BA.description:
Through this driving concept, students will analyze the impact of Reconstruction on American life and politics following the Civil
War. Using primary and secondary sources, students will analyze the tangible accomplishments of liberated Black Americans and
the significance of the 13th, 14th and 15th Constitutional amendments. Students will also analyze the political and violent
opposition that emerged as a direct response to Reconstruction. Throughout the unit, students will assess the extent to which
Reconstruction presented a turning point in American history and evaluate its impact on ongoing efforts to achieve racial
equality.

3D3FCC27466F4909BEF452380334BA58.description: Driving Concept 7: Unresolved: The Reconstruction Era (1865–1877)

CF7B741D7BCB446A8F626172ED5D8310.description:
Assess the source of a webpage or digital resource about the Civil War using strategies like lateral reading to evaluate the
reliability of the source.

B8FFD2EF96604571ACB98B35F49256D4.description: Analyze the methods of abolition and emancipation undertaken by enslaved people during the course of the Civil War.

7B501A71294A472B892CF69904E08361.description:
Use context to assess the reasons for Abraham Lincoln’s issuance of the Emancipation Proclamation, evaluating its short- and
long-term impact.

9167405D3AAD4BAC82D5F0C8FA2331BB.description: Evaluate the role of women, civilians, free Black Americans, religious minorities and Indigenous Nations in the Civil War.

3AEAE6CEA6FA4314B36BA34811DFE8AD.description:
Compare the Union and Confederate approaches to the war, including strategy, resources, technology and international
support shaped its course and outcome.

21358245C4D94C469694E4C28738E181.description:
Use primary sources to analyze the Union rationale for the Civil War, including the perspectives of Frederick Douglass,
abolitionists, and Northerners who were not pro-abolition.

1464F2B57D5A4DDA8BCED2D2A8AD65D2.description:
Use primary sources to evaluate the reasons for the start of the Civil War, including the decision of Southern states to secede
from the United States to protect the institution of slavery.

DC4E136A618146D297AFEE03FCA36FB2.description:
Evaluate the impact of territorial expansion and the conflict over the expansion of slavery on sectional tensions between
Northern and the Southern states.

1ACC531105AC46C3A2D4AEB139253FFE.description:
Through this driving concept, students will understand that the unresolved issue of slavery and debates over its expansion
divided American public into geographic and political factions that eventually resulted in the Civil War. Students will study the
role of significant leaders in the course of the Civil War, including the leadership of Abraham Lincoln. Finally, students will
investigate the short- and long-term impact of the Civil War on different factions of American society.

819EA352AC0B4E4D9311ED32DF2D8816.description:
Analyze societal confines and constraints within social reform movements of the early 19th century, including the role of
gender, sexuality, religion, and race.

3ECF0688EB934DBB817B87A984F48F2A.description:
Compare gender rights and roles in different geographic regions and communities within the United States, and evaluate the
goals and tactics, of the women’s suffrage movement.

57FD3D1E11D14773921C921D9BF8201F.description:
Evaluate the political, social, and economic opportunities and challenges faced by Indigenous Nations and Mexicans living in
land incorporated into America after 1848.

25699FA57EE248BA8594E9D77352FF8D.description:
Evaluate the reasons for Asian immigration to the United States, the political, social and economic opportunities and
challenges faced by Asian immigrants and the ways individuals demonstrated resilience.

6FDC6C3BC37E4AA2AC5E041A915EECAF.description:
Evaluate the growth and international context of the abolitionist movement, including the effectiveness of various tactics
and leaders by analyzing primary and secondary sources –– including the perspectives of abolitionists including, Sojourner Truth,
Harriet Tubman, Elizabeth Freeman, Henry Highland Garnet, and Frederick Douglass.

BE932B1A8D64458C93632564D2F2C206.description: Analyze the complex and varied lives and experiences of enslaved people and free Black Americans.

186571FE5AEE43CEACB3EA1E9BBFD2AB.description:
Use charts, graphs, and data to evaluate the institution of slavery on the economic growth of the United States between
1800 and 1861, with a particular focus on the impact of the invention of the cotton gin.

315DECFDEAE94EC8AA6261EC85D4AFCB.description:
Through this driving concept, students will consider the complexity of American History by examining primary and secondary
sources that reveal the horrors and brutality of enslavement. Students will also investigate the means by which enslaved persons
resisted and maintained humanity. Students will contextualize the emergence of varying forms of abolitionism within a broader
social and religious movement that called for reforms to American social and political life.

0C0135BF39C949BDB14C7CA7716231BB.description:
Evaluate the impact of territorial expansion, immigration, and Northern industrialization on the institution of slavery and
American politics.

8402BFF60534480594287061370B70EA.description:
Evaluate the causes and consequences of the Mexican-American War, with specific attention to the impact of the war and
the Treaty of Guadalupe-Hidalgo on Mexicans and Indigenous peoples living in the newly acquired American territories.

6B5F79BFEC2C4C8B95587CAC1B59241E.description:
Analyze the perspectives and actions (both adaptation and resistance) of Indigenous Nations in response to territorial
invasion using primary and secondary sources.

79076AA8FB5E47FEB2C5BD60AA26E3B7.description:
Compare and evaluate the actions taken and rationales provided by the United States government to acquire western or
Indigenous territory in the 1800s, with particular attention given to the policies and campaigns of President Andrew Jackson and
the consequences such actions had on the land and people.

2B21DBC38D904A4D99463EC6AA71DB5B.description: Evaluate the experiences of free Black communities in the American Northwest.

5414EA97503F4091A356F6E011062562.description:
Evaluate the reason different individuals, including Federalists, Abolitionists, and Democratic-Republicans supported and
opposed American territorial expansion.

9E84466596DB40308594D466ED58E616.description:
Compare and evaluate the different ways in which the United States acquired territory from 1800 to 1860, including an
evaluation of the Louisiana Purchase.

FA1777975AAF48B0A3B3476605043386.description:
Assess the extent to which perspectives toward American territorial expansion, including Manifest Destiny and Indigenous
resistance, changed over time, including an understanding that the removal of Indigenous Nations was not inevitable.

1CB1178695B94A7F914B1D4A11E61FA6.description:
Through this driving concept, students should study the expansion of the United States by interrogating the idea of Manifest
Destiny and analyzing the experiences of different individuals as the United States expanded west. Students will study the
treaties, financial agreements and wars that precipitated expansion, as well as the political and indigenous opposition to
territorial acquisition. Throughout this driving concept, students should analyze the continued growth of slavery and how it
perpetuated an imbalance of power between slave states and free states.

8C76963F30FF468285AA6E15A1A1DAC1.description: Driving Concept 4: Invasion and Control: Expansion of the Nation (1800-1860)

4907D55293CD42D1A5BCF6DFD2112D2A.description:
Analyze the social and political changes during the Jacksonian era, including the expansion of voting rights, from multiple
perspectives, and evaluate the legacy of these changes.

55A4361ADD824CB39790E25D230CF102.description:
Evaluate the legacy of the presidential elections of 1800, 1876, 2000, and 2020 to evaluate the significance of peaceful
transfers of power and their impact on democratic ideals.

119DB1C1BFDE425C805DD9F5423FAF90.description:
Analyze the international and domestic disputes that shaped the formation of early political parties such as the Federalists
and the Democratic-Republicans and the short-and long-term significance of these disputes.

8AB0F6A093AC442E80631A6D24A40C00.description:
Analyze the daily lives of those who were not allowed to participate in the formation of the US government or were denied
access to civil rights, such as voting and/or citizenship using primary sources (e.g., the writings of Olaudah Equiano and Harriet
Jacobs).

332E032B5FD74C8D8A05475A0B9E7E20.description:
Analyze the presidency and legacy of George Washington, including his legacy as an enslaver and as a leader who voluntarily
relinquished political power.

A2B8A887175B4B94A312BFE1FF960B93.description:
Analyze the political debate regarding the location of the national capital, the compromise that led to the establishment of
the District of Columbia and the consequences of the compromise for DC residents.

C85362EB1F484C8EB916BFB74799C1EB.description:
Evaluate the reasons for the creation of the Bill of Rights and determine the extent to which the fundamental liberties
ensured by the Bill of Rights were equitably and fairly applied to people within the United States.

C09BA89E9057416B8E17684B2168C51A.description:
Compare the US Constitution to the Articles of the Confederation, Haudenosaunee Confederacy and the British Government
by examining differences or similarities in government structure and power, as well as individual rights and liberties.

C596A0BFB1FA49A8B8EC871610049B35.description:
Evaluate the arguments of the Federalists and the Anti-Federalists, including a focus on individual rights and the size of the
republic, and explain how historical context shaped these arguments.

3F661886C8DF4AF2AC34D65CB952BF44.description:
Explain the structure, power, and function of the federal government created by the Constitution, including key
constitutional principles such as the division of power between federal and state government, the creation of checks and
balances, the sovereignty of the people, limited government, and judicial independence.

C266A247CF6744D89901A4D493B8FBA6.description:
Evaluate the issue of slavery at the Constitutional Convention through primary and secondary sources, analyzing the
attempted rationale and implications of its protection in the Constitution, including how the decision reinforced the institution of
slavery and the power of states in which slavery was prevalent.

1FBA299B74C049F084B1EBEE3D4E78D6.description:
Identify key individuals at the Constitutional Convention and evaluate the consequences of the compromises that emerged
to secure ratification by the states, including the distribution of political power, rights of the states, and the make up of the Senate
and Electoral College.

A5C3AD0E09054A2C9DCB56AB9DB84B5D.description:
Analyze the strengths and weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation, evaluating the competing arguments for and against
revision.

161D314CD37F47F8ACE388B2C3F38AC8.description:
Through this driving concept, students will analyze the context in which the representative democracy of the United States was
created –– evaluating its promise, contributions, and shortcomings. To begin their investigation, students will analyze the
government created by the founders, and assess the reasons for and the impact of compromises made during the Constitutional
Convention, as well as the Constitution’s inclusion of specific guarantees of individual liberty, and the ways they were and/or
were not universal in their intent or application. Throughout their study, students will analyze key founding documents as well as
source material from individuals who supported and opposed the adoption of the Constitution, and the impact it continues to
have on our lives today.

0FDF567F8D774CCB8821C3F13EEE3BE1.description:
Driving Concept 3: A Newly Formed, Diverse Nation: Confederation to Constitution
(1770s-1800s)

18FA281C785D4F3BB9ACFE22CFBAD75D.description:
Analyze the impact of the Revolution on the social and political status of different groups in the new nation, including but not
limited to women, Indigenous Nations, enslaved and free Black Americans, religious minorities, and white people of various
socioeconomic groups (e.g., rural farmers, Southern planters, urban craftsmen, Northern merchants, etc.).

AF0CB6348E8A49C4A4EA47919AB75E5E.description:
Compare the causes and impacts of the American Revolution to revolutions in Haiti, France, and Bolivarian revolutions in
Latin America.

32095196726346C5BB67AA502C425402.description:
Evaluate the immediate impact of the Revolutionary War on the new country’s domestic and international relations,
including the impact of the Treaty of Paris on Indigenous Nations.

A2FC7A8583B64434BD05B36F4ABDA48B.description: Evaluate the reasons for American colonial victory over the British Empire.

C20EC1E4C8D0430AA14D6753B824D01D.description:
Compare multiple perspectives of participants during the Revolutionary War, including military leaders like George
Washington and everyday efforts across colonial society.

659F4931F61D46168CC7A095B0F8A3B8.description:
Use historical context to analyze the ideals contained in the Declaration of Independence, identifying Thomas Jefferson as a
main contributor, and critiquing the extent to which such ideals have fully applied to the people of the United States –– from the
Revolutionary era to today.

A6B57109156F47C4833DD5F36920A045.description:
Evaluate the contributions of key figures during the Revolutionary era, including but not limited to, George Washington, John
and Abigail Adams, Phillis Wheatley, Benjamin Franklin, Thomas Jefferson, and James Armistead Lafayette.

25B8B3F5AA21463EA2D5C98D6BE5A27D.description:
Evaluate the economic, political, and ideological reasons for the movement for independence from England and construct a
timeline of key events including the Stamp Act, Boston Massacre, Boston Tea Party, and the Battle at Lexington and Concord.

BC319FB009E64E01867C21AEF0A366CA.description:
Compare reasons for and the consequences of different colonial responses to British economic and political policies following
the French and Indian War.

446E5EF7E7844CC4967C4DA77FB222F6.description:
Analyze the experiences, perspectives, and identities of people who were denied access (e.g., enslaved people, women, free
Black people, religious minorities,
DRAFT
etc.) to full rights across the colonies, including citizenship, marriage and voting restrictions.

35C8407CC51C4B7B9AE200087F45F8E6.description:
Evaluate the causes of the social and legal codification of race in the colonial era and the proliferations of a race-based
hierarchy, including the impact of Bacon’s Rebellion.

3AB73AE70F1842A29CC7653F196C8A96.description: Compare the different ways that Indigenous Nations resisted British colonizing forces.

49CFBEE87A4B47FE9421065236BF2155.description:
Analyze the lived experiences and culture of early colonists, free Black people, enslaved people, women, religious minorities,
and indentured servants across the colonies.

00C4D7C1159744578840A3AFC2B4E18D.description:
Analyze the experience, perspectives, and identities of Africans who were enslaved from the start of the transatlantic trade
through bondage, including the codification of race as a tool of oppression and resistance to enslavement.

45C4EFC7AE4442C18D0AD3EFF15F40FE.description:
Compare the motivations of different groups who settled in the Thirteen Colonies, and analyze the impact of these
differences on the political, demographic, religious, and social features of the Thirteen Colonies.

D8E54697698A487DA84FD583A371766F.description:
Analyze the reasons for and impact of Spanish colonization and settlement in the Southern and Western United States during
the period, including resistance to Spanish colonization by Indigenous Nations.

5B31C75630DB47E49BEF9ACC43E57BE4.description:
Identify and analyze global trade routes and their impact on the formation of the European colonies throughout the
Americas –– including North, Central, and South America and the Caribbean –– as well as the impact on African and European
society.

36A51AB550E54F33B8866AD36FF83E7B.description:
Compare the economic, religious, and political motives that led to the establishment of early, distinct European colonies in
the Americas.

0A0202E3226C434CAF8E8E95A87C9F8F.description:
Analyze how the concepts of whiteness and blackness changed across time and place (e.g., the “one-drop rule,” Benjamin
Franklin’s “Observations Concerning the Increase of Mankind,” Race in Cuba)

AA243762DF9F42D99DAFD24ADD8FC54D.description:
Through this driving concept, students will develop and refine their inquiry skills as they evaluate historical evidence to support
arguments about colonization and the American Revolution. Students will analyze multiple perspectives and interpretations,
drawing conclusions about the causes and effects of historical events in the colonial and revolutionary era. To develop an
understanding of the different ways individuals may have experienced daily life, students will study laws and interactions that
impacted Europeans colonists, people of African descent, and Indigenous Nations. Students will analyze the changing relationship between the colonial governments and Britain, analyzing the reasons that individuals and groups within the diverse
American population supported or opposed independence from the British.
Students will also contextualize concepts such as liberty, freedom, and democracy, comparing their use in justifications for
independence and the extent to which they were applied to different Americans on the basis of religion, socio-economic status
or class, race, and gender.

3C5BF8FCCD9A431BBFB5208B467B4387.description:
Assess the ways Indigenous Nations have been portrayed in American history and popular culture and the limitations of such
portrayals in understanding the diverse communities that comprise the “Native American” identity.

FB5FBE529FEB4EED8F70B19FAF1B789B.description:
Analyze the economic and cultural impact of what is often referred to as the “Columbian Exchange,” or the widespread
transfer of diseases, commodities, people, animals, and ideas as a result of European colonization and interaction with the
Americas and other parts of the world

32BAC7E664C24BDB84365BFE592EB23E.description:
Evaluate the impact of the arrival of Europeans from the perspective of Indigenous Americans, including the effects of
warfare and diplomacy, the immense loss of life and land, the impact on Indigenous sovereignty, and the role of conquest and
disease using primary and secondary sources.

974CA843A1354793A31E482B97A944F1.description:
Compare Indigenous and European perspectives of early contact, with attention to the limitations of using European sources
to understand the history and culture of Indigenous Nations.

299F261FA55F40F59531D9A3620DEDCD.description:
Analyze the impact of the arrival of European colonists in the Americas using primary and secondary sources, including
population data.

D1A677C0E545470BBEC30A91497A01AB.description:
Evaluate European colonists’ ideas about religion and conquest including the conception of the “New World” between 1400
and 1600.

20C56022F1D0466FB73479C15B8A1581.description:
Compare the different cultural and religious and/or spiritual belief systems of early Indigenous societies, with a particular
focus on the role of gender and family, including the history of two-spirit identities between 1400 and 1600.

FD7842EAC0E14461BF75B51E6E3E3AA9.description:
Compare the complex systems of governments of at least three Indigenous societies, including chiefdoms and structures that
had democratic characteristics between 1400 and 1600.

92EBA5A8A96C43D4BA9A76567B70F32F.description:
Evaluate the agricultural developments and accomplishments of at least three Indigenous societies in the Americas between
1400 and 1600ز

67A99AF6672D4FF8A57E0A3F202C3C0F.description:
Explain the development of technological and scientific innovations of at least three Indigenous societies between the 1400
and 1600.

FC17EAA59FEB459788BAA2D8B7374707.description:
Compare the different ways societies adapted to the land and climate and how they shaped their environments between
1400 and 1600.

A41EF2545C6146D8B56B1CFF1505D5A0.description: Locate and identify Indigenous Nations, tribes, and/or communities from the 1400s through the present day on maps.

F2682E5244714FFEA73FE64719A2F11B.description:
Analyze the collection and use of anthropological and archeological evidence to draw conclusions about Indigenous societies
in the Americas, including an analysis of the tension between Western anthropological/ archeological practices and Indigenous
scientific knowledge.

6D3620F16CF243D9BD6F9A5CDAE0689F.description:
Evaluate historical and cultural sources –– archaeological, genetic, and linguistic evidence, and Indigenous Nations creation
stories –– to support claims about the history of early human migration to the Americas.

2790F400E8724362B41A7F0CC2982D37.description:
Through this driving concept, students will analyze the scientific and cultural innovations of diverse, Indigenous societies across
the Americas, with particular attention to the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries. Using historical evidence, students will interrogate
the origins of the idea that the Americas were a lightly populated wilderness prior to European contact by studying the complex
and highly organized societies of Indigenous communities and nations of the Eastern Coast of North America along with the
chiefdoms of the Southeast. Students will review primary and secondary sources –– including both Indigenous and European
accounts –– to analyze the geographical, political, and social impact of early interactions, with themes of both conquest and
resilience.

5605E96A7F564D159C29B921FD2DA6F6.description:
Driving Concept 1: Indigenous Nations and Early European Colonization: Political, Social,
and Economic Structures of the Americas in the 15th and 16th Century

document.title: Washington, DC K-12 Social Studies Standards Revised Standards

1CD8D66E919E423CA144CE51B2D8E9C9.description:
Analyze the characteristics and causes of at least one contemporary issue facing the global community, compare proposals
for addressing the issue, and propose a course of action for making change.

32DCA3F0AB6F41F4B308C210FB43A1E9.description: Use maps to examine global trade markets and to evaluate the spatiality of global supply chains.

18C3A03454404BF4890F7EA25C3EF7BF.description: Evaluate the credibility of online sources and claims about climate change using strategies like lateral reading.

602547571754460494A8CB0FC150D1C8.description:
Identify and explain the human causes and results of climate change, including on species extinction, and compare the
responses of at least three individuals, groups, or governments around the world.

906E12844F3A456280578FD5B53442B1.description:
Evaluate the positive and negative effects of globalization, and the differing impact of globalization on at least three
regions.

FCEBBD76B6544BD9A957E42BFE4C1E53.description: Analyze the various causes of globalization, including advancements in communication and technology.

1A15007C48CB40049FF2CB7D07AA8719.description:
In this driving concept, students synthesize their understanding of world geography and contemporary global issues. By
examining international and supranational organizations and systems, students will return to the study of power and bias that
was the foundation for the course. Students will explore real world examples of the role these systems play in modern events,
and further consider ways to take action as a global citizen.

D7E7A167C1264FD5ABA2FD8A9CD639DF.description: Driving Concept 8: Thinking and Acting Globally

77BDA95F915043FFAA05B01E2CF65ED5.description:
Identify a Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) and assess options for individual and/or collection options for taking action
to address the causes and impacts of challenges facing a region, city or country in Oceania.

9F7BEE57F99243D19763D860A7BAA783.description:
Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology influence the connections between people and
affect the spread of idea/or cultural practice within Oceania and between Oceania and other regions.

A18817F74DCA41A193F3065A0986531E.description:
Analyze the reasons for, and consequences of, the migration of people within, from, and/or to at least one region or
country within Oceania over time, and assess the impact of migration on the region, with specific attention to the role of climate
change on migration from Oceania.

1380531AFF96474A8398AC88CFD36825.description: Analyze the impact of climate change on at least one region, country, or city within Oceania.

21E336975C03402394C6BEBF370F93B6.description:
Use physical, cultural, and economic maps to draw regions on Oceania and compare these to the existing region's economic
communities.

5E1F36B9FE9E4F549A1521F340B43D22.description:
Analyze maps of Oceania that represent a variety of environmental (landforms, bodies of water, natural resources) and
cultural characteristics (languages, borders, religions, etc.) to assess geographic patterns that make up the continent.

DEB4D6416F3D4102B7975772A5C44ABC.description:
Analyze different geographic representations of Oceania, created by different groups of people over time to support claims
about the history and geography of Oceania.

68C99949F03245AC8F59A7AB9637B5FF.description:
In this driving concept, students analyze the geography of Oceania, and the political, economic, social, and cultural impact of
geography on the people and history of the region. Utilizing a variety of maps, students analyze the role of Oceania in global
economics and history, as well as contextualize contemporary issues within the region. It is recommended that teachers use a
case study approach during this driving concept.

910EDDD6D480483191C96ADAD41B8723.description:
Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology influence the connections between people and
affect the spread of ideas/or cultural practices within North America.

B2B7D152DA454966BB7C49DF69B3B7FD.description:
Analyze cultural, political, and economic forces that impact urbanization in at least one city in North America, and evaluate
the impact of these forces on the structure of that city.

92738CD5FB8F4030B794AE204473A191.description:
Analyze the reasons for, and consequences of, migration of people within, from, and/or to one region or country within
North America over time, and assess the impact of migration on the region.

62609C9E26884AA183155C53261C7FC2.description:
Assess the ways in which changes in land use over time have impacted the economy, ecology, population, exposure to
disease or climate change in one region, country or city within North America.

0C3F31805FA8474DA6F34BEAB4F67543.description:
Analyze maps of North America that represent a variety of environmental (landforms, bodies of water, natural resources)
and cultural characteristics (languages, borders, religions, etc.) to assess geographic patterns on the continent.

E75CB26EAB844173A19F2660D970CCA4.description:
Analyze different geographic representations of North America, created by different groups of people over time to support
claims about North American history and geography.

F865BB7EC231475496621A19E13F8E53.description:
In this driving concept, students continue their regional studies through the geography of North America, with an emphasis on
human environment interactions. Utilizing a variety of maps, students analyze the impact of a changing environment on the
region and the world, as well as contextualize contemporary issues within the region. It is recommended that teachers use a case
study approach during this driving concept.

C1836261A84B40E7818C5DB8E9B937F8.description:
Identify a Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) and assess options for individual and/or collection options for taking action
to address the causes and impacts of challenges facing a region, city or country in Europe.

A2481D812ABB49B2BBE798250EEBA743.description:
Analyze at least one cultural element of a country located in Europe (e.g. art, literature, music, dance, cuisine, philosophy,
religious or political thought), including its local significance and influence on other societies.

0BAA8EEBCA9F4F6EA427C41EF6645549.description:
Analyze cultural, political, and economic forces that impact urbanization in at least one city in Europe and evaluate the
impact of these forces on the structure of that city.

2FE74B13B9FA4212B5AEB5817DFE7483.description:
Analyze the reasons for, and the consequences of, the migration of people within, from, and/or to one region or country
within Europe over time and assess the impact of migration on the region.

222EC90130184F47B02D03D71AE6A676.description:
Assess the ways in which changes in land use over time have impacted the economy, ecology, population, exposure to
disease or climate change in one region, country or city within Europe.

2CC839C0CC664D28AC24DFBC7E3D2D37.description:
Use physical, cultural, and economic maps to draw regions in Europe and compare these to the existing region's economic
communities.

A62EC39FBEE340A59A4D21DB5D735AD7.description:
Analyze maps of Europe that represent a variety of environmental (landforms, bodies of water, natural resources) and
cultural (languages, borders, religions, etc.) characteristics to assess geographic patterns on the continent.

F96A63A023554F148A19FABD68DE2319.description:
Analyze different geographic representations of Europe, created by different groups of people over time to support claims
about European history and geography.

AEFE468825364D46A04101A8D50F93F9.description:
In this driving concept, students analyze the geography of Europe, and the political, economic, social, and cultural impact of
geography on the people and history of Europe. Utilizing a variety of maps, students analyze the role of Europe in global
economics and history, as well as contextualize contemporary issues within the region. It is recommended that teachers use a
case study approach during this driving concept.

1287300E2C264768B195EABCECB938F5.description:
Identify a Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) and assess options for individual and/or collection options for taking action
to address the causes and impacts of challenges facing a region, city or country in Latin America or the Caribbean

9E466A918ABD4C62B9D1DBF77FAC42BF.description:
Analyze at least one cultural element of a country located in Latin America or the Caribbean (e.g. art, literature, music,
dance, cuisine, philosophy, religious or political thought), including its local significance and influence on other societies.

7CE4DFF0E35D409EA3670837F868785F.description:
Analyze cultural, political, and economic forces that impact urbanization in at least one city in Latin America or the
Caribbean and evaluate the impact of these forces on the structure of that city.

124D87B1FBC040869A49445F9D42FB0A.description:
Analyze the reasons for, and consequences of, the migration of people within, from, and/or to one region or country in
Latin America or the Caribbean over time and assess the impact of migration on the region.

DC22F7CE3DF2407EAFE470FDE0988E04.description:
Evaluate the influences of long-term, human-induced climate change on patterns of conflict, cooperation, and migration on
one region, country or city within Latin America or the Caribbean.

F420DFF2BD174DA2BBE9621FD6EDF95E.description:
Assess the ways in which changes in land use over time have impacted the economy, ecology, population, exposure to
disease or climate change in one region, country, or city within Latin American or the Caribbean.

7E8B606FECEA4F2C8560B63C818F7908.description:
Evaluate the reasons for patterns of conflict and cooperation between one region or country within Latin American or the
Caribbean and another region or country.

4FCFA08217184775995DFF7614B8162A.description:
Use physical, cultural, and economic maps to draw regions in Latin America and the Caribbean and compare these to the
existing region's economic communities.

BE82DB062AAD4BAABEC9305A60AB58F8.description:
Analyze maps of Latin America and the Caribbean that represent a variety of environmental (landforms, bodies of water,
natural resources) and cultural (languages, borders, religions, etc.) characteristics to assess geographic patterns on the
continent.

6B2AA7C40DAF414E860FC0F843783957.description:
Analyze different geographic representations of Latin America and the Caribbean, created by different groups of people
over time to support claims about Latin American and Caribbean history and geography.

E279871AFB02495A93E15C495010F252.description:
In this driving concept, students continue their regional studies through the geography of Latin America and the Caribbean, with
an emphasis on how geography drives the economics, history, and civics of the region and impacts contemporary life. Utilizing a
variety of maps, students analyze the role of Latin America and the Caribbean in global economics and history, as well as
contextualize contemporary issues within the region. It is recommended that teachers use a case study approach during this
driving concept.

BEF8880A187F44138843B9C7EF71C6B9.description: Driving Concept 4: Latin America and the Caribbean

AF802E2A8E324383886E5038868A4D6C.description:
Identify a Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) and assess options for individual and/or collection options for taking action
to address the causes and impacts of challenges facing a region, city or country in Asia.

E5AF1EE1BEAC49E7818992CF7ED3E7BD.description:
Analyze at least one cultural element of a country located in Asia (e.g., art, literature, music, dance, cuisine, philosophy,
religious or political thought), including its local significance and influence on other societies.

B0FEFA1512E048ACA7473DAD388FA0C5.description:
Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology have influenced the connections between people
and affected the spread of at least one idea and/ or cultural practices within Asia and between Asia and other regions.

9AD0F785239D4E8DB7E0EA59EF7B2513.description:
Evaluate the reasons for, and the impact of, the migration of people within, from, and/or to one region or country within
Asia over time.

86A32C996575448996E66F10CA7867C2.description: Analyze the impact of climate change on at least one region, country, or city within Asia.

445982BAD57044A8971134610E5B6169.description:
Analyze cultural, political, and economic forces that impact urbanization in at least one city in Asia and evaluate the impact
of these forces on the structure of that city.

FBAB978260B242AAB1BC7415FF47A2D3.description:
Assess how the environmental characteristics of Asia influenced the economic development of at least one region or
country within Asia and the region or country’s role in global trade patterns over time.

C477F76C34C34BE39D4936A5DC922C1B.description:
Assess the ways in which changes in land use over time have impacted the economy, ecology, population, exposure to
disease or climate change in one region, country, or city within Asia.

AD17975088A94208AC4307A90E13FEF0.description:
Evaluate the reasons for patterns of conflict and cooperation between at least one country or region within Asia and
another country or region.

500BDF6B5634451983575E5FB5B27F95.description:
Use physical, cultural, and economic maps to draw regions on the Asian continent and compare these to the existing
regional economic communities.

054F0560A7FC4CCA9B9FDBBD175DDE47.description:
Analyze maps of Asia that represent a variety of environmental (landforms, bodies of water, natural resources) and cultural
(languages, borders, religions, etc.) characteristics to assess geographic patterns on the continent.

0266F84472C743038D5C3309099CBAAB.description:
Analyze different geographic representations of Asia, created by different groups of people over time to support claims
about Asian history and geography.

730767744EF44DA4BD0921E640735664.description:
In this driving concept, students continue their regional studies through the geography of Asia, with an emphasis on regional
diversity. Utilizing a variety of maps, students investigate the role of different regions of Asia in global economics and history, as
well as contextualize contemporary issues within the region. It is recommended that teachers use a case study approach during
this driving concept.

1374D949A27D42F2924A857712E79CDF.description:
Identify a Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) and assess options for individual and/or collection options for taking action
to address the causes and impacts of challenges facing a region, city or country in Africa.

7BE695E106F145219E07C3308E79FE5E.description:
Identify ways that global climate policy could impact equitable access to economic, social, and public health opportunities
for at least one group of people in Africa.

A1936D5C249649CFAC3F68F2220478F0.description:
Analyze at least one cultural element of a country located in Africa (e.g., art, literature, music, dance, cuisine, philosophy,
religious or political thought), including its local significance and influence on other societies.

17B0BEF029324735B89790AB85323A98.description:
Analyze cultural, political, and economic forces that impact urbanization in at least one city in Africa, and evaluate the
impact of these forces on the structure of that city.

9EB532969B934860850C888D538B85FF.description:
Analyze geographic data to explain the reasons for the voluntary and forced migration of people within, from, and/or to at
least one country, region, or city within Africa over time, and analyze the development of the African diaspora.

0223F96162454948B75F1D61F313E83E.description:
Explain how population distribution, natural resources, and the history of at least one country or region within Africa have
impacted changes in land use over time.

7F952F6CC4514DB7A0FF28312289D559.description: Evaluate the impact of climate change on people in at least one region, country, or city within Africa.

193457FB45BA4B60B2578171270FC540.description:
Evaluate the reasons for patterns of conflict and cooperation between at least one country or region within Africa and
another country or region , including the impact of colonialism.

15C671A3B48E4489A974CC85A024C30E.description:
Use physical, cultural, and economic maps to draw regions on the African continent and compare these to the existing
region's economic communities.

535924485CBC48679B2300188FCA4567.description:
Analyze maps of Africa that represent a variety of environmental (landforms, bodies of water, natural resources) and cultural
characteristics (languages, borders, religions, etc.) to assess geographic patterns on the continent.

C94437CBBB774D818C443E001611369D.description:
Analyze different geographic representations of Africa, created by different groups of people over time to support claims
about African history and geography.

B85EDD7C7AB34B83AF5B29415AFEFB74.description:
Through this driving concept, students build on their geography skills, analyzing the geography of Africa, and the political,
economic, social, and cultural impact of geography on the people and history of Africa. Through this exploration, students evaluate the diverse regions within Africa. For this driving concept, Africa will serve as a case study for analyzing how generations
of ingenuity contributed to the cultural and intellectual diffusion of ideas around the world. It is recommended that teachers use
a case study approach during this driving concept.

9F4ABA7F28334184966998D3830D2AF9.description:
Evaluate the strengths and limitations of different geographic tools, data sets, and sources for understanding the lived
experiences of individuals in different parts of the world.

84B32E8896EB4F17B85E4CBD8A93538D.description:
Explain how terms and language used to describe different regions and nations can influence our understanding of those
places and the people who live there.

763DD605E4B447F682BF237DCCECDC3B.description:
Describe the purpose, creation, evolution, and impact of international borders, and evaluate the impact of the creation of a
specific border.

523F699AE7904DB181A4FA4CB5CBBF58.description:
Evaluate the ways in which continents are divided, and develop a claim about the strengths and limitations of the current
approach.

00AB3E4326F94D52A31DE09EDE5578E2.description: Analyze how the environment and physical geography shape human behaviors and identities.

90445D30368D4790A410EF363C938C7A.description:
Analyze the impact of the perspective of common map projections on widespread understanding of world geography, and
explain how maps can convey a point of view.

8D580DFA2402412697F7038C1FF0E0FE.description:
Through this driving concept, students analyze the history of maps and mapping and the ways that the discipline of geography is
used to express and maintain power. Students will assess what gives a location a sense of “place,” as well as how humans and
the environment interact to change each other over time. Teachers should use case studies to evaluate how geography
influences human behavior and the development of communities, as well as how communities change over time. Students will
build on their understanding of geography skills and global history, including their understanding of colonization from
elementary social studies to analyze how geography drives human decision making and impacts daily life.

C40974F67EB84D3DBE3BCE6A511C1F03.description: Driving Concept 1: The Power of Maps

document.title: Washington, DC K-12 Social Studies Standards Revised Standards

58EDE67E5D174F62AE23384C0DB03D55.description:
Analyze methods of impacting political change in Washington, DC, and develop a plan for taking action to address an issue
of local, national, or global concern.

0FA00F1F2DDA44558C8184F2DEB3D05F.description:
Evaluate the impact and influence of historical movements for justice and equality on modern social movements and
organizations.

3F8C385338AD4833B6D1F64F42ABECF3.description:
Compare the efforts and impact of diverse groups and organizations inspired by the African American Civil Rights
movement to address inequalities in American society, including but not limited to: the gay rights movement, the Stonewall Uprising, the American Indian Movement (AIM), the United Farm Workers, the Women’s Liberation Movement, the Asian
American Movement, disability rights movement, Chicano Movement and Latinx resistance.

CB43B04A755C49CF947933A75943BF99.description:
Evaluate the impact of key moments and figures in the fight for Black equality and voting rights including, but not
limited to, the Montgomery Bus Boycott, Freedom Rides, sit-in protests, the Little Rock Nine, and the March on
Washington.

CB927C8D3A1B43E09274A94190F76822.description:
Evaluate the reasons for and resistance to segregation in the North, including the impact of redlining and uprisings in
the North and West.

F2913D9237364D109772A84DF8E4CD49.description:
Evaluate different strategies for resistance to Jim Crow laws in the South, such as boycotts, legal battles and direct
action in the United States organized by grassroots groups such as Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC),
Southern Christian Leadership Conference (SCLC), Black Panthers, etc.

17A7B714FF144840A1B1F8A9340F8D24.description:
Evaluate the impact of Tape v. Hurley, Piper v. Big Pine School, Mendez v. Westminster and Brown v. Board of Education,
Topeka on school segregation and the movement for equality.

CE0CD52509484A34BAF9D7271DAE105E.description:
Analyze the work of activists and grassroots acts of resistance following the end of slavery to determine when the Civil
Rights Movement began, including but not limited to Ida B. Wells, W.E.B. Du Bois, Anna Pauline Murray and A. Philip Randolph.

3ED6002E5E8C41F99B3B7E238FB39F2E.description:
Students will explain that the Civil Rights Movement not only started long before the early 1950s and extends long afterwards to
the present day, but how its aims also intersected beyond race into gender, sexuality, class, religion, and sovereignty. Students
will analyze the grassroots efforts of everyday people organizing and working together for social change and a more just,
equitable, and secure world.

29F10A45FE2E417EAA036A808C73121C.description: Driving Concept 7: The Long Civil Rights Movement

4F47C8DCCD7B4147A6BAE5DA7D41126F.description:
Compare the different experiences of servicemembers when they returned to the United States after the war, including
white, Black, Latinx, Indigenous and Asian American servicemen.

8E544BAEEA044D74B7B5C11BBAB40ABB.description:
Using primary sources from the perspective of American citizens of Japanese descent, analyze the struggles and resistance
of those who were incarcerated during World War II.

2EDC2A0BC0CB41508AF4D7B22BBA0894.description:
Analyze changes at home as the US mobilized for and entered the war, including social, economic, and political
wartime opportunities for women and communities of color including Black and Latinx groups (e.g., women of color as
riveters and war material assembly workers, Navajo coders).

CC6FE9FD04094339B40E1776731D67A1.description:
Describe the causes and consequences of major events of World War II including Pearl Harbor, D-Day and the decision to
drop the atomic bomb on Japan.

575A72FBA00B401E877E5283F932F01F.description:
Explain the causes of World War II and the rise of fascism in Italy and Germany, and explain how bias and prejudice led to
the scapegoating of marginalized groups in Europe, including Jewish, Romani, Slavic, disabled, Jehovah’s Witnesses and LGBTQ+
communities.

5B40938BE3D747D5A643A33E3F3D30A8.description:
Through this driving concept students will explain the causes of World War II, the US’s role in the conflict and what that meant
for American populations at home and abroad. Students will evaluate how the war changed the cultural, political, and economic
landscape for citizens after the war’s end and into the 1950s.

069A6013CD9F4446ADF9BEA95E85225B.description: Driving Concept 6: World War II and Postwar US

C01F1416564647B0A025BB39FFB69470.description:
Analyze the rise in Black art, music, literature, businesses, and queer culture in the Black Renaissance period, including but
not limited to Harlem and DC (e.g., Black Broadway).

8241F7F4FB3D46F3AF8FCD8F1BD08378.description: Evaluate the reasons for and impact of the Great Migration.

03FF61EE23C643949B1BA7D2892C2BC6.description:
Explain how white supremacist groups founded in the aftermath of emancipation, such as the Ku Klux Klan, enacted terror
against Black people and also Jewish, Catholic, Latinx, and Asian American communities.

5A316DD586444815A4FE4FBC3406E88A.description:
Analyze how laws passed after the end of slavery, such as the so-called “Black Codes,” impacted Black Americans’
ability to work, vote, and move in public space, and analyze the lived experiences of Black citizens after the Civil War.

B41A0559B95547F7BA6E82E808E34B21.description:
Explain the grassroots efforts by Black Americans to gain access to the American economy, political institutions, and
social equality.

9460789952B4452EA0FBDB35234E3C32.description:
Analyze the early political successes of the Reconstruction era, including the election of approximately 2,000 Black
Americans to local, state, and national office.

E870F40F34744D238297D06DD9856BFB.description:
Evaluate the impact of the 13th, 14th and 15th amendments on the lived experiences of formerly enslaved persons in
the South, including the promise and shortcomings of each amendment.

0B507E57A45B40FF9B7AC258C0C5640C.description:
In this driving concept, students will analyze how the policies of Reconstruction and the backlash against multiracial democracy
shaped American politics and society after the Civil War and through the 1920s. Students should understand the promise of the
13th, 14th and 15th amendments and how freedpeople worked to access economic and political opportunities following the Civil
War. Students should also analyze the role of white supremacy in the backlash to Reconstruction.

25B9EEF4576241FFB0C8212F89E662DB.description: Driving Concept 5: Reconstruction and the Early Struggle for Equality

96660563925B48778B99EA1A18951732.description: Use primary and secondary sources to analyze emancipation in Texas and subsequent efforts to memorialize emancipation.

B17340EB21AF474E9DF36041BC4085A6.description:
Evaluate the political and social impact of the end of the Civil War and the assassination of Abraham Lincoln on different
individuals in America, including the experiences of emancipation.

E6E54A171BB64A9594053C59524A4EDA.description: Evaluate the impact and legacy of the Gettysburg Address and the Emancipation Proclamation.

B31C4852E0CD41D4AD8CD1F2CF4B1B8F.description:
Evaluate why many Black soldiers fought for the Union Army, but Indigenous soldiers fought for both the Confederacy and
the Union.

68C345359BEF4BD1A51FE33EB2D384C5.description: Identify two major Civil War battles and their effects on the outcome of the war.

770AC713A95840829BEEFD98F8D2820D.description:
Analyze how economic pressures related to the slave economy determined whether states remained with the Union or
joined the Confederacy.

600E75084B8045989CDC3FA8FB742753.description:
Analyze the impact of abolitionists on the fight for freedom, including reformers Frederick Douglass, William Lloyd Garrison,
Harriet Beecher Stowe, Harriet Tubman, Sojourner Truth, Martin Delany, and John Brown.

D823AF5C7D7F49128E5AE5104D772644.description:
Explain that arguments about slavery, especially the expansion of the slave system into new territories, caused secession
and the Civil War.

AEB0CC5B6F12492AAE169F509D9FDEC1.description:
Explain how expansion and key events between the Constitutional Convention and the attack on Fort Sumter ultimately
led to the Civil War.

81D4A0930B5B4F9EA0598BCC40F14C43.description:
In this driving concept, students will analyze the Civil War, its causes, leadership during the war and its consequences. Students
will use primary sources to explain the connection between the institution of slavery and the Civil War. Students will also
evaluate the different lived experiences of Americans during the Civil War.

40460AD50E66435B96AACC4F9B462E50.description:
Describe how the Underground Railroad developed in the United States, including the work of activists from the District of
Columbia in assisting enslaved people fleeing to the North.

A4761294A03E4B13926484F2166AA79A.description:
Explain how some contemporary music forms, including but not limited to, gospel, blues, and rock and roll, trace their
roots to enslaved people.

AA9503B4A9D74574B01DCE7CCA396F22.description: Discuss how the experience of enslaved people differed based on geographic location and labor performed.

5E3DC4485B854811B134685E3225A801.description: Compare and contrast how the system of slavery operated in the North and the South.

79B703E3AE124294B08A724B9FD079ED.description:
Analyze Compare the strategies of the work and organizations of key abolitionists Harriet Tubman, Venture Smith,
Sojourner Truth, Nat Turner, and Olaudah Equiano.

012A0DDBC71B428FAF9251B27594D0F9.description: Explain how local, state, and federal laws, including slave codes, protected the institution of slavery.

ADF2E3B7214E40FEB9EC32142A444916.description:
Evaluate how enslaved Africans practiced religion covertly through singing spirituals in the fields, gathering in hush harbors
on Sundays for ring shouts, and fusions of Protestant Christianity and African-based spiritualities like vodoun and hoodoo.

D2F23C53D2174469A0536CE97AB0E0CA.description:
Describe how enslaved Africans in early America used religion, writing, speeches, rebellion, sabotage, and maroon
communities as resistance against the institution of chattel slavery.

1BF62C5C1B29405D9190ED1E8F7B97E8.description:
Explain that white enslavers adopted and spread false beliefs about racial inferiority and evaluate the impact of that
ideology today.

66D122683F744364956D26B61F6ABBAC.description: Explain the importance of language when discussing challenging topics (e.g., “enslaved person” rather than “slave”).

3DC1AF5E54FF481394DF4E49A161F116.description:
In this driving concept students analyze the history of enslavement and resistance in the United States. Students compare the
differences in the practice of slavery in the North and South as well as how enslaved Africans fought against these practices
through everyday actions and acts of resistance including uprisings.

AFCBB1DF40CA4368AB6507AAB6DAE73F.description:
Compare the different artistic, cultural, political, and spiritual traditions of current-day Indigenous Peoples, and how
those practices and ways of life persevered and still thrive today, including Two-Spirited gender identities.

86734C4AB5404E6FB14187ED4B14C5FF.description:
Identify and describe the lived experiences of people who came to the West, including Asian, and African Americans, as
well as their motivations for movement and their experiences upon arrival.

25F0B7EBC6AF43D384D597101771EDE3.description:
Analyze the lived experiences of different immigrant communities between 1850-1900, (e.g., religious minority, Irish,
German, Mexican, Italian, British, Southeast Asian, Chinese, and Japanese communities).

96425BF753904BCC980788D23BE7AB73.description:
Evaluate the environmental impact that settler colonialism had on the Great Plains region, West Coast, Northwest, and
Southwest.

40080E00E95A44738FFEBA7998BB1747.description:
Explain Indigenous resistance to territorial invasion, cultural and religious assimilation, and attack including efforts to
maintain sovereignty and independence (e.g., Geronimo, the Battle of Little Bighorn, and Ghost Dance movement).

2B291D20274E462885B02420C97E73DB.description:
Describe the causes of the Texas Independence movement and Mexican War from the perspective of Tejanos, enslaved
Texans, Mexicans, American settlers, and Indigenous Nations with a focus on the impact of these events on individual lived
experiences.

C747A8E22776420080E74A033EC5FE68.description: Analyze the experiences and legacies of Black Americans in the Northwest Territory.

7A8D65E3263D4DA78FC3DED6C463930F.description:
Using primary sources, evaluate the legacy of American settlers including the treatment of Indigenous Nations during
the Lewis and Clark expedition and resistance to settler colonialism.

A88CCFF068CC47FDBF4382EA3789CABE.description:
Use primary sources and Indigenous histories to explain the causes and consequences of significant events in territorial
conquest of sovereign Indigenous Nations territories between 1781 and 1877, including but not limited to, the Louisiana
Purchase and the Trail of Tears.

C75F6A533D8E4CF296A4E15C6631C61A.description:
Compare and contrast maps of Indigenous Nations and land at the start of each century from 1700 to the present with
a special focus on areas west of the Mississippi River.

50103192DB71470B946046986E77D6CF.description:
Evaluate historical perspectives about US imperial expansion including Manifest Destiny and American exceptionalism from
multiple perspectives including Indigenous Nations, countries and peoples in the Pacific, Caribbean, Asia and Americas.

4E43C3134E8E479E88507C82514CE9AA.description:
In this driving concept, students will evaluate the impact Westward Conquest had on the lives and legacies of different
populations, with a focus on Indigenous Nations. Students should evaluate the cause of and opposition to territorial conquest
and expansion, using multiple perspectives and context to evaluate primary source accounts.

886B04E581F8421D87A82FEB96B07A0E.description: Driving Concept 2: War and Conquest in the West

E860C0FF54B8469A88F89A8A4A12C496.description:
Evaluate the credibility of online sources and claims about one moment in American history using strategies like lateral
reading.

F5C3FF05E7ED4F40823EE0823FA40517.description:
Compare different ways individuals and communities have used artistic expressions and acts of joy to resist oppression in
American history.

0A2FFB0AC92445F3BAA2C54D70479C7C.description:
Compare multiple primary source accounts of a significant policy in American history and make a claim about why different
individuals were differently impacted by a policy decision.

71B3929A71B94104A8585CACDF980F46.description:
Compare multiple accounts of one significant event in American history and make a claim about which account is more
useful in understanding the past.

5304EF4DE8CC41949C89AC05C6955CCB.description:
Compare multiple accounts of one significant event in American history and analyze the reasons for differences in each
account.

4A854AB7675C47B79D44FDB6E815E37E.description:
Analyze how maps of the United States and surrounding territories created by different peoples between 1776 and the
present day convey different ideas about the history of the United States, Indigenous Nations, Mexico, Canada and
surrounding territories.

E8E5679DEC544F23B044616DE6964392.description:
In this driving concept, students will use historical thinking skills to develop claims about the utility of different sources in
understanding the past. This driving concept prepares students to analyze different perspectives and experiences throughout
American history, and ask questions about authorship, context, and perspective in historical source material.

05166F302F8343A1A0BDDA499D50C305.description: Driving Concept 1: Inquiry in American History

document.title: Washington, DC K-12 Social Studies Standards Revised Standards

38FE645ED263492D819FA1E1243770C8.description:
Evaluate the creation of the United States and the ways it may serve as an example (both for its strengths and limitations)
to other democracies around the world.

F92FC5E4CD0F44D9BF889C2B76182EFD.description: Analyze the reasons for, and impact of, the expansion of rights, including the right to vote, in the United States over time.

E9C93853E12E485780E9C05108CBAF40.description:
Evaluate the credibility or perspective of online sources and claims about the history or application of the United States
Constitution using strategies like lateral reading.

A9FA7BCA2C144875854E6611B1AA2C8E.description: Analyze the political motivations that led to Washington, DC being established as the capital of the United States.

F913D18D32464FA9942D1360C1493162.description:
Explain protections that the Bill of Rights provides to individuals and the importance of these 10 amendments to the
ratification of the US Constitution.

53FA40580DB94E1B9B1B42903A7D91C7.description: Explain the role of the courts and the judicial branch of government, and identify their power to evaluate laws.
